versions.version: Leptonica 1.87.0 (commit 13275a2), in builds with JPEG 2000 support enabled via HAVE_LIBJP2K / OpenJPEG.

solutions.value: The manufacturer has confirmed the fix in the jp2kio.c file in the master branch of the official Leptonica repository. It is recommended that you apply the fix and recompile the library.

supportingMedia.value: The manufacturer has confirmed the fix in the jp2kio.c file in the master branch of the official Leptonica repository. It is recommended that you apply the fix and recompile the library.

descriptions.value: Out-of-bounds read vulnerability in the pixReadMemJp2kCore() function in Leptonica, located in jp2kio.c. The function retrieves the output dimensions only for component 0 and uses a common index to iterate through the buffers of all components. If the remaining components have smaller dimensions, the traversal exceeds the bounds of their sample buffers, which are allocated by OpenJPEG. When processing a specially crafted JPEG 2000 image, data read from adjacent dynamic memory may be incorporated into the pixels of the decoded image and result in information disclosure to anyone who can access the output.

cna.title: filelock: StrictSoftFileLock creates its claim directories without the lock mode, so another local user with a write bit on them can end a live hold

descriptions.value: filelock is a platform-independent file lock for Python. From version 3.30.0 until version 4.2.1,  StrictSoftFileLock  and  AsyncStrictSoftFileLock  on POSIX systems create coordination and claim directories without applying the caller’s restrictive lock mode. A permissive umask or inherited default ACL can leave these directories writable by another local user, allowing that user to delete an active holder’s claims. Another authorized process can then acquire the lock while the original holder remains in its critical section. An attacker can also plant malformed claims to prevent acquisition. This issue is fixed in version 4.2.1.

descriptions.value: @fastify/middie is the Express-style middleware engine for Fastify. In versions from 9.0.0 through 9.3.5, the use() function joined a path-scoped middleware's mount path to the plugin scope prefix in a way that could diverge from the path Fastify's router serves, most often when the scope prefix ended in a slash, and also for array mount paths and for mount paths written without a leading slash. When the two paths disagreed, the middleware was silently skipped while the route handler still ran, so path-scoped middleware such as authentication, authorization, or rate limiting could be bypassed by a single unauthenticated request. The issue is fixed in @fastify/middie 9.3.6, and users should upgrade to 9.3.6 or later. As a workaround, enforce authorization in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after the router has resolved the request.

cna.title: Robots::Validate versions from 0.4.3 before 0.4.10 for Perl report clients as imposter robots when User-Agent matcher state carries over from a previous request

solutions.value:
Upgrade to Robots-Validate v0.4.10 or later.

Deployments with Algorithm::AhoCorasick::XS should upgrade to v0.4.11, which fixed a bug with using that version.

descriptions.value:
Robots::Validate versions from 0.4.3 before 0.4.10 for Perl report clients as imposter robots when User-Agent matcher state carries over from a previous request.

Each Robots::Validate object holds one pure-Perl Aho-Corasick search machine and feeds every User-Agent into it without resetting its state. A User-Agent that ends part-way through a robot name leaves the machine mid-match, so the next User-Agent checked by the same object can complete that name. That client's address is then checked against the robot's DNS rule, which it fails.

A remote client can use this to make a site that blocks bad robots block other visitors where the prefix User-Agent string is a suffix of a robot being validated.

Note that deployments with Algorithm::AhoCorasick::XS are also affected, since it was unused due to a different bug.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-130 Excessive Allocation

Initialization of a resource with an insecure default vulnerability in OpenText Advanced Authentication Server allows Excessive Allocation.

This issue affects Advanced Authentication Server: from 6.4.0.0 through 6.4.3.x, from 6.5.0.0 through 6.5.0.x, and from 6.6.0.0 through 6.6.1.0.



The fix for this is issue is to create a secure configuration.  The 6.6.2.0 release has a best practice entry if the configuration is unsecure.



A secure configuration is to NOT allow creation/recreation of Unauthenticated Endpoints.  If creation/recreation of Unauthenticated Endpoints is required, you should only allow it from trusted networks.  



To remedy this issue, change your configuration to NOT allow creation/recreation of Unauthenticated Endpoints. cna.title: Active Storage: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Storage filename handling

descriptions.value: Active Storage makes it simple to upload and reference files in cloud services and attach those files to Active Record objects. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, ActiveStorage::Filename#base and #extension_with_delimiter, and therefore #extension, pass the stored filename unmodified to File.basename and File.extname, which raise ArgumentError when the name contains a NUL byte. Active Storage stores the client-supplied filename verbatim, so a user who is permitted to upload an attachment could persist such a filename on databases that accept NUL bytes in string columns, such as SQLite and MySQL/MariaDB. Each subsequent request that builds a variant or preview of the blob, opens it, or renders it as an Action Text attachment then raises, possibly resulting in a persistent DoS vulnerability for the pages that display the blob until it is purged or its filename is corrected. Applications that use PostgreSQL are not affected, because PostgreSQL rejects the row. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

descriptions.value: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. From 2.0.0 until 2.9.1, the pure-Ruby Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode implementation decodes invalid Punycode A-labels instead of returning them unchanged. Labels that decode to ASCII text or fail to convert back to the same A-label can therefore make Addressable::URI#display_uri show a trusted-looking host while host, normalized_host, and the connection target retain the attacker-controlled encoded host. A trusted-name comparison using Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode output can also treat two different hosts as the same without displaying the URI. The native libidn implementation, to_ascii, and normalized_host are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: Improve Wikidata enrichment and return MISP standard

x_patch2vuln.subject: Improve Wikidata enrichment and return MISP standard
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The vulnerability is remediated by properly escaping user-supplied text as a SPARQL string literal using json.dumps with ensure_ascii=False, which neutralizes quotes, backslashes, newlines, and control characters. Additional hardening includes strict validation of the language tag, numeric configuration values, text length, and UUID format before query construction; validation of Wikidata response structure and entity URI format before importing results; replacement of raw exception formatting with generic error messages that do not expose upstream details; use of the modern Wikidata SPARQL endpoint with POST method; a proper MISP user-agent string; and a bounded request timeout.
assumptions: The CAPEC-143 mapping is the closest available pattern; no SPARQL-specific CAPEC exists in the catalog. The underlying technique (query injection via unsanitized string concatenation) is identical to SQL injection.

CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker has authenticated access to a MISP instance with the wiki expansion module enabled. The actual privilege level required depends on MISP role configuration, which is not specified in the patch.

The affected version range is unspecified; the patch does not include version tags or release boundaries. The vulnerability existed in module version 0.2 (as indicated by the old moduleinfo) and was fixed in version 1.0.
The CVSS VI:L rating accounts for both the query manipulation and the old error-message information disclosure. If only the injection is considered (without the error leak), VI could be rated N.

The patch is treated as a single vulnerability fix (SPARQL injection) with associated hardening changes (error sanitization, input validation, endpoint update). The caller asserts all changes relate to the same vulnerability.
No evidence of active exploitation, PoC, or in-the-wild usage was found in the patch or metadata.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: The patch rewrites the wiki.py handler to: (1) escape user text via json.dumps(text, ensure_ascii=False) before embedding in the SPARQL query; (2) validate language tags with a regex, numeric settings (max_results 1-25, timeout 1-60), text length (1-2000 chars), and UUID format; (3) switch from string concatenation to a properly escaped SPARQL literal; (4) use the modern https://query.wikidata.org/sparql endpoint with POST method and a MISP user-agent; (5) validate Wikidata response bindings and entity URIs against a strict pattern before creating annotation objects; (6) replace the mutable shared misperrors dict and raw exception formatting with a ModuleError class and generic error strings; (7) add a 313-line test suite (tests/test_wiki.py) covering injection vectors, invalid inputs, malformed responses, and error sanitization; (8) update documentation and module metadata to reflect the new misp_standard output format and configuration options.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The module is invoked over the network via the MISP API. AC:L: The injection requires only crafting a text value with SPARQL metacharacters; no race conditions or complex prerequisites. AT:N: No need to manipulate the attack target. PR:L: Requires authenticated access to a MISP instance with the wiki module enabled. UI:N: No user interaction beyond the API call. VC:N: The queried data is public Wikidata; no confidential MISP data is exposed. VI:L: An attacker can alter the enrichment results (integrity of advisory annotations) and the old error path could leak internal details. VA:N: No meaningful availability impact on the MISP system. SC/SI/SA:N: No impact on external systems beyond the public Wikidata service. Overall severity is low given the limited blast radius.

capecRationale.rationale: CAPEC-143 describes injection of query language fragments through unsanitized input into a dynamically constructed query. Although the CAPEC name references SQL specifically, the attack pattern is identical: an attacker supplies input containing query-language metacharacters (quotes, braces, keywords) that alter the structure of the query sent to an interpreter. SPARQL injection follows the same pattern. This is the closest available CAPEC; no SPARQL-specific CAPEC exists in the catalog. The uncertainty is that the CAPEC is SQL-specific in naming, but the underlying technique (query injection via string concatenation) is the same.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The module dynamically constructs a SPARQL query by concatenating untrusted user input directly into the query string without neutralizing special elements. This is the same pattern as code/query injection: the intended query structure is modified by attacker-controlled input. SPARQL is a query language interpreted by the Wikidata endpoint, making this a code injection into a query interpreter.

The old code formatted raw exception objects into the error response string ('wikidata API not accessible {}'.format(e)), which could expose internal details such as proxy credentials, full query text, or upstream response bodies. The fix replaces this with generic error messages.

events.description: Corrective change authored (7a2a7e3d9e0f67f6732bd8050ab7da79e7b344d9): Improve Wikidata enrichment and return MISP standard
Patch retrieved from the supplied URL; retrieval time is used as the default availability time.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-143 SQL Injection

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by properly escaping user-supplied text as a SPARQL string literal using json.dumps with ensure_ascii=False, which neutralizes quotes, backslashes, newlines, and control characters. Additional hardening includes strict validation of the language tag, numeric configuration values, text length, and UUID format before query construction; validation of Wikidata response structure and entity URI format before importing results; replacement of raw exception formatting with generic error messages that do not expose upstream details; use of the modern Wikidata SPARQL endpoint with POST method; a proper MISP user-agent string; and a bounded request timeout.

descriptions.value: The Wikidata Lookup expansion module (wiki.py) in MISP misp-modules contained a SPARQL injection vulnerability. The handler function constructed a SPARQL query by directly concatenating the user-supplied text value into the query string without any escaping or parameterization: 'SELECT ?item WHERE { ?item rdfs:label"' + request.get("text") + '" @en }'. An authenticated MISP user with access to the module could supply a crafted text attribute value containing SPARQL syntax (quotes, closing braces, UNION, SERVICE, LIMIT, etc.) to alter the structure of the query sent to the Wikidata SPARQL endpoint. This could allow an attacker to modify the query logic, extract unintended data, or cause the query to fail in ways that expose internal error details. Additionally, the old error handling path formatted raw exception objects into the response string ('wikidata API not accessible {}'.format(e)), potentially leaking internal information such as proxy credentials, query contents, or response bodies. The module also used a spoofed browser user-agent string and the deprecated Wikidata endpoint. The vulnerability required authenticated access to the MISP instance and the ability to invoke the wiki expansion module with a text attribute. The impact is limited to manipulation of the enrichment query and potential disclosure of internal error details; it does not directly compromise the MISP server or its stored data.

cna.title: Action Mailbox: Possible signature replay in Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress

descriptions.value: Action Mailbox routes incoming emails to controller-like mailboxes for processing in Rails. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, the Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress authenticates a request with an HMAC of the timestamp and token parameters concatenated without a separator, and ActionMailbox::Ingresses::Mailgun::InboundEmailsController::Authenticator#recent? rejects only timestamps more than 2 minutes in the past. Because the signature does not fix the boundary between the two values, a captured signed request can be presented with a timestamp far in the future, which the ingress then accepts indefinitely. An attacker who obtains one signed Mailgun webhook request, but not the signing key, could submit arbitrary inbound email that Action Mailbox processes as genuine, possibly leading to forged messages attributed to the sender of the attacker's choosing. Applications that receive inbound email through the Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress are affected. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of GGUF files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a heap-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute arbitrary code in the context of the current process. Was ZDI-CAN-34558.

cna.title: Misinterpretation of Input in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, which reads each string literal as the database engine reads it - a backslash as an escape only on MySQL/MariaDB, on PostgreSQL with standard_conforming_strings off and in PostgreSQL's E'...' strings - when it looks for the marker, so that no value can reach the comment where the marker is honoured, and which reads literals the same way when it masks them in the slow-query log line and the trace. Until then, on SQL Server and SQL Server Compact keep logging off or the log device on files (the defaults); on PostgreSQL 6.3.3 to 6.3.7, and on MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL before 6.2.19, no setting of the server avoids it.

descriptions.value: Misinterpretation of SQL statement text in the database layer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.3.7 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to have a failed database write reported to the server as successful. The layer answers a failed statement as a success when it finds the marker [IGNORE-ERRORS], which is meant only for the server's own schema statements (its upgrade scripts and the database log's tables), and statements carry values from outside - an envelope address, the user name of a failed logon, a message's headers - in their text on MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL, and in the batches of the database log on every engine. Up to 6.2.18 the marker was honoured anywhere in a statement, a value included, on MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL. From 6.2.19 it was honoured only inside a comment, but the layer read a backslash inside a string literal as an escape, which SQL Server, SQL Server Compact and PostgreSQL with standard_conforming_strings on (its default) do not, so that on those engines a value holding a backslash could make the layer take part of the statement's literals for statement text and find the marker there: on PostgreSQL from 6.3.3 for every statement carrying an outside value that holds a backslash, with no setting changed for a message delivered into a local mailbox (through an internationalised (SMTPUTF8) envelope sender) and for the IP range an auto-ban writes (named after the user name of the failed logon), and on SQL Server and SQL Server Compact for the database log, when the server logs to the database (logging is off, and the log device is files, by default). A statement run outside a transaction that then failed - a constraint, a deadlock, a lock or statement timeout, a full disk, and up to 6.2.18 a lost connection - was answered as a success, and its caller went on as if the row had been written: a message delivered into a local mailbox could be counted as delivered with no row to show it and no failure notice to its sender, and a message accepted with 250 could be left with no queue row and never delivered (up to 6.2.18, and on PostgreSQL from 6.3.3 when every recipient's address carries the marker too, which needs an address that takes any local part); an auto-ban whose IP range was not written could be logged and counted as applied, with no error reported, while the address stayed unbanned; and message metadata (written only when message indexing is on), entries of the database log and rows of features an administrator turns on could be lost without an error. On MySQL/MariaDB up to 6.2.18 the caller was handed whatever identifier the client library still held for the connection - 0, or that of an insert its last successful statement made, in whatever table - under which a queued message's recipients were then written, so that another message still in the queue could be delivered to them as well. This flaw gives a value no way to change what a statement does, and no privilege is gained.

cna.title: pgEdge Postgres MCP Server write confirmation skipped for writes that begin with a reading keyword

descriptions.value: pgEdge Postgres MCP Server enables SQL queries against PostgreSQL databases through Model Context Protocol compatible clients. Prior to 1.1.0, the bundled CLI and web clients classified query_database statements only by their first keyword before deciding whether to display a write confirmation. SELECT INTO, data-modifying common table expressions beginning with WITH, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE of a write were treated as reads and could execute without confirmation on an allow_writes connection. Read-only connections remain protected by PostgreSQL transaction access mode, and EXPLAIN without ANALYZE and SELECT FOR UPDATE remain classified as reads. This issue is fixed in 1.1.0.

cna.title: Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix

descriptions.value: Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. Prior to 4.13.16, mount() and app.mount() can remove a dynamic mount prefix using the route-pattern length rather than the matched-prefix length, allowing a crafted path to be forwarded as a protected inner route while the outer application routes the original path. Since 4.12.21, rebuilding the forwarded URL from the decoded pathname can also convert a decoded backslash to a slash and collapse parent-directory segments, again causing the mounted application to receive a protected path. An unauthenticated client can use either applicable path transformation to reach a mounted route without authentication or authorization middleware scoped to a subpath inside the mount prefix. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.16.

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.4 or later, whose database schema 6102 converts every MySQL and MariaDB table to utf8mb4, and which runs only on a database upgraded to its schema; 6.3.8 also fixes a separate way round the auto-ban. Until then, converting the IP range table as that step does (ALTER TABLE hm_securityranges ENGINE=InnoDB, ROW_FORMAT=DYNAMIC, CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_general_ci) lets the database store such a name, and setting MaxInvalidLogonAttempts to 1 closes this way round, since every failed logon then reaches the limit by itself, and a guess at an account, made under a name the table can hold, is banned under it.

descriptions.value: The auto-ban of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.0 through 6.3.3, with a MySQL or MariaDB database, can be kept from banning an address after repeated failed logons, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to go on guessing account passwords from a single address without being banned. The server makes its MySQL tables in MySQL's utf8 character set, which holds no character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, sends its statements as UTF-8 over a utf8mb4 connection and leaves the database's default strict mode in place. From 6.2.0 it decodes the user name of a SASL PLAIN logon as UTF-8, so the name can hold such a character. When the failed logons counted from one address reach MaxInvalidLogonAttempts (3 by default), the server clears that address's count, saves an IP range named "Auto-ban: " followed by the user name of the logon that reached the limit, and drops the connection. If such a character is in the part of the user name that the range's name keeps (the name is cut to 100 characters), the database refuses the range: no range is saved, the address is not refused, and, its count having already been cleared, it is given the next full set of attempts. An attacker can in this way spend all but the last attempt of each set on password guesses, and make the last under such a name. On Windows, POP3 AUTH PLAIN reaches it on a server as installed, and IMAP AUTHENTICATE PLAIN where IMAP SASL authentication is turned on (off by default); on Windows and on Linux (from 6.3.0), SMTP AUTH PLAIN reaches it where plain-text authentication is allowed (off by default), and ManageSieve and CardDAV where they are turned on (off by default). Each failed save is reported in the server's error log. A database whose strict mode has been turned off stores the character as a question mark and makes the first such ban, but refuses every later ban named after the same user name, or after one holding other such characters in their place, as a duplicate while the first stands, since the server cannot look up a name holding such a character there.

cna.title: SMTP and POP3 response injection when using STARTTLS

descriptions.value: If an attacker was able to perform a man-in-the-middle attack on an SMTP or POP3 server connection using STARTTLS, the attacker could inject server responses before the TLS handshake completed. Thunderbird would process these responses after the handshake, as if they had been received from the server over the encrypted connection. This could be used to make Thunderbird report a different outcome for sending or fetching mail, and to show attacker-controlled text in error messages. The encrypted connection itself was not compromised, and credentials were not exposed. Connections using SSL/TLS instead of STARTTLS were not affected. This vulnerability was fixed in Thunderbird 160 and Thunderbird 153.7.

cna.title: Addressable: Denial of service in URI path normalization

descriptions.value: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. Prior to 2.9.1, Addressable::URI.normalize_path repeatedly scans and rewrites paths while removing only one nested dot segment per pass, producing quadratic work. URI#normalize, URI#normalized_path, URI#join, URI#==, and URI#=== inherit the behavior, so processing a sufficiently long attacker-controlled URI can consume a worker thread and cause denial of service on every Ruby implementation. URI.parse alone and code that never normalizes, compares, or joins untrusted URIs are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

cna.title: Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file read and remote code execution in Active Storage video previews, analysis and image processing

descriptions.value: Active Storage makes it simple to upload and reference files in cloud services and attach those files to Active Record objects. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, ActiveStorage::Blob#open writes a blob to a tempfile whose name carries the extension of the uploaded filename, and hands that path to ffprobe (VideoAnalyzer, AudioAnalyzer), ffmpeg (VideoPreviewer) and ImageMagick (ImageAnalyzer, the :mini_magick variant processor). These tools select a decoder from the file extension when the content does not identify its own format, so an attacker who chooses the filename and declares the content type of an upload chooses which decoder processes it. An FFmpeg built with AviSynth support treats a file with the .avs extension as an AviSynth script and evaluates it, which could disclose files readable by the application process through the preview image, or load a native library the attacker has also uploaded, possibly leading to remote code execution in the FFmpeg process. ImageMagick selects its coders and delegates from the extension in the same way. An application is affected if it accepts uploads from untrusted users and analyzes video or audio attachments, generates video previews, or processes images with ImageMagick. The AviSynth attack additionally requires an FFmpeg built with --enable-avisynth and the AviSynthPlus runtime on the host. Upstream FFmpeg and the common Linux distribution and Homebrew packages do not enable it; the GPL builds distributed for Windows and Linux from ffmpeg.org do. Other decoders that FFmpeg or ImageMagick select from the extension may be reachable without AviSynth. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

descriptions.description: CWE-646: Reliance on File Name or Extension of Externally-Supplied File

descriptions.value:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unlimited recursion depth in constructed-form string decoding.

Any constructed-form string element causes the decoder to recurse on the element's contents. The BER encoding controls nesting depth at four bytes per level, with no bound checked. Perl recursion is heap-allocated, so the process grows without a stack crash.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust memory with a small deeply nested constructed string.

solutions.value: Upgrade to Convert-ASN1 0.37 or later.

cna.title: Overly Restrictive Account Lockout Mechanism in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, in which a failed sign-in at the web services listener from loopback or from an address in WebServicesTrustedProxies is counted against the user name alone, towards the per-name lockout (AccountLockoutThreshold in hMailServer.ini, 0, off, by default), and never towards a ban of the address, as for an address in AutoBanNeverBan; a failure from any other address counts as before. A proxy at another address that is not listed, forwarding to the HTTPS port, is not taken for a proxy and is charged as before, as a load balancer is at the mail listeners, until its address is in WebServicesTrustedProxies; from 6.3.8 a ban its clients earn also closes the web services listener to it. Through a proxy the per-name lockout is then the limit on the guesses at one account, so turn it on there. Until then, put the proxy's address in AutoBanNeverBan (127.0.0.1 and ::1 for a proxy on the same machine), which keeps the auto-ban from counting that address's failed logons on any protocol; turning the auto-ban on failed logons off, or setting MaxInvalidLogonAttempts or AutoBanMinutes to 0, also avoids it, for every address. From 6.3.6 the never-ban list by reverse name spares a proxy at another address whose forward-confirmed reverse name it covers, lifting the ban once the name is confirmed; it cannot name loopback.

descriptions.value: The web services listener of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.3 through 6.3.7 counts every failed CardDAV, CalDAV or Autodiscover sign-in from a proxy it trusts - one on the same machine, or one named in WebServicesTrustedProxies, whose X-Forwarded-Proto it believes - against the proxy's own address, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker who can reach the proxy to have that address banned from the server's mail listeners. The listener, off by default (WebServicesHttpPort and WebServicesHttpsPort 0), signs an account in with HTTP Basic over HTTPS for CardDAV from 6.3.3 and for CalDAV and Outlook Autodiscover from 6.3.4. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, which the server trusts when it is on the same machine or named in WebServicesTrustedProxies, the listener takes the client's HTTPS from the proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto header, but it does not believe X-Forwarded-For and sees the proxy's address for every client. Each failed sign-in counted towards the auto-ban against that address, so that failed sign-ins through the proxy from anybody, under any user name, reaching MaxInvalidLogonAttempts (3 within 30 minutes by default) wrote an IP range that refused the proxy's address at the SMTP, POP3, IMAP and ManageSieve listeners for AutoBanMinutes (60 by default), and could write it again each time it lapsed. For a proxy on the same machine that address is the loopback address, so that a webmail on that machine, local scripts that submit mail and the other local clients of the mail listeners were shut out; for a proxy at another address that also carries mail, every mail client behind it was. Such a proxy forwarding to the listener's HTTPS port, re-encrypting, was counted against in the same way, and listing it in WebServicesTrustedProxies did not spare it. The auto-ban is on by default and AutoBanNeverBan, which spares an address, is empty by default; the listener itself went on serving the proxy.

descriptions.description: CWE-645: Overly Restrictive Account Lockout Mechanism

cna.title: Magic Login Mail or QR Code <= 2.07 - Unauthenticated Privilege Escalation via Account Takeover to Host Header Injection in curpageurl() Magic-Login URL

affected.product: Magic Login Mail or QR Code

descriptions.value: The Magic Login Mail or QR Code plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Privilege Escalation via Administrator Account Takeover in versions up to, and including, 2.07. This is due to the `curpageurl()` function falling back to the raw `$_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']` value — with no validation against the site's configured origin via `home_url()` or `site_url()` — when `get_the_permalink()` returns empty or false, allowing an attacker-controlled Host header to become the URL origin of the magic-login link generated by `generate_url()` and delivered to the target via `wp_mail()`. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to intercept the one-time uid and token pair sent to a targeted Administrator's email and replay them against the real site, causing `autologin_via_url()` to call `wp_set_auth_cookie()` and establish a full Administrator session on the targeted account. Exploitation requires the `[magic_login]` shortcode to render on a path where `get_the_permalink()` returns empty or false (such as a 404 page or a block-theme header template part), the web server to forward non-canonical Host headers, the attacker to know the target administrator's email address, and the administrator to click the attacker-originated magic-login link. Successful exploitation gives the attacker control of a distinct, already-privileged Administrator account; it does not promote the attacker's original account. Successful exploitation additionally requires an action by an administrator — the attacker cannot trigger the vulnerability on their own.

solutions.value: Upgrade Docker Sandboxes to version 0.53.0 or later.

workarounds.value: Publish services using an explicit host port instead of an automatically assigned port. Stop the listening service when withdrawing access until upgrading.

descriptions.value: Docker Sandboxes can silently republish a sandbox service after an operator removes its automatically assigned host-port mapping. An attacker able to reach the restored endpoint may regain access to the service. Both TCP and UDP mappings are affected. Exposure is limited to the original bind address, which defaults to loopback. The issue is fixed in version 0.53.0.

cna.title: Action Pack: Missing SameSite attribute on session cookies from Action Pack session stores

descriptions.value: Action Pack is a framework for handling and responding to web requests. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, Action Pack session stores other than ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore (CacheStore, MemCacheStore, and third-party stores built on AbstractStore, AbstractSecureStore or the session mixins) write the session cookie without a SameSite attribute, regardless of config.action_dispatch.cookies_same_site_protection, which defaults to :lax. Only CookieStore applies the configured policy. In browsers that do not treat a cookie without the attribute as SameSite=Lax, a cross-site request could carry the session cookie, possibly leading to cross-site request forgery against actions that do not verify an authenticity token, such as those of API-only applications. Applications are affected when they use a session store other than CookieStore and do not pass same_site: to config.session_store. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

cna.title: Action Pack: Possible cache poisoning in Action Pack content negotiation

descriptions.value: Action Pack is a framework for handling and responding to web requests. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, Action Pack negotiates the format of a rendered response from the Accept, X-Requested-With and, for XHR requests without Accept, Content-Type request headers, but ActionController::Rendering#_set_vary_header adds Vary: Accept only when the request carries a usable Accept header and the response has no Vary header yet. A response to a request without Accept, or to an XHR request, therefore omits the headers that selected its representation, and a response whose Vary the application set before rendering (for example Vary: Accept-Language) never gains Accept. A shared cache that honours Vary could store such a response and serve it to later clients that request a different representation, possibly leading to cache poisoning in which visitors receive, until the entry expires, a page without its layout or HTML in place of JSON. The attacker cannot choose the content of the response. Applications that render negotiated responses from actions marked public (for example with expires_in ..., public: true) behind a shared cache that honours Vary, such as Thruster or Rack::Cache, are affected. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

cna.title: Quick Page/Post Redirect 5.2.1 - 5.2.3 - Backdoor via Off-Repository Update Channel

descriptions.value:
The Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4 was distributed with a hidden update mechanism that fetched Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4 updates from its author's own server instead of WordPress.org, which was used to push a backdoored build to sites, allowing the attacker controlling that server to inject arbitrary content into pages and to deliver arbitrary code to affected sites.

Version 5.2.1, as published on WordPress.org, bundled the Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4 Update Checker library (updater/ directory) configured to poll https://anadnet.com/updates/?action=get_metadata&slug=quick-pagepost-redirect-Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4. In March 2021 that server delivered a modified 5.2.3 build, different from the 5.2.3 later published on WordPress.org, which kept the update channel and added a the_content filter that, for logged-out visitors on single posts and pages, fetched content from https://w.anadnet.com/bro/3/ (passing the site host, request URI and visitor User-Agent) and prepended the response to the post (observed serving SEO spam links to search engine crawlers). Because the version string matched a later WordPress.org release, affected sites were not offered a clean update until 5.2.4.

Indicators of compromise:
- Outbound requests to anadnet.com or w.anadnet.com
- An updater/ directory (Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4 Update Checker, Puc v4p10) inside wp-content/Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4/quick-pagepost-redirect-Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4/
- The strings filter_the_content_in_the_main_loop, ppr_pro, QQQEND or w.anadnet.com in page_post_redirect_Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4.php
- page_post_redirect_Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4.php with MD5 ad717da18cf8a2b69899c0d7dafee05a (tampered 5.2.3)

Remediation: remove the Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4 (it has been closed on WordPress.org), or at minimum reinstall the clean 5.2.4 from WordPress.org, delete any leftover updater/ directory, verify the files with "wp Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4 verify-checksums quick-pagepost-redirect-Quick Page/Post Redirect Plugin WordPress plugin before 5.2.4", clear the opcode cache, and treat any site that ran the tampered build as potentially compromised.

cna.title: Active Support: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Support safe_constantize

descriptions.value: Active Support is a collection of utility classes and standard library extensions used by Rails and other Ruby projects. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, when constant lookup raises LoadError, ActiveSupport::Inflector#safe_constantize (and String#safe_constantize) builds a regular expression from the requested constant name without escaping it, so a caller that passes untrusted input lets the attacker choose the source of a pattern that the application compiles. Crafted patterns can trigger defects in Ruby's regular expression compiler, possibly leading to a crash of the server process, and repeated requests could keep the application unavailable. Action Cable passes the channel value of each subscribe command to safe_constantize before any channel lookup, so an unauthenticated client can reach this code when the application mounts Action Cable and accepts connections from untrusted clients without an added authentication check. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

descriptions.value:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via zero-length BIT STRING content.

A BIT STRING with zero content octets passes -1 to substr as the length. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the decoded value is nearly all of the input that follows the element. In the constructed form each zero-length segment copies the rest of the input again, so memory grows with the square of the input size.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust memory with a short constructed BIT STRING. The resulting value also contains bytes from adjacent input.

Improper Certificate Validation in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, which on Windows refuses before connecting, with HM7534 in the error log, a root certificate file name whose bytes in the code page outside ASCII also read as UTF-8, for PostgreSQLSslRootCert and TlsCaFile alike and whichever database client is loaded, and hands an Oracle MySQL client the name in UTF-8, which names the same file. Until then, name the root certificate file by a path in ASCII alone, which reads as the same name in the code page and in UTF-8 and which every affected version hands over unchanged; where a name outside ASCII must stay, make sure no one else can create the file or folder that the name's UTF-8 reading names.

descriptions.value: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.25 through 6.3.7 on Windows, with a PostgreSQL database, the connection's sslmode require, verify-ca or verify-full, and a root certificate file named by PostgreSQLSslRootCert (from 6.2.25) or, with TlsMode=verify-full and neither PostgreSQL key set, by TlsCaFile (from 6.3.4), hands the file's name to libpq as bytes in the system's ANSI code page (up to 6.3.5 as Latin-1 bytes, which on code page 1252 are the code page's own for U+00A0 to U+00FF), and libpq looks for the file by those bytes and then hands the same bytes to OpenSSL, whose file opening on Windows reads a name as UTF-8 first and opens the file at that reading when one is there. When every byte of the name outside ASCII also reads as UTF-8 - for example U+00C3 U+00A9, the bytes C3 A9 on code page 1252, which are U+00E9 in UTF-8 - the database server's certificate was checked against the file at that other name whenever one was there, which allows a local attacker who can create that file but cannot change the configured one, as any user can by default beside a file an administrator keeps under ProgramData, or beside a folder directly under the system drive's root whose permissions the administrator restricted, and who can intercept the connection to the database server or stand in for it, to have hMailServer trust a certificate authority of the attacker's own and read and modify the traffic between hMailServer and its database, the database password included; the file alone, holding no authority that issued the database server's certificate, stops hMailServer from connecting to its database. The same applies in 6.3.4 through 6.3.7 to TlsCaFile when an Oracle MySQL client library has been put in place of the bundled MariaDB Connector/C, since that client opens the file through OpenSSL in the same way; the bundled MariaDB Connector/C opens the file in the code page and is not affected, and neither are the Linux builds. The configuration is not the default: by default no root certificate file is named.

descriptions.value: @grpc/grpc-js implements the core functionality of gRPC purely in JavaScript, without a C++ addon. The affected matchers are used for route selection, xDS credential identity matching, and RBAC URL path, principal name, server name, and header rules. An ALLOW policy using an alternation can consequently accept a method, certificate identity, or header value outside the intended set, while a DENY policy becomes broader rather than permissive. This issue is fixed in versions 1.13.2 and 1.14.2.

cna.title: Uncontrolled Search Path Element in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, which on Windows always hands the bundled client its plugin folder in the bytes the client reads it in - the ANSI code page, or UTF-8 where that is the code page - or, where the code page lacks a character of the path, by the folder's short (8.3) name, which is the same folder; where neither can be written, it hands a folder under the Windows system folder that holds no plugin and that only administrators can create, so that a plugin found only in the installation's plugin folder is not loaded and the connection's error says why, and where even that folder cannot be written, it refuses the connection before attempting it, with error HM7537 in the log. It never hands Latin-1 bytes, the empty value or a folder the current drive or folder completes: that closes the service's case and the database commands' case alike. Before 6.3.8, install hMailServer in a folder whose path is ASCII alone, as the default folder under Program Files is, and start hMailServer.exe's database commands, and DBSetup when it finishes an installation, from a folder on the system drive. For a new installation of 6.3.4 or 6.3.5 with an external database, whose setup runs two or three of the commands in the Bin folder itself, only an installation folder whose path is ASCII avoids it. An installation whose path is ASCII is not affected; on a system whose code page for non-Unicode programs is 1252, the service is not affected unless the path holds a C1 control character (U+0080 to U+009F) whose byte code page 1252 reads as another character, but before 6.3.8 a path holding a character above U+00FF reaches a database command started from another drive on any code page. Setting MARIADB_PLUGIN_DIR in the service's environment does not help, since the client takes the option first and every affected version sets it.

descriptions.value: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.3 through 6.3.7 on Windows, with a MySQL or MariaDB database, hands the bundled MariaDB Connector/C the folder of its authentication plugins (the plugin folder in the installation's Bin folder) as Latin-1 bytes, which the client reads in the system's ANSI code page when it builds a plugin's path and loads the plugin with LoadLibraryExA, which allows a local authenticated user to execute code as the hMailServer service's account (LocalSystem, or the service's virtual account for a new installation from 6.3.4) by creating the folder those bytes name in the code page and placing in it a DLL with a plugin's name, when the installation folder's path holds a character between U+0080 and U+00FF whose byte the code page reads as another character, and none above U+00FF, and the user can create that other folder (by default any authenticated user may create a folder directly under the root of the system drive). The server converted the path with the C runtime's wcstombs_s in the C locale, which writes each character up to U+00FF as the byte of the same value: on code page 1252 those bytes are the same letters, while on another code page, such as 1251, or on a UTF-8 code page, they name another folder. The client loads the plugin the database server names in its greeting, unless it is built in, and any plugin the server names in an authentication switch, and tries again at each connection while a load fails, so with a MySQL 8.0 or later server, whose greeting names caching_sha2_password by default, the DLL is loaded at the next connection the service makes, whatever plugin the database account uses; a DLL's entry point runs when it is loaded. A path holding any character above U+00FF was handed over as an empty string, whatever the code page, from which the client makes a plugin's name at the root of the current drive: for the service, whose current folder is System32, that is the root of the system drive, where by default only administrators can create a file, but the server's own database commands (hMailServer.exe --check-database, --upgrade-database and the others from 6.3.4, and the /Debug and /Test console modes from 6.2.3) run in the folder they are started from - the product tells administrators to run them from an elevated prompt in the Bin folder, and the setup of 6.3.4 and 6.3.5 ran two or three of them itself with the Bin folder as their working folder for a new installation with an external database - so a DLL that a local authenticated user placed under a plugin's name at the root of a drive other users may write, such as a FAT or exFAT volume, was loaded into the administrator's process at the command's first connection to a MySQL 8.0 or later server. 6.3.8 fixes both cases: it hands the folder in the code page's bytes or by its short (8.3) name, and where neither can be written, a folder under the Windows system folder that holds no plugin and that only administrators can create, or else refuses the connection before attempting it; it never hands the empty value or a folder the current drive completes. The configuration is not the default: the default installation folder, under Program Files, is ASCII. Linux builds set no plugin folder and are not affected.

cna.title: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, whose JSON reader keeps an object's member names in an ordered set, whose cost does not depend on which names are chosen, and holds a REST request body and a mailed TLS-RPT report to 10,000 members in an object; the reply to a password-protected message is held to 2 MB. Until then, clear each domain's report mailbox, or move it off the domains the server hosts, so that no report is read by the server; and switch OpenPGP in the webmail off (portal_enabled under /api/v1/settings/openpgp), and off for any domain or account that holds openpgp_portal_enabled on, which refuses the reply to a password-protected message before its body is parsed; clearing the public base URL is not enough, since links already made stay usable. For the routes that take an account or an API key, only limiting who can reach the REST API avoids it (RestApiPort 0, the default, turns it off), or a reverse proxy in front of it that holds request bodies well below 16 MB. Restarting the service ends a busy thread.

descriptions.value: Inefficient algorithmic complexity in the JSON reader of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.6 and 6.3.7 allows a remote attacker to hold the server's mail delivery threads or its REST API's worker threads, making mail delivery, the REST API and the webmail unavailable. 6.3.6 fixed CVE-2026-107574, in which reading a JSON object searched the member names already read for each new name, by keeping the names in a hash set; the set uses the standard library's hash, which takes no secret, so member names chosen to fall in one bucket of it still cost time growing with the square of their number. Against the released reader, one such object of 16 MB took about 5 seconds to read in the Linux build, and one of under 6 MB about 23 seconds in the Windows build, where objects of the same sizes with other names took under a tenth of a second. A remote unauthenticated attacker reaches the reader by mailing such an object as a TLS-RPT report, up to 16 MB once decompressed, to a hosted domain's report mailbox, where an administrator has set one; it is read on a mail delivery thread (ten by default), and those threads deliver all mail, local and outbound, so a stream of such reports stops all delivery for as long as it continues. It is also reached without an account through the reply to a password-protected message, with the message's link alone, where the REST API is on (it is off by default) and a public base URL for such links is set; and by any account through the webmail's routes granted 16 MB, and by an application's API key through the send API. Each such request holds one of the REST API's four worker threads, in the process that also serves SMTP, IMAP and POP3.
Buffer overflow in Turbolev in Google Chrome prior to 157.0.8103.78 allowed a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page. (Chromium security severity: High)

cna.title: Addressable URI normalization resolves some dotted path segments to the wrong path

descriptions.value: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. From 2.2.5 until 2.9.1, Addressable::URI.normalize_path can resolve a path containing leading parent segments and later parent segments to a different path than an RFC 3986 resolver. URI#normalize, URI#join, URI#==, and URI#=== inherit the result. An application that authorizes the Addressable-normalized path but sends the original URI to another resolver can allow access outside the intended path allowlist. Applications that use the same normalized value for authorization and the request, or reject parent segments, are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

cna.title: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access ('Link Following') in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, whose setup holds every folder from the root of the volume down to the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel open and, before anything changes, refuses with exit code 7 a junction, a symbolic link or a mount point on the way that anybody but SYSTEM, the Administrators and TrustedInstaller owns, may change or may remove - a junction made at a drive's root and left with the permissions the root hands down among them - and a folder on the way that another account may rename or remove, or empty, naming each with the icacls that deals with it. Until then, install hMailServer under Program Files, or at a path with no link on it below folders that only administrators may change. For a link that is meant to be on the path, make it the administrators' alone from an elevated Command Prompt - icacls "<link>" /L /setowner *S-1-5-32-544, then icacls "<link>" /L /inheritance:r /grant:r *S-1-5-18:F *S-1-5-32-544:F *S-1-5-32-545:RX - and check where it leads (dir /al of the folder that holds it); make the Administrators the owner of each folder above the program folder that other accounts may change, and take away their right to change it; then restart Windows. Where another account owned or could change such a link or folder while the installation was there, reinstall into a new folder as the hMailServer documentation, ServiceAccount.md, "Reinstalling into a new folder", says.

descriptions.value: Improper link resolution in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.7 allows a local authenticated user to run code as the mail server's service account or as an administrator when the path to the program folder passes through a junction, a symbolic link or a mount point that the user controls or that every user may change, such as a junction made at the root of a drive, which takes the root's permissions, or through a folder that every user may rename. Setup installed the programs through any such link without first checking who controls it, or whether a folder above the program folder may be renamed, and the service is registered to run the programs by that path, so the programs are installed where a link another account controls leads, or that account can later make the path lead to a folder it controls; the service, which runs as LocalSystem or as its virtual account, and the programs administrators run from Bin are then started from there. 6.3.7's fix for CVE-2026-107571 does not cover this: its hardening of the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel does not change a folder reached through a link that the administrators do not alone control, and setup does not refuse such a path: it installs through the link and at most reports afterwards that the folders could not be hardened. The default installation under Program Files is not affected.

descriptions.description: CWE-59: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access ('Link Following')

cna.title: Incorrect Default Permissions in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, whose setup makes a new program folder, every folder above it that is not there, and Bin and ControlPanel in it, with permissions of their own from the moment each exists - SYSTEM and the Administrators full control, Users read and execute, nothing inherited, the Administrators the owner - before Inno Setup makes a folder or copies a file, each made by its name relative to the folder above it, which setup holds open. Until then, install hMailServer under Program Files, or into a new folder inside a folder that only administrators may change. To install elsewhere, first make the program folder from an elevated Command Prompt and give it a protected set of permissions - icacls "<program folder>" /inheritance:r /grant:r *S-1-5-18:(OI)(CI)F *S-1-5-32-544:(OI)(CI)F *S-1-5-32-545:(OI)(CI)RX, then icacls "<program folder>" /setowner *S-1-5-32-544 - check with dir /q /a "<program folder>" that nothing has been made in it, and restart Windows before running setup, so that nothing opened in it before its permissions were set stays open.

descriptions.value: Incorrect default permissions in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.7 allow a local authenticated user to run code as the administrator who installs the product, when it is installed into a new program folder in a location whose permissions let every user write, such as the root of a drive. 6.3.7 fixed CVE-2026-107571 by giving the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel permissions that only administrators may change, but its setup lets Inno Setup make a new program folder first, with the permissions the folder above hands down, and replaces them only afterwards, tens of milliseconds later (33 to 139 milliseconds in the project's test runs). In that time any local account may make files and folders in the new folder, which keep that account as their owner, among them the Bin folder that setup then copies the programs into. Setup runs programs from Bin with the administrator's elevated rights, registering the service among them, before its hardening at the end of setup takes such a folder back, and those programs load a library placed in Bin in place of the system's. The default installation under Program Files, whose folders give ordinary users read and execute only, is not affected.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via quadratic bigint loop in os2ip.

Every INTEGER or ENUMERATED longer than four content octets reaches os2ip, which iterates over each content octet with $result = ($result * 256) + $octet. Each multiplication operates on a bigint that grows by one octet per step, so decoding an n-octet value takes O(n^2) bigint work. Nothing limits content length before this loop runs.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust CPU with a single oversized INTEGER or ENUMERATED value.

solutions.value: Upgrade to Convert-ASN1 0.37 or later.

descriptions.value: Action View is a framework for handling view template lookup and rendering and provides view helpers for building HTML. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, ActionView::Helpers::TextHelper#highlight substitutes each matched phrase into the :highlighter string without escaping it and returns the result marked HTML-safe. credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, which on Windows hands OpenSSL the name of each of these files in the code page and refuses, with HM7536 in the error log, a name with a character the code page does not have or whose bytes outside ASCII also read as UTF-8, so that nothing is read from or written to a refused file: a listener whose certificate or key file is refused does not start, a refused client-certificate CA file verifies no certificate, the object store's refused CA file allows no request, and the ACME client orders no certificate. Until then, name every TLS file, the ACME directory and the program and data folders by paths in ASCII alone, which read as the same name in the code page and in UTF-8 and which every affected version hands over unchanged; where a name outside ASCII must stay, keep each of its characters at or below U+00FF and one the system code page writes as its Latin-1 byte (on code page 1252, U+00A0 to U+00FF; none under a UTF-8 code page) - change any other name to ASCII - and make sure no one else can create the file or folder that the name's UTF-8 reading names.

descriptions.value: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.3.7 on Windows hands OpenSSL the names of its own TLS files - the listeners' certificates, chains, private keys and Diffie-Hellman parameters, a port's client-certificate CA file (from 6.2.19), the object store's CA file (from 6.3.4) and the ACME client's keys and certificates - as Latin-1 bytes, which on code page 1252 are the code page's own for U+00A0 to U+00FF, and OpenSSL's file opening on Windows reads a name as UTF-8 first and opens the file at that reading when it is there, or creates it there when its folder is. When every byte of a configured name outside ASCII also reads as UTF-8 - for example U+00C3 U+00A9, the bytes C3 A9, which are U+00E9 in UTF-8 - the server used the file at that other name whenever one was there, which allows a local attacker who can create that file or its folder but cannot change the configured one, as any user can by default beside a file an administrator keeps under ProgramData, to have a port that logs on by client certificate (from 6.2.25) accept certificates from a certificate authority of the attacker's own and so sign in over the network as any mailbox without its password; to have the server trust such an authority for its object store and, intercepting that connection, read and modify the messages it stores; to receive the private keys the ACME client writes, the key of a certificate issued for the server's names among them; or to keep TLS ports from starting. The configuration is not the default: by default these files have names in ASCII, client certificates are off on every port, and the object store and ACME are off. The Linux builds are not affected.

cna.title: pgEdge Postgres MCP Server SQL injection through custom pl-do tool parameters

descriptions.value: pgEdge Postgres MCP Server enables SQL queries against PostgreSQL databases through Model Context Protocol compatible clients. Prior to 1.1.0, custom pl-do tools interpolated JSON arguments into a PostgreSQL DO block delimited by fixed dollar-quote tags. An argument containing $mcp_custom_tool$ could terminate the block and inject arbitrary SQL statements, while $mcp_args$ could inject procedural code into a plpgsql block. Because the statement used the simple query protocol, injected text could include additional statements and transaction control, bypassing read_only and accessing data or modifying resources available to the connecting role. The issue requires at least one pl-do custom tool; sql and pl-func tools pass arguments as bind parameters and are not affected by this injection mechanism. This issue is fixed in 1.1.0.

cna.title: Action Pack: Possible restoration of destroyed sessions in Action Dispatch CacheStore

descriptions.value: Action Pack is a framework for handling and responding to web requests. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, ActionDispatch::Session::CacheStore writes a session back to the cache at the end of each request that loaded it, without checking that the session's cache entry still exists. When a concurrent request destroys the session, through reset_session on logout or by deleting its cache entry on the server, a request that loaded the session earlier and finishes later restores it under its original session ID. Logout and server-side revocation could therefore fail to end a session, and an attacker who holds a stolen session cookie could keep that session valid across the victim's logout. Applications that use config.session_store :cache_store are affected, with any cache backend. ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore is not affected, nor is ActionDispatch::Session::MemCacheStore with Dalli 4.0.0 or later, whose session store does not write back a session that was deleted. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

cna.title: Active Support: Possible XSS vulnerability in Active Support MessagePack serializer

descriptions.value: Active Support is a collection of utility classes and standard library extensions used by Rails and other Ruby projects. From 8.1 until 8.1.4.1, ActiveSupport::MessagePack serializes an ActiveSupport::SafeBuffer as its bytes alone and deserializes it as a new SafeBuffer, so a buffer that is no longer html_safe? (for example, one mutated in place with gsub!) is restored as html_safe. If such a buffer holds untrusted input and is stored through a MessagePack serializer, rendering it after it is loaded bypasses ERB auto-escaping, possibly leading to XSS. Applications on Rails 8.1 are affected if they use a MessagePack serializer, such as config.action_dispatch.cookies_serializer = :message_pack or :message_pack_allow_marshal, or serializer: :message_pack for Rails.cache, ActiveSupport::MessageVerifier or ActiveSupport::MessageEncryptor, and store a SafeBuffer that was mutated in place with untrusted input. Rails 8.0 and earlier do not serialize SafeBuffer with MessagePack and are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 8.1.4.1.

Alternatively, make `mount/3` match its first argument as a map (`%{} = params`), or define `handle_params/3` in the LiveView. In both cases a mount without a route raises, and the join fails.

descriptions.value:
Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in phoenixframework phoenix_live_view allows an authenticated user to mount a router-mounted LiveView without the on_mount hooks of its live_session via a phx_join message that carries neither a "url" nor a "redirect" key.

The catch-all clause of the private Phoenix.LiveView.Channel.authorize_session/3 in lib/phoenix_live_view/channel.ex accepts a join without a URL for any session, including a root LiveView mounted at the router. The channel then mounts the LiveView with no route, and only a route adds the live_session hooks to the mount lifecycle. Checks that those hooks perform on the connected mount do not run, and event checks that they attach through attach_hook/4 are never attached. The attacker needs a valid session token for the LiveView, which only the HTTP render issues, after the hooks pass there. on_mount hooks declared in the LiveView module still run.

This issue affects phoenix_live_view: from 0.16.0 before 1.0.20, from 1.1.0-rc.0 before 1.1.34, and from 1.2.0-rc.0 before 1.2.14.

x_proofOfConcept.value:
The target application has a live_session whose on_mount hook halts the mount for a suspended account and attaches a :handle_event hook with attach_hook/4 that denies the delete_post event to users who are not admins. The LiveView at /posts does not define handle_params/3.

* Sign in as a user without the admin role and load /posts over HTTP. Keep the session cookie, the CSRF token from the page, and the id, data-phx-session, and data-phx-static attributes of the element that has data-phx-main.
* Open the LiveView websocket at /live/websocket with the session cookie and the CSRF token.
* Send a phx_join message on the topic lv:<id>. The payload has "params" (with "_csrf_token" and "_mounts": 0), "session", and "static". It has no "url" key and no "redirect" key.
* The server replies with status ok. The LiveView is mounted without the live_session hooks.
* Send an event message of type click for the event delete_post. The LiveView handles the event, and the post is deleted.

The same join with the "url" key set to the page URL runs the hooks, and the delete_post event is denied. If the account is suspended after step 1, the join with "url" is refused, and the join without "url" still succeeds.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Join authorization. The private Phoenix.LiveView.Channel.authorize_session/3 in lib/phoenix_live_view/channel.ex has three clauses. The "redirect" clause resolves the route and checks that it stays in the same live_session. The "url" clause requires, for a session where Phoenix.LiveView.Session.main?/1 is true, that the route for the URL matches the view and the live_session of the session. The third clause matches any other join parameters and returns the session with no route and no URL. Nested LiveViews need this clause because they have no URL. The clause does not call Phoenix.LiveView.Session.main?/1, so it also accepts a root LiveView that was mounted at the router.

2. Mount with no route. With no route, mount/3 receives :not_mounted_at_router as its params. The private load_lifecycle/2 adds the on_mount hooks of the live_session only when it receives a %Phoenix.LiveView.Route{}. Without a route it returns the lifecycle of the LiveView module alone. The live_session layout is skipped in the same way.

3. Result. The signed session token, the static token, the CSRF token, and the session cookie are all valid, so the join succeeds. The LiveView runs without the live_session hooks. Hooks that halt the mount do not run, and hooks attached with attach_hook/4 for :handle_event or :handle_info are never attached.

Conditions that stop the mount. A LiveView that defines handle_params/3 raises on a mount without a route. A LiveView whose mount/3 matches its params as a map raises. A LiveView that reads an assign that a skipped hook sets raises. In these cases the join fails.

The official JavaScript client always sends "url" or "redirect" for a root LiveView. Only nested views join without either key.

cna.title: WP Instant Feeds <= 1.3.4 - Unauthenticated Stored Cross-Site Scripting via 'data[images][][url]' Parameter

descriptions.value: The WP Instant Feeds plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'data[images][][url]' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.3.4 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. cna.title: llama.cpp MTMD Multimodal GGUF File Parsing Integer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

descriptions.value:
llama.cpp MTMD Multimodal GGUF File Parsing Integer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of llama.cpp. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of audio multimodal projector GGUF files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in an integer overflow before allocating a buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute arbitrary code in the context of the current process. Was ZDI-CAN-30980.

cna.title: Gwenhywfar 4.99.8beta before 5.14.2 Stack Buffer Overflow via GWEN_TLV_Buffer_To_DB()

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: Gwenhywfar 4.99.8beta before 5.14.2 Stack Buffer Overflow via GWEN_TLV_Buffer_To_DB()

descriptions.value: Gwenhywfar 4.99.8beta before 5.14.2 contains a stack-based buffer overflow in GWEN_TLV_Buffer_To_DB() in src/parser/tlv.c when decoding BER-TLV tags into a fixed 128-byte buffer. Attackers can supply a record with about 127 or more tag continuation bytes or a truncated multi-byte tag, such as via a malicious chip card's EF_SSD file read by libchipcard's ZKA driver, to crash the application.

Successful exploitation requires that a staff member or administrator opens the affected ticket and clicks the attacker-planted link on the ticket-detail screen, as the VenoBox payload is triggered on click rather than on page load. Successful exploitation additionally requires an action by an administrator — the attacker cannot trigger the vulnerability on their own.

cna.title: Node.js is vulnerable to a remotely triggerable uncaught exception in TLS servers via deferred handshake callbacks

descriptions.value: A deferred-callback use-after-destroy in Node.js TLS server handshake handling allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to terminate the server process. When a TLS server uses any of the SNICallback, OCSPRequest, newSession, or resumeSession hooks, or server.addContext(), the corresponding OpenSSL callbacks are deferred, and the deferred code does not handle the underlying socket being destroyed between scheduling and execution. By sending a client hello that reaches the vulnerable path (for example, no SNI together with an OCSP request) followed by padding and a socket FIN, an attacker makes OpenSSL deliver the client hello and the end-of-file in the same tick, so the socket is destroyed before the deferred callback runs and the process raises an uncaught exception instead of emitting an 'error' event. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x and 24.x.

supportingMedia.value: A deferred-callback use-after-destroy in Node.js TLS server handshake handling allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to terminate the server process. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x and 24.x.

cna.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection') in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.2.19 or later, which substitutes parameters in a single pass that never re-examines a value already written into the statement, and gives each parameter a name no other parameter's name and ordinal can form. There is no complete workaround for earlier versions on MySQL/MariaDB or PostgreSQL, since the recipient row is written for every queued message; keeping message indexing (MessageIndexing) and greylisting off, as they are by default, removes those two paths only. SQL Server and SQL Server Compact installations need no action for this issue.

descriptions.value: SQL injection in the database layer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.2.18, when the server uses MySQL/MariaDB or PostgreSQL, allows a remote attacker to alter SQL statements the server runs. On those two engines parameters are not bound: SQLStatement::GenerateFromCommand wrote each value into the statement's text as a quoted literal with a separate string replacement over the whole text per parameter, so a value holding the name of a parameter substituted after it had that name replaced, inside the value, by the later value with its own quotes, which ended the literal early and placed the later value in the statement as SQL. The row the server writes for each recipient of a queued message carries the recipient's address twice, so in the default configuration an authenticated user who may send mail reaches it by sending to an address of their choosing. A remote unauthenticated sender reaches the same statement through a message the server sends to the envelope sender, such as a delivery failure notice or an automatic reply, and, when greylisting or message indexing is enabled (both are off by default), through the greylisting record's envelope addresses or through the message metadata the server stores for IMAP SORT, which carries four header fields of a received message. An altered statement runs with the privileges of the server's database account; on PostgreSQL, whose client call runs every statement in the text it is given, further statements can follow it, while on MySQL/MariaDB, where one statement is run per call, the change is confined to the statement it is in. SQL Server and SQL Server Compact, where parameters are bound, are not affected.
