descriptions.value:
flowintel contains an information disclosure vulnerability in its case history feature. When a user views the history of a case they are authorized to access, the history output includes references to other cases (linked, unlinked, or forked) without verifying whether the requesting user has permission to view those referenced cases. This exposes the identifiers and titles of cases that the user should not be able to discover.

The vulnerability affects multiple output paths:
- Browser-based case history view
- API history endpoint
- Plain-text history download
- Markdown history download
- Report timeline generation

An authenticated user with access to any single case can enumerate the existence and identifiers of other cases by reading the history of a case they can access. This bypasses the intended per-case access control model and may reveal the existence of sensitive investigations, their identifiers, and associated metadata to unauthorized users.

The raw audit storage is not modified; the issue is solely in the presentation layer failing to filter references to inaccessible cases before returning history data to the user.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-128 Application Metadata Discovery

descriptions.description: CWE-200 Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

solutions.value: A new visibility-aware history retrieval function was introduced that parses each history record for case references (link, unlink, fork events) and checks the requesting user's access to every referenced case before including that record in the output. Records referencing inaccessible cases are omitted from the response. The filtering is applied consistently across all history output paths (browser view, API, text download, Markdown download, and report timelines). Administrative users retain full unfiltered access. The raw audit log storage remains unchanged to preserve forensic integrity.

cna.title: flowintel: Unauthorized Disclosure of Linked Case References in Case History

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: The affected version range is assumed to be all versions prior to 4.1.0 based on the explicit context providing affected_version '0' and fixed_version '4.1.0'. The exact earliest affected version is not confirmed by the patch itself.
The CAPEC-128 mapping is the closest available pattern; no CAPEC specifically covers cross-object information disclosure through a legitimate read endpoint. The mapping is approximate.
CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker needs at least one valid authenticated session with access to any case. If the application allows unauthenticated history access in some deployment, PR would be N.
The patch commit message references 'Tool: Codex' which is noted as the AI tool used for implementation but is not credited as a vulnerability finder or reporter.

The vulnerability requires the attacker to already have access to at least one case; it does not allow access to cases with no prior relationship to the attacker's accessible cases beyond those referenced in history.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker leverages a legitimate application endpoint (case history) to discover metadata about other resources (case identifiers, titles, and relationships) that they are not authorized to access. This is the closest CAPEC pattern to the observed information disclosure through a functional endpoint. The mapping is approximate because CAPEC-128 typically refers to version/configuration discovery, whereas here the disclosed metadata is application data (case references) rather than system metadata. No more specific CAPEC pattern for cross-object information disclosure via a legitimate read endpoint exists in the CAPEC catalog.

x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N - The vulnerability is exploitable over the network via the web application. AC:L - Exploitation requires only viewing the history of any accessible case; no special conditions or race conditions are needed. AT:N - No prior attack or manipulation of the target is required. PR:L - The attacker must be an authenticated user with access to at least one case. UI:N - No user interaction beyond normal application use is required. VC:L - The vulnerable component (case history endpoint) leaks limited information (case IDs and titles of referenced cases). VI:N - No integrity impact. VA:N - No availability impact. SC:L - Subsequent components (other cases) have their existence and identifiers exposed to unauthorized users. SI:N - No integrity impact on other systems. SA:N - No safety impact.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: A new visibility-aware history retrieval function was introduced that parses each history record for case references (link, unlink, fork events) and checks the requesting user's access to every referenced case before including that record in the output. Records referencing inaccessible cases are omitted from the response. The filtering is applied consistently across all history output paths (browser view, API, text download, Markdown download, and report timelines). Administrative users retain full unfiltered access. The raw audit log storage remains unchanged to preserve forensic integrity.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Added a new function get_visible_history() in common_core.py that: (1) verifies the user can view the current case, (2) groups raw history lines into logical records using timestamp-based event boundaries, (3) extracts referenced case IDs from link/unlink/fork messages using regex patterns, (4) checks can_view_case() for each referenced case, and (5) excludes records referencing inaccessible cases. Updated download_history(), download_history_md(), the browser history endpoint, the API history endpoint, and the report timeline generator to call get_visible_history() instead of the raw get_history(). Added helper functions _history_case_references() and _history_record_complete() to handle legacy multiline link records and ambiguous formats. Changed download_history() to serve content via BytesIO instead of reading a file path directly.

cna.title: Org.keycloak:keycloak-model-jpa: case-variant realm urls bypass proxy restrictions

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When configured with a database that uses case-insensitive collation, Keycloak resolves realm URLs regardless of letter casing. A remote attacker can exploit this behavior by sending requests with alternate letter casing to bypass upstream reverse proxy access controls that rely on case-sensitive path matching. This issue can expose restricted authentication endpoints intended only for internal access, though Keycloak's internal authentication mechanisms remain intact.

cna.x_redhatCweChain: CWE-178: Improper Handling of Case Sensitivity

workarounds.value:
Configure upstream reverse proxies, load balancers, or API gateways to enforce case-insensitive path matching (such as case-insensitive regular expressions or URI normalization) for rules restricting realm access. Alternatively, enforce network-level restrictions (such as IP allowlisting or dedicated internal interfaces) instead of URL path filtering alone.

Apply the revised configuration by reloading the proxy service:
`systemctl reload <proxy_service>`

Warning: Reloading or restarting the proxy service may momentarily disrupt active client connections. Ensure that proxy path normalization accurately handles all character casing variants.

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Alexander Schwartz (IBM) for reporting this issue.

descriptions.value:
flowintel contains an authorization flaw in its recurring reminder notification subsystem. When a user is subscribed to recurring notifications for a case, the system does not re-verify the recipient's current access rights to that case before generating or displaying the notification.

As a result, a user who previously had access to a private case and later had that access revoked can still:
- Receive recurring reminder notifications containing case-related content.
- View stored reminder notifications in their notification list, including notification counts, even though they no longer have permission to view the underlying case.

The vulnerability affects both the notification creation path (recurring reminder generation) and the notification display path (listing and counting stored reminders). The issue arises because the authorization check performed at subscription time is not re-applied at delivery or retrieval time.

Security impact is limited to information disclosure: an unauthorized user may observe case titles, reminder messages, and associated metadata that they no longer have permission to access. No integrity or availability impact is indicated by the patch.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-66 Exploiting Incorrectly Configured Security Levels

solutions.value: The fix introduces an authorization re-check at two points: (1) before creating a recurring reminder notification, the system now verifies the recipient's current case visibility and skips delivery if access has been revoked; (2) when listing or counting stored notifications, the system now filters out case-related reminder notifications for which the viewing user no longer has case access. This ensures that both the creation and display paths enforce current authorization state rather than relying on a one-time check at subscription time.

cna.title: flowintel: Stale Authorization Allows Notification Disclosure After Case Access Revocation

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: The affected version range is inferred from the explicit context (affected_version: 0, fixed_version: 4.1.0); the patch itself does not contain version strings.

The CAPEC-66 mapping is the closest available match; no CAPEC specifically covers stale-authorization or missing re-authorization at notification delivery time. This uncertainty is noted in the CAPEC rationale.
CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker is an authenticated user who previously had case access; the patch does not specify whether unauthenticated access is possible.
CVSS VC:L assumes the disclosed information is limited to notification content (case titles, reminder messages) rather than full case data; the patch only addresses notification visibility.
The patch does not indicate whether the vulnerability is exploitable remotely or requires local access; AV:N is assumed based on the web-application nature of the product.
The commit message references 'Tool: Codex' which is noted as the AI tool used for implementation but is not credited as a vulnerability finder or reporter.

capecRationale.rationale: The notification subsystem operated with a lower security enforcement level than the case-access subsystem: it did not enforce the same access-control checks that governed case visibility. An attacker (or a user whose access was legitimately revoked) could exploit this misconfiguration to continue receiving case-related notification content. This is the closest CAPEC to the pattern of a component not enforcing the security level configured elsewhere in the application. The mapping is uncertain because no CAPEC specifically describes stale-authorization or missing re-authorization at delivery time; CAPEC-66 is selected as the best available match for a security-level enforcement gap between components.

x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The application is a web-based platform accessed over the network. AC:L: No special race condition or complex setup is required; the user simply needs to have previously had case access and then have it revoked. AT:N: No manipulation of the target is needed. PR:L: An authenticated user with a valid account and prior case subscription is required. UI:N: Notifications are delivered and displayed automatically without requiring victim interaction. VC:L: Limited confidentiality impact; case-related notification content (titles, reminder messages) is exposed to a user who no longer has case access. VI:N, VA:N: No integrity or availability impact is evidenced. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N: The affected data resides within the same application scope; no cross-scope impact is indicated.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces an authorization re-check at two points: (1) before creating a recurring reminder notification, the system now verifies the recipient's current case visibility and skips delivery if access has been revoked; (2) when listing or counting stored notifications, the system now filters out case-related reminder notifications for which the viewing user no longer has case access. This ensures that both the creation and display paths enforce current authorization state rather than relying on a one-time check at subscription time.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In recurring_notification.py, the create_notification function now imports can_view_case and, for each recurring notification subscriber, fetches the User record and calls can_view_case(case, recipient); if the check fails, the notification is skipped via continue. In notification_core.py, the DEADLINE_ICONS tuple is extended to include the clock icon (fa-solid fa-clock), a new helper _is_case_deadline_notification is added to identify case-related deadline/reminder notifications by icon or notification_type, and _visible_deadline_notifications is updated to use this helper so that reminders for inaccessible cases are excluded from the returned list. The test file is updated to create a real Case object for the reminder notification fixture instead of using a hardcoded case_id.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Recheck private case access for recurring

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Recheck private case access for recurring

weaknessRationale.rationale: The system performed an authorization check at subscription time but failed to re-enforce it at notification delivery and display time. The authorization decision was not re-evaluated when the user's access to the case changed, resulting in continued access to case-related notification content. This is a failure to properly enforce authorization at the point of access rather than a complete absence of authorization logic.

In the recurring notification creation path, no authorization check existed at all before generating the notification for a subscriber. The check was entirely absent, not merely insufficient, making CWE-862 a defensible secondary mapping for the creation path specifically.

cna.title: Mailer Trusts Replies That a Man in the Middle Injects Right After STARTTLS

descriptions.value:
Since Symfony 7.3, the require_tls option of EsmtpTransport refuses to send a message over a connection that isn't encrypted. It prevents a network attacker from stripping STARTTLS. But after the server's 220 reply to STARTTLS, the transport started the TLS handshake without checking whether more data had already arrived.

An attacker in the middle of the connection could add cleartext replies right after the 220. The transport then read them as if they came from the encrypted session. The attacker could make the transport skip AUTH, or report a message as sent while the server had rejected it.

Connections that use implicit TLS, with smtps:// or port 465, are not affected. Since Symfony 8.1, the Amazon SES SMTP transport enables require_tls by default on ports other than 465 and 2465. So ses+smtp:// DSNs are affected without setting the option.

The transport now refuses to start TLS when the server sends data right after its answer to STARTTLS, and throws a TransportException instead.

flowintel contains an authorization bypass in its task completion workflow for privileged cases. Users with lower-privilege roles (editor, queuer) were able to mark tasks as completed without the required approver review (Admin, Case Admin, or Queue Admin), undermining the approval workflow.

The vulnerability was exploitable through multiple paths:
- Direct task completion via browser UI or REST API
- Changing a task's status to "Finished", which implicitly completed the task
- Creating a new task in a privileged case with the completed flag already set
- Using UUID aliases or Matrix delegation to reach the same endpoints

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with at least editor or queuer role
- A privileged case with tasks in a non-completed state

Security impact:
- Bypass of the mandatory approver review process for privileged cases
- Unauthorized modification of task completion state
- Potential to mark sensitive work as finished without proper oversight

descriptions.value:
A vulnerability exists in the flowintel application's calendar functionality that allows unauthorized access to private case data. The task calendar queries failed to enforce visibility checks on the parent case associated with tasks. Specifically, tasks assigned to a user or belonging to the user's organization were returned in calendar views (including browser and API ICS feeds) without verifying whether the user had permission to view the parent case. This allowed users to potentially discover and access details of private cases they were not authorized to view, leading to information disclosure.

The issue affected the default task visibility logic and the assigned-only task queries. The fix ensures that case visibility is rechecked in addition to task assignment or organization membership, preventing the exposure of private case data in calendar outputs.

CAPEC-126 Forced Browsing

The fix ensures that tasks are only visible if the user has permission to view the parent case, in addition to being assigned to the task or belonging to the same organization. This prevents the disclosure of private case data in calendar views and ICS feeds.

cna.title: Unbounded exponent in Fraction validation

descriptions.value:
Validating an untrusted string in exponent notation into a Fraction field computes the full power of ten without any bound: an input of a few bytes takes seconds to validate.

String inputs are passed to the Fraction constructor. For strings in exponent notation (e.g. '1e8000000'), CPython computes the corresponding power of ten as an integer (in Lib/fractions.py).

The issue was fixed in commit 69ed168e9ad465eef4c8d81efb152a93b604daf5. For strings in exponent notation, the exponent is now parsed before calling the Fraction constructor, and exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into Fraction fields (in both JSON and Python mode, including in strict mode), using Pydantic from 2.10.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.0.

From 2.14.0, exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected, matching the maximum number of digits accepted for integers.

supportingMedia.value:
Summary

Validating an untrusted string in exponent notation into a Fraction field computes the full power of ten without any bound: an input of a few bytes takes seconds to validate.

Details

String inputs are passed to the Fraction constructor. For strings in exponent notation (e.g. '1e8000000'), CPython computes the corresponding power of ten as an integer (Lib/fractions.py):

exp = m.group('exp')
if exp:
    exp = int(exp)
    if exp >= 0:
        numerator *= 10**exp
    else:
        denominator *= 10**-exp

The issue was fixed in commit 69ed168e9ad465eef4c8d81efb152a93b604daf5. For strings in exponent notation, the exponent is now parsed before calling the Fraction constructor, and exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected.

Impact

Denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into Fraction fields (in both JSON and Python mode, including in strict mode), using Pydantic from 2.10.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.0.

From 2.14.0, exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected, matching the maximum number of digits accepted for integers.

cna.title: Dnsmasq: dhcpv6 relay remote crash via stale pointer in relay_upstream6()

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Akin Yilmaz (DecompilerAI) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value:
Disable the DHCPv6 relay feature if it is not required, or restrict network access to the DHCPv6 relay port.

1. If DHCPv6 relay capability is not needed:
Remove or comment out all `dhcp-relay` entries in `/etc/dnsmasq.conf` or in configuration files under `/etc/dnsmasq.d/`, then restart the service:
```
systemctl restart dnsmasq
```

2. If DHCPv6 relay is required, restrict incoming traffic on UDP port 547 to trusted network interfaces or subnets using firewalld:
```
firewall-cmd --remove-port=547/udp --permanent
firewall-cmd --reload
```
Alternatively, configure rich rules in firewalld to permit UDP port 547 only from designated DHCPv6 clients and relay sources.

Caveats:
Disabling the relay configuration or restricting UDP port 547 prevents clients on blocked interfaces or subnets from forwarding DHCPv6 requests. 

Warning: Restarting or reloading the dnsmasq service will momentarily interrupt active DNS resolution and DHCP operations.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in dnsmasq, where a memory handling issue exists in its Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) relay processing. A remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability by sending a sequence of network packets to a system configured as a DHCPv6 relay. This causes the service to write data to previously freed memory and crash, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).

cna.title: Validation bypass of extra data keys in JSON model validation

descriptions.value:
When validating JSON data into a model allowing extra data, the keys of extra data aren't validated against the key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__, resulting in extra data not matching the declared type. This is the case if you define __pydantic_extra__ as e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=r'^x_')], int].

The validate_json_by_iteration() method (in pydantic-core/src/validators/model_fields.rs), used to validate JSON data into models, only validates the values of extra data, and stores the keys as is.

The issue was fixed in commit 4c65dbda9970a488e2ff21c8693fc6f6d70a3358.

Impact: validation bypass, as extra data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted JSON data into models allowing extra data (with extra='allow'), with a key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__ (e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=...)], int]), using Pydantic from 2.13.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.2.

Python mode validation isn't affected.

The validate_json_by_iteration() method (in pydantic-core/src/validators/model_fields.rs), used to validate JSON data into models, only validates the values of extra data, and stores the keys as is (L605-L623):

        match validator.validate(py, value, state) {
            Ok(value) => {
                model_extra_dict.set_item(&py_key, value)?;
                fields_set.add(py_key)?;
            }
            // ...
        }
    }
    // ...
}

The issue was fixed in commit 4c65dbda9970a488e2ff21c8693fc6f6d70a3358.

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel's chatbot component used a single shared MCP (Model Context Protocol) session and process-wide environment variable to pass per-user API credentials to a child process. Because the session and the ambient FLOWINTEL_API_KEY environment variable were shared across all concurrent requests, a user's authenticated identity could be applied to another user's tool invocation, or a stale/ambient credential could be inherited by a new request.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with access to the chatbot interface.
- Concurrent or overlapping chatbot tool invocations from different users, or a request made after another user's credentials were written to the process environment.

Impact:
- A lower-privilege user could read data belonging to a higher-privilege user (e.g., private investigation cases).
- A user whose session was invalidated (deleted, password changed, key revoked) could still operate under a previously cached ambient credential.
- The parent process environment was mutated with user-specific secrets, creating a persistent credential leak surface.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-126 Session Hijacking

descriptions.description: CWE-200 Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

solutions.value: The shared persistent MCP session and process-wide API key mutation were removed. Each chatbot tool invocation now spawns its own short-lived MCP child process with credentials resolved fresh from the authenticated request context. If the user's identity or API key is unavailable, the invocation is rejected before any child process is launched, preventing fallback to ambient or stale credentials. Each transport is deterministically closed on success, failure, or timeout, eliminating residual credential exposure.

The Serializer Doesn't Enforce #[Ignore] on the Class Picked by a Discriminator Map or object_to_populate

supportingMedia.value:
When it denormalizes data into a class, the Serializer computes which attributes it may write from the `#[Ignore]` and `#[Groups]` metadata. It did that for the requested class, but wrote into another class in two cases. The first case is the class that a discriminator map picks from the data. The second is the class of the object passed with the `object_to_populate` or `deep_object_to_populate` option.

When the requested class has no `#[Ignore]` attribute and the context sets no groups, nothing was restricted. A client could then set a property that the picked class marks with `#[Ignore]`, constructor arguments included:

```php
#[DiscriminatorMap(typeProperty: 'kind', mapping: ['email' => EmailNotification::class])]
abstract class Notification {}

class EmailNotification extends Notification
{
    #[Ignore]
    public bool $skipModeration = false;
}
```

With a `#[MapRequestPayload] Notification $notification` argument, the payload `{"kind":"email","skipModeration":true}` set `skipModeration`. With groups in the context, a property outside these groups could be set too. This happened when another class of the map had a property with the same name in one of the groups. The same happened with `#[Ignore]` when the requested class declares the map itself. On 5.4, `ObjectNormalizer` also returned such properties when normalizing an object whose class declares the map itself.

This affects `ObjectNormalizer`, `PropertyNormalizer` and `GetSetMethodNormalizer`.

The Serializer now resolves the class it writes into first, and computes the allowed attributes for that class. The type property of a discriminator map is also written only when the metadata of that class allows it.

cna.title: @fastify/express vulnerable to path-scoped middleware bypass via request URL decoding and normalization mismatches

descriptions.value: @fastify/express is a compatibility layer that lets Express middleware run inside the Fastify web framework. In versions before 4.0.10, the plugin passes Express a request URL that does not always match the path Fastify's router dispatched, so path-scoped Express middleware can be skipped while the route handler still runs. Several request forms trigger the mismatch, including percent-decoding that rewrites a backslash to a slash or double-decodes an encoded percent sign, and a request target that begins with an asterisk, so the middleware and the handler disagree on the path or on parameter and query values. An unauthenticated client can therefore reach a handler that an authentication, authorization, or rate-limiting middleware was meant to protect, with no special configuration required. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.10, and users should upgrade to 4.0.10 or later.

MISP contains an authorization and input-validation flaw in its event push mechanism. When a user with push permissions initiates a push of events to a remote MISP instance, the system fails to enforce two critical checks: (1) it does not verify that an event is published before including it in the push, allowing unpublished (i.e., not yet publicly shared) events to be transmitted to the remote server; and (2) it does not verify that the pushing user has read access to the event, causing events the user cannot fetch to be sent as empty event shells, thereby disclosing the existence and metadata of events the user is not authorized to view. Additionally, the remote server's reply selecting which offered events to accept is used without validating that the selected identifiers actually correspond to events in the offered set, potentially allowing the remote to reference events outside the intended scope. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with push permissions on the source MISP instance and a configured push target. The security impact is unauthorized disclosure of confidential threat-intelligence data (unpublished events and events restricted by user permissions) to a remote MISP instance that should not receive them.

assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; all versions prior to this commit are assumed affected.
PR:L assumes the attacker needs a standard authenticated user with push permissions; if push is restricted to administrators only, PR could be H.

VC:L assumes the disclosed data (unpublished events, inaccessible event metadata) constitutes a low confidentiality impact; if the events contain highly sensitive threat intelligence, the impact could be higher.
CAPEC-126 is the closest available mapping; no CAPEC precisely describes 'missing authorization on outbound data push in a trusted inter-system exchange.'

The remote server's ability to reference non-offered events (CWE-20 component) is assessed as low impact because the events would still need to exist and be accessible on the source; the primary impact is the authorization bypass (CWE-862).
The 'Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5' credit is included as listed in the commit metadata; its role as a remediation developer is inferred from the co-authorship line.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix enforces three security controls in the push path: (1) an explicit check that the event's 'published' flag is set before the event is eligible for push, returning a descriptive error if it is not; (2) a guard that skips any event for which the pushing user's fetch returns empty, preventing transmission of inaccessible events as empty shells; and (3) validation of the remote server's event-selection reply so that only UUIDs present in the originally offered event list are accepted, discarding any identifiers the remote references that were not part of the push offer.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/Event.php, a new early-return check is added at the top of uploadEventToServer() that rejects the push if $event['Event']['published'] is empty. In app/Model/Server.php, three changes are made: (a) in the push() loop, a 'continue' statement is added when fetchEvent() returns empty, skipping inaccessible events; (b) the lastpushedid fallback logic is corrected to preserve the existing value when both successes and fails are empty; (c) in getEventIdsForPush(), the remote's JSON reply is validated as an array, filtered to string values, and then cross-referenced against the UUIDs in the $request (offered events) array so that only UUIDs present in both sets are returned.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The push occurs over the network between MISP instances. AC:L: Triggering a push is a standard user action with no special race or timing conditions. AT:N: No manipulation of the attack target is required. PR:L: An authenticated user with push permissions is required. UI:N: No additional user interaction beyond initiating the push. VC:L: Confidential event data (unpublished events, events the user cannot access) is disclosed to the remote server. VI:N, VA:N: No integrity or availability impact on the source. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N: The remote server receives data but its own confidentiality, integrity, and availability are not compromised.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The push mechanism does not enforce that events are published or that the pushing user has read access before transmitting them to a remote server, constituting a missing authorization check on data egress.

The remote server's reply selecting events to accept is used without validating that the referenced identifiers belong to the set of events actually offered in the push request, allowing out-of-scope references.

capecRationale.rationale: The MISP push mechanism relies on a trusted relationship between the source and remote MISP instances. The source trusts the push flow and the remote's reply without enforcing proper authorization (published status, user access) or validating the remote's selection against the offered set. The closest CAPEC is Leverage Trusted Relationship because the vulnerability arises from insufficient validation within a trusted inter-system data exchange. Uncertainty: no CAPEC perfectly captures 'missing authorization on outbound data push'; CAPEC-126 is the best available match for a trusted-relationship data-flow flaw.

PR:L assumes the attacker needs at least editor-level access to create or modify case/task fields, based on the editor_required decorator visible in the surrounding code. If the application allows unauthenticated case creation, PR would be N.
The CVSS secondary-scope impact (SC:L, SI:L) assumes the victim's spreadsheet application executes injected formulas; actual impact depends on the specific application and its security settings.
CAPEC-117 (CSV Injection) is selected as the closest match; if this CAPEC ID is not present in the target CAPEC version, CAPEC-66 (Leverage Executable Code) would be the next-best alternative.

The fullwidth Unicode formula triggers (＝, ＋, －, ＠) are included in the fix, suggesting the developers considered non-ASCII bypass vectors; the CVSS does not separately account for this as it does not change the base score.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: New file app/utils/csv_utils.py defines csv_safe_cell(value) which returns an empty string for None, prepends an apostrophe to strings that start with tab/CR/LF or whose lstrip()-ed form begins with =, +, -, @, or fullwidth equivalents (＝, ＋, －, ＠), and otherwise returns the value unchanged. In app/tools/tools.py the _cases_to_csv function is modified so that both case rows and task rows are wrapped with a dict comprehension applying csv_safe_cell to every field before writer.writerow. The user manual (doc/user-manual.md) gains a note explaining the apostrophe-prefixing behaviour and that JSON exports preserve original text.

UI:A – the victim must actively open the CSV in a spreadsheet application for the formula to execute. VC/VI/VA:N – the primary system (flowintel) suffers no direct confidentiality, integrity, or availability impact. SC:L – the secondary system (spreadsheet) may leak data via formula functions. An attacker stores formula-like text in application fields; when the CSV is opened in a spreadsheet, the formula executes. CAPEC-117 is the most specific and directly applicable pattern. descriptions.value:
flowintel allows users with editor-level access to author case and task fields, including aggregated tags. When these records are exported as CSV, the field values are written verbatim into the output file.

Because no sanitisation is applied to user-supplied text before CSV serialisation, an attacker can store values that begin with spreadsheet formula triggers (such as =, +, -, @, or their fullwidth Unicode equivalents, or leading control/whitespace characters). When a victim opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application (e.g. Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc), the stored text is interpreted and executed as a live formula rather than displayed as literal text.

This can lead to unintended data manipulation within the spreadsheet, potential data exfiltration via formula functions, or execution of downstream commands depending on the spreadsheet application and its configuration.

The vulnerability requires the victim to actively open the CSV file in a spreadsheet application; the flowintel application itself is not directly compromised.

cna.title: Doctrine Remember-Me Token Provider Accepts Outdated Tokens Under the Series of Their Copy, Also After Logout

descriptions.value:
DoctrineTokenProvider keeps a copy of the previous token of a remember-me cookie. This way, concurrent requests sent with that token are still accepted for 60 seconds. The copy is stored in another row, under a series derived from the series of the cookie. Since Symfony 6.4.45, 7.4.18 and 8.1.6, a copy is stored for every series that the remember-me handler generates. Before, copies were stored only for the series created before Symfony 5.4.19, 6.0.19, 6.1.11 and 6.2.5.

A cookie could use the series of the copy instead of its own series. The copy then matched as a current token, so the limit of 60 seconds didn't apply and the theft detection didn't trigger. Logging out deleted only the row of the original series, and the copy stayed.

An attacker who got hold of a remember-me cookie could then keep logging in as its user after the user logged out. This works when the token was rotated at most once since the attacker got the cookie.

DoctrineTokenProvider now accepts only the series formats that the remember-me handler generates, whatever the collation of the database. It also deletes the copy together with its token.

supportingMedia.value:
`DoctrineTokenProvider` keeps a copy of the previous token of a remember-me cookie. This way, concurrent requests sent with that token are still accepted for 60 seconds. The copy is stored in another row, under a series derived from the series of the cookie. Since Symfony 6.4.45, 7.4.18 and 8.1.6, a copy is stored for every series that the remember-me handler generates. Before, copies were stored only for the series created before Symfony 5.4.19, 6.0.19, 6.1.11 and 6.2.5.

A cookie could use the series of the copy instead of its own series. The copy then matched as a current token, so the limit of 60 seconds didn't apply and the theft detection didn't trigger. Logging out deleted only the row of the original series, and the copy stayed.

An attacker who got hold of a remember-me cookie could then keep logging in as its user after the user logged out. This works when the token was rotated at most once since the attacker got the cookie.

`DoctrineTokenProvider` now accepts only the series formats that the remember-me handler generates, whatever the collation of the database. It also deletes the copy together with its token.

cna.title: Org.keycloak:keycloak-services: pre-revocation id tokens can mint fresh uma rpts after realm not-before

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When an administrator revokes tokens by setting a not-before revocation cutoff, Keycloak fails to enforce this boundary when processing User-Managed Access (UMA) grant requests using ID token claims. An authenticated remote user with an active session can submit a previously revoked ID token to receive a fresh Requesting Party Token (RPT). This flaw allows an attacker to bypass token revocation and retain unauthorized access to protected resources.

descriptions.description: Use of a Key Past its Expiration Date

cna.x_redhatCweChain: CWE-324: Use of a Key Past its Expiration Date

workarounds.value:
Explicitly terminate active user sessions when revoking tokens, or disable User-Managed Access (UMA) authorization on clients where fine-grained authorization is not needed.

To reduce exposure:
- In the Keycloak Administration Console, navigate to the target realm, select 'Sessions', and explicitly terminate active sessions for the relevant user or realm rather than relying solely on the not-before timestamp cutoff.
- For OpenID Connect clients that do not require fine-grained resource permissions, ensure that 'Authorization Enabled' is set to 'OFF' in the client settings.

Caveats:
Terminating active user sessions will immediately disconnect active sessions and require users to re-authenticate. Disabling authorization services on a client disables the issuance of Requesting Party Tokens (RPTs) for that client. These configuration changes take effect immediately and do not require restarting the Keycloak service.

FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its task management workflow. When a user reopens a completed task (by toggling its completion state or changing its status to a non-finished value) or creates a new task within a completed privileged case, the parent case is automatically revived (un-completed, status reset to Created, finish date cleared). The system failed to enforce the required Admin or Case Admin privilege check before performing this case revival side effect.

A user with basic task-level permissions (e.g., editor, queuer, or queue admin) could trigger the revival of a completed privileged case through the browser interface or the REST API, without holding the elevated role required for case-level operations. This could disrupt case lifecycle management, clear completion metadata, and potentially expose the case to further unauthorized modifications.

The vulnerability affects both the browser-based task completion/status-change endpoints and the corresponding API endpoints, as well as the task creation flow.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-114 Forced Browsing

solutions.value: The fix introduces explicit authorization checks (can_reopen_case and can_reopen_task) that require Admin or Case Admin privileges before a completed privileged case can be revived as a side effect of task reopening or task creation. Denial is enforced at the core model layer and at both the browser and API endpoint layers, with audit logging of denied attempts. Legitimate task creation is preserved, but the automatic case revival is suppressed for unauthorized users.

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel's alerting module contained an authorization bypass in the alert access control logic. When an alert was linked to a private case, the system relied solely on connector ownership (user or organization) to determine access, without verifying that the requesting user still held valid membership in the associated private case.

This meant that a user who was a connector owner of an alert could continue to read alert details, review history, raw payloads, and action comments, and could perform review-status updates or case-creation actions, even after their access to the linked private case had been revoked or they were never a member of that case.

Additionally, a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap existed: after a review-status update or a competing case-creation claim was committed, the response could disclose private case identifiers or review history to a user whose access had been concurrently removed by another session linking the alert to a private case.

Impact:
- Unauthorized disclosure of private case data (review comments, raw payloads, action history) through alert endpoints.
- Unauthorized modification of alert review status and creation of cases from alerts the user should no longer access.
- Leakage of a competing case identifier to an unauthorized user during concurrent case-creation races.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-114 Forced Browsing

descriptions.description: CWE-362 Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Inadequate Locking

solutions.value: The fix enforces private case visibility as a mandatory gate before any connector-ownership check can grant alert access. If an alert is linked to a private case and the user cannot view that case, access is denied regardless of ownership. A post-commit re-verification is added after review-status updates and after detecting a competing case-creation claim, ensuring that concurrent association changes do not result in unauthorized data disclosure in the response.

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

assumptions: The affected version range is inferred from the explicit context (affected_version '0', fixed_version '4.1.0'); no explicit changelog or release notes are available to confirm the exact first vulnerable release.

The CAPEC-114 mapping is the closest available pattern; the actual attack is a logic flaw in authorization ordering rather than classic forced browsing, but no more specific CAPEC exists for missing authorization checks in API endpoints.

CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker must be an authenticated user with connector ownership; if the product allows unauthenticated access to alert endpoints, PR would be N, but the patch evidence (session-based auth, API keys in tests) supports authenticated access.

The TOCTOU component (CWE-362) requires a concurrent session to link the alert to a private case at the precise moment of the response; this is a secondary vector and the primary issue is the missing authorization check (CWE-862).
The commit message references 'Tool: Codex' which is noted as the AI tool used to assist in development; no credit is assigned for this as it is not a person or organization.

Because the authorization logic did not enforce private case membership, the server returned sensitive case data and accepted state-changing actions. This is the closest CAPEC to the observed pattern of accessing a resource by directly specifying its identifier without the required authorization context. Uncertainty: the attack does not involve guessing URLs but rather exploiting a logic flaw in an existing authorized endpoint; however, CAPEC-114 remains the best available match for direct resource access bypassing intended access controls.

AC:L: No special race condition or complex setup is required; a connector owner whose case access was revoked can simply call the alert endpoints. AT:N: No manipulation of the target is needed. PR:L: The attacker must be an authenticated user with connector ownership of the alert. UI:N: No victim interaction is required. VC:L: Confidential impact is limited to alert-level data (review comments, raw payload, action history) rather than full case contents. VI:L: The attacker can modify review status and create cases, but cannot alter case data directly. VA:N: No availability impact. SC/SI/SA:N: No impact on other systems.

If an alert is linked to a private case and the user cannot view that case, access is denied regardless of ownership. A post-commit re-verification is added after review-status updates and after detecting a competing case-creation claim, ensuring that concurrent association changes do not result in unauthorized data disclosure in the response.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In can_user_view_alert, the private-case membership check was moved before the connector-ownership checks and made unconditional (no longer gated on case.is_private), so any user lacking case access is denied even if they own the connector. The unused import get_present_in_case was removed. 33 regression tests were added covering revoked access, connector scope, concurrent case-link transitions, and authorized-user preservation.

cna.title: Validation bypass of aliased fields in TypedDict and dataclasses allowing extra data

descriptions.value:
When extra data is allowed, providing both the alias and the name of an aliased TypedDict or dataclass field makes the unvalidated value (provided under the name) overwrite the validated one (provided under the alias), resulting in validated data not matching the declared type.

Extra items are stored in the same dictionary as the fields (the returned dictionary for TypedDict, the instance __dict__ for dataclasses). As only the alias is marked as used, the field name is treated as an extra item, and its unvalidated value overrides the validated one. The TypedDict validator (pydantic-core/src/validators/typed_dict.rs) and the dataclass validator (pydantic-core/src/validators/dataclass.rs) share this logic.

The issue was fixed in commit 34491f5328f168f14e3769cd5f0f83c0af0f4778.

Impact: validation bypass, as data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted data into TypedDict or dataclass types with aliased fields and extra data allowed (with extra='allow', or with the extra_items argument for TypedDict), using Pydantic V2 (up to and including 2.14.1).

Pydantic models (BaseModel) are not affected, as extra data is stored separately from fields.

Summary

As only the alias is marked as used, the field name is treated as an extra item, and its unvalidated value overrides the validated one (pydantic-core/src/validators/typed_dict.rs):

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a vulnerability in the cryptographic signature verification of protected events. When a MISP instance signs a protected event for synchronization, it strips all whitespace from the JSON body before computing the PGP signature (preg_replace("/\s+/", "", $data)). The receiving instance performs the same whitespace-stripping before verification. Because the signature covers only the whitespace-free representation, a network relay positioned between two MISP instances can insert whitespace characters into JSON object keys (effectively renaming fields) or into identifier values such as UUIDs, timestamps, and distribution fields without invalidating the signature. The receiving instance accepts the modified event as authentic.

The vulnerability affects the protected event synchronization path: event creation (EventsController::add), event editing (EventsController::edit), event viewing (EventsController::view1), and server-to-server pull synchronization (ServerSyncTool, Server model). An attacker with a network position to intercept and modify traffic between MISP instances can alter the semantic content of protected events while the PGP signature still validates, undermining the integrity guarantees that protected events are designed to provide.

The fix introduces two complementary mechanisms. First, a post-verification scan rejects any received body that contains whitespace in JSON keys (except under Galaxy cluster 'meta' keys) or in identifier-like values (uuid, id, timestamp, distribution, date). Second, a new exact-byte signature scheme (x-pgp-signature-v2) signs the body as transmitted, without whitespace normalization. MISP 3.0 and later peers exchange this exact-byte signature; older peers retain the legacy whitespace-stripped signature. A signature_version field is embedded in protected events so that a 3.0 receiver refuses a body carrying that marker if only the legacy signature is present. Both mechanisms together close the whitespace-injection vector while preserving backward compatibility with pre-3.0 instances.

Flowintel's community data launcher script passes the admin API key as a command-line argument to a child Python helper process. On Unix-like systems, process arguments are readable by all local users via standard tools such as ps or by reading /proc/<pid>/cmdline, allowing any local user to observe the key while the helper process is running.

An attacker with local access to the host can capture the admin API key during the brief window in which the helper process is active. Possession of the key grants full administrative access to the Flowintel REST API, enabling unauthorized creation, modification, or deletion of threat intelligence data, users, roles, and organisations.

Preconditions:
- The victim must invoke the community data import or deletion command (launch.sh -tdc or -dtdc) with the API key supplied as a positional argument.
- The attacker must have a local user account on the same host and be able to observe process listings during the helper execution window.

Impact:
- Disclosure of the Flowintel admin API key to any local user.
- Subsequent full administrative control over the Flowintel instance via its REST API.

Affected: <4.1.0
CAPEC-66 Exploiting Trusted Input in Untrusted Context

descriptions.description: CWE-200 Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

solutions.value: The launcher no longer forwards the admin API key in the child process command line. The key is now passed exclusively through the FLOWINTEL_ADMIN_API_KEY environment variable, which is not visible in process listings. A hidden terminal prompt (read -r -s) is provided for interactive use, and the Python helper reads the key from the environment by default. Legacy positional and --api-key argument forms remain functional for backward compatibility but emit a warning documenting the exposure risk.

Flowintel disabled TLS certificate verification for all MISP API connections and used unverified SSL contexts for IMAP and SMTP STARTTLS mail connections. This allowed an on-path (man-in-the-middle) attacker positioned between Flowintel and its MISP or mail servers to impersonate the remote server and intercept sensitive data.

Affected connections include:
- All MISP HTTPS API calls (event retrieval, attribute search, event creation, connectivity checks, and API validation)
- SMTP STARTTLS connections used for sending email notifications
- IMAP TLS connections used for fetching mail archives and testing connectivity

An attacker who can observe or intercept network traffic between Flowintel and the MISP or mail server could:
- Capture MISP API keys and mail credentials (SMTP/IMAP passwords)
- Read all threat intelligence data exchanged (events, attributes, objects, reports)
- Inject or modify threat intelligence data returned to Flowintel

The vulnerability required no authentication on the part of the attacker and no user interaction; it was exploitable by any party with a network position between Flowintel and its configured MISP or mail endpoints.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-119 Man-in-the-Middle

solutions.value: The fix introduces a shared TLS utility module that enforces certificate and hostname verification by default for all MISP and mail connections. MISP clients now receive a proper SSL verification context instead of ssl=False, and IMAP/SMTP connections use a verified ssl.SSLContext. Operators may configure a private CA bundle path or explicitly disable verification (which fails closed on malformed input). The previous urllib3 warning suppression is removed, and upgrade documentation warns that previously accepted self-signed or mismatched certificates will now cause connection failures.

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel contains multiple authorization and credential management vulnerabilities affecting connector instances, MISP helper tools, and case templates.

- Connector instance metadata, connectivity checks, and case listings accepted instance IDs without verifying if the acting user had visibility or ownership rights, allowing unauthorized access to sensitive configuration and data.
- Case template serialization and creation processes exposed connector instances attached to templates regardless of the user's permissions, potentially leaking credentials or instance details to users who should not have access.
- Editing connector instances allowed changes to URLs or sharing scopes without requiring re-authentication of API keys, enabling the reuse of another user's credentials in a new context or the leakage of shared keys to unauthorized endpoints.
- Outbound MISP connector keys were incorrectly accepted for authenticating incoming alerts, bypassing the intended separation between outbound integration credentials and inbound alert source authentication.

These issues allow authenticated users to access unauthorized connector data, manipulate credential scopes, and potentially exploit credential confusion between different security contexts.

descriptions.value: Missing authorization in Kibana Cases alert attachments can allow an authenticated user with permission to add case comments or attachments to modify case-link metadata in documents they are not authorized to access. An attacker can add false case links and prevent legitimate case linkage by exhausting the alert's case-link limit. Writes are limited to the kibana.alert.case_ids field in indices that Kibana's internal account can read and update and whose mappings accept that field. One of the two authorization defects was fixed earlier in 8.19.22, 9.4.8 and 9.5.5; the fixed versions listed in this advisory address both defects.

configurations.value:
All of the following conditions must hold:
- The attacker must have Cases read and create_comment (Create comments & attachments) privileges, or Cases all, for the Cases feature matching the case owner in the affected space: generalCasesV3, securitySolutionCasesV3 or observabilityCasesV3.
- The attacker must have access to an existing case where they can add an attachment, or permission to create such a case.
- For one of the two authorization defects, the attacker must additionally have permission to read an alert of an authorized rule type and consumer. Permission to read the unauthorized target alert is not required. The other defect does not require an alert-read privilege.
- The target index must be readable and writable by Kibana's internal account, and its mapping must accept kibana.alert.case_ids. The attacker does not need Elasticsearch read or write privileges on the target index.

workarounds.value: Grant affected users Cases read access without create_comment in each relevant space, and remove attachment permissions from every role granting them. Another role granting Cases all or create_comment would preserve access. This also prevents ordinary comments and attachments; downgrading Cases all to read removes case creation, editing, and connector push permissions.

Upgrade Kibana versions 9.5.0 through 9.5.5 to 9.5.6.

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its user directory and assignment endpoints that allows authenticated users to access data belonging to other organisations.

When the LIMIT_USER_VIEW_TO_ORG setting is enabled to restrict directory visibility to the caller's organisation, several API endpoints (user lookup by ID, last name, Matrix ID, and role-based listings) did not consistently enforce the organisation boundary. An authenticated non-admin user could retrieve profiles of users in other organisations by supplying their identifiers.

Additionally, OrgAdmin users could retrieve the task assignments of any user in the system, including tasks and case titles from private cases to which they had no access. The assignment endpoints did not verify that the requested user belonged to the caller's organisation or that the underlying cases were visible to the caller.

Security impact:
- Exposure of user identities (names, Matrix IDs, roles) across organisation boundaries
- Disclosure of task assignments, case titles, and workflow details from private cases
- Potential enumeration of other organisations' membership and case activity

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0
CAPEC-100 Parameter Tampering

descriptions.description: CWE-200 Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

solutions.value: The fix introduces a centralised visibility-scoping function that applies the configured organisation limit consistently across all user directory queries (by ID, name, Matrix ID, and role). Assignment endpoints now verify that the requested user belongs to the caller's organisation and that the underlying cases are visible to the caller before returning any task data. Revoked case access also removes corresponding tasks from assignment views and statistics. Admin access and the global directory (when the limit is disabled) are preserved.

cna.title: XSS in symfony/ux-icons via Text That Sanitized Icons Contain Unescaped: Incomplete Fix for CVE-2026-55877

descriptions.value:
The fix for CVE-2026-55877 (GHSA-6v8j-33hc-mv84) sanitizes the SVG of icons before they are rendered inline. When the sanitizer changes an icon, it writes the icon out again as HTML. HTML writes the content of some elements, like <style>, without escaping it. But inside an <svg>, browsers parse the content of a <style> element as markup. Escaped markup in such an element then becomes live in the page:

<path onclick="x"/><style xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"><img src=x onerror=alert(1)></style>

The event handler of the <path> element only makes the sanitizer change the icon. Depending on the version, this affects every <style> element, or the elements of the XHTML namespace, like <style>, <xmp> or <noembed>.

On 2.x, the elements of the XHTML namespace were also kept. An XHTML <form> or <base> element then becomes live where icons are parsed as XML, like in the Google Maps bridge of ux-map.

Applications are exposed when an attacker can influence the SVG of the icons they render. The sources are the same as for CVE-2026-55877, like local icon files and the responses of the Iconify API.

On 2.x, the sanitizer now writes icons out as XML, which escapes their text, and only keeps the elements of the SVG namespace. On 3.x, it now only keeps the elements of the SVG namespace.

@fastify/reply-from is a Fastify plugin that forwards an incoming HTTP request to an upstream server. In versions before 12.9.1, when the plugin forwards a request whose body is not written to the upstream connection, such as a GET, HEAD, or TRACE request that carried a body, or a request with a falsy JSON body, it still forwards the client's Content-Length header while sending no body. The upstream server then treats the bytes of the following request as the unfinished body, which an attacker can use to desynchronize the connection and smuggle a request. The issue is fixed in @fastify/reply-from 12.9.1, and users should upgrade to 12.9.1 or later.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Regular sync, pulls and feeds no longer edit

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Regular sync, pulls and feeds no longer edit
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces a privilege gate on organisation detail updates during sharing group capture. A new static context flag (captureRemote) is set by Feed and Server pull code paths to indicate whether the capture originates from an internal link. A new authorization check (__mayUpdateOrgDetails) permits overwriting organisation fields only when the operation is an internal sync or the acting user holds perm_site_admin or perm_sync_internal. All other sync, pull, and feed operations are restricted to matching or creating organisations without editing their existing details.
assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; the fix is applied to the main development branch and the exact version boundary is unknown.

PR:L assumes the attacker holds a sync user account (perm_sync) or controls an external feed/pull source; if the attacker must first compromise a feed, the effective privilege requirement could be higher.

VI:L assumes that overwriting organisation metadata (type, nationality, sector, contacts) constitutes a limited integrity impact; if downstream consumers rely on these fields for access decisions, the impact could be higher.
CAPEC-114 is selected as the closest available pattern; no CAPEC specifically models data-integrity abuse through a replication/sync channel, so the mapping is approximate.
The Co-Authored-By line credits Claude Opus 5.5 as a remediation developer; this is recorded as it appears in the commit metadata but the role is inferred from the co-authorship context.
AT:N assumes no special conditions on the target are needed beyond a standard MISP deployment with sync, pull, or feed functionality enabled.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In SharingGroup.php, a static $remoteCapture flag and captureRemote() wrapper are added; captureSG() now computes an $updateOrgDetails boolean via __mayUpdateOrgDetails() and passes it to captureSGOrgs(), which forwards it to Organisation::captureOrg() instead of the previous $force parameter. Feed.php wraps both downloadAndSaveEventFromFeed() and downloadFromFeedInitiator() in SharingGroup::captureRemote(false, ...). Server.php refactors pull() to detect the internal flag from the server record and wraps the actual pull in SharingGroup::captureRemote($internal, ...). A regression test class (OrganisationDetailsSyncScope) in tests/testregressions.py verifies that a plain sync user cannot modify org details, while an internal-sync user and a site admin can.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application; sync, pull, and feed operations occur over HTTP. AC:L: exploitation requires only pushing a sharing group with a newer modified date and a roster containing modified organisation details; no race conditions or special timing are needed. AT:N: no attack-target manipulation is required. PR:L: the attacker needs a low-privileged sync user account (perm_sync) or control of an external feed/pull source; no admin credentials are required. UI:N: no user interaction is needed; the overwrite occurs automatically during capture. VC:N: no confidential data is disclosed. VI:L: organisation metadata (type, nationality, sector, contacts) can be silently altered, a limited integrity impact. VA:N: no availability impact. SC/SI/SA:N: the impact is confined to the MISP instance's own organisation records with no cross-scope effect.

capecRationale.rationale: The application incorrectly adjusted the effective privilege level during sync, pull, and feed operations: external data sources and low-privileged sync users were granted the ability to modify organisation records that should have been restricted to site admins or internal-sync users. The attacker exploits this over-privileged code path by pushing a sharing group roster containing modified organisation details. CAPEC-114 is the closest match because the core issue is that the application's privilege model did not correctly scope what operations a given role or data source may perform on organisation records. Uncertainty: no CAPEC pattern specifically describes data-integrity abuse via a sync/replication channel, so CAPEC-114 is selected as the best available approximation.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The sharing group capture path performed organisation detail updates without checking whether the acting user or data source was authorized to modify those fields. Any sync user, external feed, or non-internal pull could overwrite organisation records, indicating a missing authorization check on the write operation.

The authorization model did not distinguish between creating/matching an organisation and editing its details during sync, pull, or feed operations. The privilege boundary between regular sync users and internal-sync/site-admin users was not enforced for organisation field updates.

descriptions.value: MISP contains an authorization flaw in the sharing group capture logic. When a sharing group is re-captured with a newer modified timestamp and an updated roster, the application unconditionally overwrote the type, nationality, sector, and contacts fields of every organisation listed in the roster, including the host organisation. This behaviour was reachable by any user holding the perm_sync role, and additionally by any external server pulled from or any feed fetched, because those operations execute with the privileges of the site administrator who initiated them. As a result, a low-privileged sync user or a malicious/compromised external feed or pull source could silently corrupt organisation records on the receiving MISP instance without any site-admin or internal-sync authorization. The vulnerability does not disclose data or affect availability; the impact is limited to integrity of organisation metadata (type, nationality, sector, contacts). The fix restricts organisation detail updates to internal sync operations (pulls over links flagged as internal, or senders holding perm_sync_internal) and site administrators; all other sync, pull, and feed operations may only match existing organisations by UUID or create new ones, without modifying their stored details.

cna.title: The Unanimous Strategy Grants access_control Rules When Only One of Their Roles Matches: Regression of CVE-2020-5275

descriptions.value:
With the unanimous access decision strategy, an access_control rule that lists several roles requires all of them. That's the behavior restored by the fix for CVE-2020-5275. Since Symfony 5.4, the access decision manager asked each voter once about all the attributes of a rule. RoleVoter grants access as soon as the user has one of the roles. So a user who had only one of these roles was granted access:

security:
    access_decision_manager:
        strategy: unanimous

- { path: ^/admin, roles: [ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_AUDITOR] }

supportingMedia.value:
With the `unanimous` access decision strategy, an `access_control` rule that lists several roles requires all of them. That's the behavior restored by the fix for CVE-2020-5275. Since Symfony 5.4, the access decision manager asked each voter once about all the attributes of a rule. `RoleVoter` grants access as soon as the user has one of the roles. So a user who had only one of these roles was granted access:

```yaml
security:
    access_decision_manager:
        strategy: unanimous
    access_control:
        - { path: ^/admin, roles: [ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_AUDITOR] }
```

Only attributes decided by the same voter were affected. For example, a role combined with `allow_if` still required both.

With the unanimous strategy, voters are asked about each attribute separately again, as before Symfony 5.4. Access is denied as soon as one of the attributes is denied.

descriptions.value: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions from 7.1.0 up to but not including 11.6.10, when the plugin is registered with websocket support enabled, it opens the upstream WebSocket connection with a header set built by the default header rewriter, which forwards the client cookie but never sets the upstream origin option, so the browser origin header is dropped while the authenticating cookie is forwarded. Many WebSocket servers defend against cross-site hijacking by checking the origin and treat a missing origin as a trusted non-browser client, so behind the proxy that check never sees the foreign origin. A malicious page visited by a logged-in user can therefore open a WebSocket through the proxy to an upstream that authenticates the handshake with a cookie, and read or send messages on the user's behalf. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later. As a workaround, provide a header rewriter that sets a correct origin, or validate the origin before the proxy.

cna.title: XSS in symfony/ux-icons via SVG Content That Browsers Parse as HTML: Incomplete Fix for CVE-2026-55877

descriptions.value:
The fix for CVE-2026-55877 (GHSA-6v8j-33hc-mv84) sanitizes the SVG of icons before they are rendered inline. Browsers parse an inline

, or . They then parse the rest of the icon as HTML, and they also parse the content of and <desc> elements as HTML. The sanitizer only checked icons as SVG, so an icon could contain markup that becomes live once parsed as HTML. For example, after a <p> element, a comment can end a <style> element early and add an <img> element with an event handler: <p/><style><!--</style><img src=1 onerror=alert(1)>--></style> In the same way, an icon could add a <base> element to the page, which changes where its relative links and forms go. It could also add a <meta> element that redirects the page. Comments were kept too, while browsers end a comment at <!--> or <!--->. The rest of such a comment then became live markup, even without any HTML element before it. Applications are exposed when an attacker can influence the SVG of the icons they render. The sources are the same as for CVE-2026-55877, like local icon files and the responses of the Iconify API. The sanitizer now removes comments and the elements that make browsers switch to HTML, and only keeps the text of <title> and <desc> elements. It also makes sure that markup in CDATA sections and attribute values can't end a <noscript> element around the icon.

FlowIntel contains multiple security flaws in its note variable resolution, chatbot API tooling, and AI report generation.

- Note variable references (e.g. cross-case or cross-task lookups) were resolved using the viewing user's privileges rather than the destination case's audience. An authenticated user with access to a shared or imported note could embed references to private cases, causing sensitive case data to be pulled into AI report requests, exports, and MISP sends without the referenced case's audience having granted read access.

- The chatbot API tool permitted the language model to invoke any FlowIntel API endpoint, including administrative routes and state-changing GET operations, without an allow-list or path validation. An attacker who can influence the model's instructions (e.g. via untrusted case content) could induce data modification or access restricted endpoints.

- AI report generation passed the Ollama bearer token and full case content as command-line arguments to a child process, exposing them in the system process table to any local user.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-126 Exploiting Incorrectly Implemented Authentication Schemes
CAPEC-12 Application Configuration Error

descriptions.description: CWE-200 Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

solutions.value: Three remediations are applied: (1) Note variable resolution now enforces an audience-based authorization check so that cross-case and cross-task references only expand when the destination case's assigned organisations can read the referenced case; (2) the chatbot API tool is restricted to an explicit allow-list of reviewed read-only and search operations, with administrative endpoints always blocked, path validation against injection and SSRF, and write operations gated behind an explicit CHATBOT_ALLOW_WRITES configuration flag; (3) AI report requests are delivered to the child process via a private anonymous temporary file on stdin instead of argv, keeping credentials and case content out of the process listing.

cna.title: @fastify/swagger-ui vulnerable to documentation authentication bypass via the unprotected /static route

descriptions.value: @fastify/swagger-ui is the plugin that serves Swagger UI documentation for Fastify applications. In versions 2.1.0 through 6.1.4, the authentication hooks that applications register to protect the documentation are applied to every route the plugin adds except the bundled static asset instance. When the option that serves bundled UI files from a local directory is enabled, that instance exposes every file in the directory without credentials, so a specification file an operator meant to keep behind the documentation login becomes reachable by an unauthenticated client who knows or guesses its name. Access is read-only and limited to files in that directory. The issue is fixed in @fastify/swagger-ui 6.1.5, which applies the same authentication hooks to the static asset route, and users should upgrade to 6.1.5 or later.

CAPEC-66 is the closest available mapping; no CAPEC specifically covers 'inconsistent authorization enforcement across multiple endpoints of the same application'.

The assumption that the attacker must belong to the same organization as the event creator (orgc_id match) is based on the existing perm_modify_org and perm_publish checks that were already present; the new check is an additional gate on top of those.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-66 Exploiting Incorrectly Configured Access Control

solutions.value: A shared authorization check (isProtectedFromSyncUser / assertNotProtectedFromSyncUser) was introduced in the Event model and enforced across all write paths. The check denies any non-internal, non-site-admin sync user from modifying a protected event through any route other than events/edit with a valid signature. The check is now invoked in the ACL component (modify, publish, tag), in the CryptographicKeys, Events, and Tags controllers, and in the Event, EventReport, Galaxy, and MispAttribute models, closing every previously unprotected write path.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains an authorization bypass affecting the event protection mechanism. In MISP, a protected event is designed to be modifiable only through the events/edit endpoint with a valid cryptographic signature. However, the protection check was enforced solely on that single route. All other write endpoints that operate on an event—attributes (add, edit, delete), objects (delete), events (populate, publish, unprotect, upload_sample, upload_analysis_file), tags (attach, detach), event reports (edit, delete), galaxy clusters (attach, detach), and cryptographic keys (add, delete)—lacked the equivalent check.

As a result, an authenticated user holding the sync permission (perm_sync) who is neither a site administrator nor an internal sync user (perm_sync_internal), and who belongs to the same organization as the event's creator (orgc_id), could modify, delete, or add data to a protected event without providing a valid signature. This included the ability to unprotect the event entirely, publish it to other instances, and add cryptographic signing keys that would subsequently permit signed edits, effectively nullifying the protection mechanism.

The vulnerability requires an authenticated sync user account within the event's creator organization. No user interaction or special network conditions are required; standard API calls to the affected endpoints are sufficient. The security impact is a loss of integrity over protected threat-intelligence events: an attacker can inject, alter, or remove attributes, objects, tags, reports, and galaxy cluster associations, and can remove the protection flag or add signing keys to enable persistent unauthorized modification.

cna.title: Validation bypass of Pydantic V1 dataclasses allowing extra data

descriptions.value: When extra data is allowed (extra=Extra.allow), providing a __pydantic_initialised__ key when validating a Pydantic V1 dataclass makes it considered as already validated, resulting in field values not being validated. The __init__() method of Pydantic V1 dataclasses stores all the provided keyword arguments in the instance __dict__ before validation, so a __pydantic_initialised__ keyword argument overrides the internal flag used to skip validation of already validated instances. As a result, data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted data into Pydantic V1 dataclasses allowing extra data. The issue was fixed in Pydantic 1.10.27. Users relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2 should upgrade to 2.14.2 or later.
