@symfony/stimulus-bridge lazy-controller-loader: arbitrary code execution via unsanitized Stimulus magic comments

descriptions.value:
The @symfony/stimulus-bridge npm package includes a Webpack loader called lazy-controller-loader that supports "magic comments" placed above a Stimulus controller import, for example /* stimulusFetch: 'lazy' */, to control lazy loading behavior. To read those options, the loader extracted the raw text of any stimulus* comment and evaluated it as JavaScript using Node's vm.runInNewContext(). The Node.js node:vm module is not a security sandbox, and a crafted comment can break out of the VM context using well-known techniques to run arbitrary Node.js code within the build process.

This is a build-time vulnerability: it does not affect browsers or end users. The code executes on the developer machine or CI/build server during a Webpack or Symfony Encore build. Realistic attack vectors include a malicious Stimulus controller introduced through a compromised dependency, or a pull request that triggers an automated CI build. An attacker who can get such a file into the build can read files and environment variables available to the build process, exfiltrate CI secrets, tamper with generated build artifacts, and run commands with the permissions of the build user.

The loader no longer evaluates comment content as JavaScript. It now parses each comment as an object expression using a real JavaScript parser and extracts only plain literal values. Any non-literal value, such as a function call, an identifier, or a sequence expression, is rejected and reported as a build error instead of being executed. Legitimate option values like 'lazy' and 'eager' continue to work without any changes required on the user's side.

cna.title: Tool result data shaped like a file is rebuilt as a file download or provider file reference when message history is reloaded

descriptions.value: When message history is serialized and loaded again, a tool result that contains a JSON object in the serialized shape of one of Pydantic AI's file types is rebuilt as that file. A third party who controls data a tool returns, such as a record that an MCP server or a function tool returns from an external system, can use this to make the application download a URL on its local network, or make the model provider read an s3:// object or uploaded file with the application's credentials. Applications are affected when tool results can contain third-party data, message history containing those results is serialized and loaded again (stored history, history a UI adapter holds on the server, or Temporal, DBOS or Prefect durable execution), and the model is one Pydantic AI downloads files for, one that honors force_download, or one whose provider resolves non-HTTP file URLs or uploaded files. History that a client submits through the Vercel AI or AG-UI adapter in the default mode is not affected. The issue is fixed in pydantic-ai and pydantic-ai-slim 1.107.10 and 2.66.0.

flowintel contains an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability affecting multiple endpoints that manage child records of cases and tasks. An authenticated user with access to one case or task could read or modify records belonging to other cases by supplying identifiers of those records directly in the request.

Affected operations include:
- Reading task notes, subtasks, and URL tools by referencing their IDs without verifying they belong to the authorized task
- Retrieving task assignees for a task belonging to a different case
- Editing or deleting timeline events and timeline event links belonging to another case
- Editing or removing case connectors belonging to another case
- Invoking connector module operations (MISP, generic connectors, worker calls) by combining an authorized case with a connector link from a different case

The root cause is that the application authorized the parent resource (case or task) in the URL but then fetched or operated on the child record independently without verifying the child's ownership relationship to the authorized parent.

Security impact: an authenticated user can exfiltrate sensitive threat intelligence data from cases they do not have access to, and can modify or delete timeline entries, connector configurations, and other records in unauthorized cases, leading to data integrity loss and potential disruption of incident response workflows.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0
CAPEC-1 Tamper with URLs

descriptions.description: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

solutions.value: The fix enforces ownership validation by requiring the authorized parent case or task ID in every core method that reads or writes child records. Before returning data or performing writes, each child record's case_id or task_id is explicitly compared against the resolved parent. Mismatched records are rejected with a 404 or 403 response. Connector module context building now verifies connector-to-case ownership before preparing module data, resolving credentials, or executing sync operations. Instance visibility checks are applied consistently across both web and API routes.

cna.title: Privilege Escalation via Directly Uploaded Integration Packages in Kibana

descriptions.value: An issue in Kibana allows Elasticsearch transforms in directly uploaded integration packages to run with Kibana's internal system identity instead of the installing user's privileges. A user with Integrations: All and Agent policies: All privileges in a single Kibana space could access or modify data they are not authorized to access, including agent policies from other spaces. This could disclose sensitive information or lead to command execution on managed Elastic Agent hosts.

supportingMedia.value: An issue in Kibana allows Elasticsearch transforms in directly uploaded integration packages to run with Kibana's internal system identity instead of the installing user's privileges. A user with Integrations: All and Agent policies: All privileges in a single Kibana space could access or modify data they are not authorized to access, including agent policies from other spaces. This could disclose sensitive information or lead to command execution on managed Elastic Agent hosts.

scenarios.value: Remote Command Execution on Elastic Agent via Direct Package Upload

configurations.value:
All of the following conditions must hold:
- The attacker has both Fleet Integrations: All and Agent policies: All privileges in at least one Kibana space.

workarounds.value: Restrict the combination of Fleet Integrations: All and Agent policies: All privileges to fully trusted administrators until Kibana is upgraded.

solutions.value: Upgrade Kibana versions 8.14.0 through 8.19.23 to 8.19.24.
Upgrade Kibana versions 9.0.0 through 9.4.9 to 9.4.10.
Upgrade Kibana versions 9.5.0 through 9.5.5 to 9.5.6.

For Kibana: Review and reinstall affected integration packages

Upgrading Kibana does not change the stored authorization of transforms in previously installed integration packages. Review directly uploaded and custom integration packages containing transforms. Uninstall affected packages whose transforms retain Kibana's internal system authorization, then reinstall any packages still needed after upgrading so their transforms use the installing user's privileges.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Pulls and feeds no longer update sharing

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Pulls and feeds no longer update sharing
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces a proper authorization check for remote capture operations. The captureRemote method now receives the full server context (or null for feeds) and stores both the internal flag and the remote organization identifier. A new __remoteMayUpdate method verifies that, for non-internal pulls, the remote organization is a member of the target sharing group (as owning org, in the SharingGroupOrg list, or via an all_orgs entry). For feeds (server is null), the update is always refused. When the check fails, the sharing group record is left unchanged while the pulled data still attaches to it, preserving data integrity without granting unauthorized metadata modification.

solutions.value: The fix introduces a proper authorization check for remote capture operations. The captureRemote method now receives the full server context (or null for feeds) and stores both the internal flag and the remote organization identifier. A new __remoteMayUpdate method verifies that, for non-internal pulls, the remote organization is a member of the target sharing group (as owning org, in the SharingGroupOrg list, or via an all_orgs entry). For feeds (server is null), the update is always refused. When the check fails, the sharing group record is left unchanged while the pulled data still attaches to it, preserving data integrity without granting unauthorized metadata modification.

descriptions.value: MISP contains an authorization flaw in the handling of remote pull and feed operations. When a non-internal pull or a feed processes incoming data and encounters an existing sharing group, the application did not verify that the remote server's organization was actually a member of that sharing group before allowing the group's metadata to be updated. The captureRemote mechanism previously stored only a boolean flag indicating whether the link was internal, and the authorization check in captureSGExisting relied solely on that flag. For non-internal pulls and feeds, the check was insufficient: a remote server whose organization was not a member of the target sharing group could still cause the group record to be modified (for example, altering the local flag, the modified timestamp, or other group properties). A feed, which has no associated server organization at all, could likewise trigger an update to an existing sharing group's metadata. The security impact is an integrity violation: an authenticated remote entity with sync or feed privileges can alter sharing group attributes that govern how data is distributed among organizations, potentially changing the local flag or other access-relevant properties of groups it does not belong to. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with the ability to initiate a pull or feed (a sync user or feed administrator) and a target sharing group that exists on the local instance. No unauthenticated access or user interaction is required.

cna.title: XSS in symfony/ux-icons via Attribute Names That the Sanitizer Reads Differently Than Browsers: Incomplete Fix for CVE-2026-55877

descriptions.value:
The fix for CVE-2026-55877 (GHSA-6v8j-33hc-mv84) sanitizes the SVG of icons before they are rendered inline. The checks matched attribute names as written in the icon, while browsers and the renderer read some names differently.

On 2.x, fromFile() keys the attributes of the root <svg> element by their local name. A handler like x:onload passed the check, and was then rendered as onload, which runs on load. HTML parsers also read attribute names case-insensitively, so a SMIL animation with ATTRIBUTENAME="href" could set a javascript: URL on a link. And an href in the XLink namespace under another prefix, like q:href, wasn't checked. On 3.x, the sanitizer writes it out as xlink:href, and XML parsers resolve the prefix on both branches.

Applications are exposed when an attacker can influence the SVG of the icons they render. The sources are the same as for CVE-2026-55877, like local icon files and the responses of the Iconify API.

The sanitizer now checks attributes by local name. It also finds the attributeName of animations in any case, and ignores the prefix of its value.

flowintel contains an authorization flaw in its user deletion functionality. Organization-scoped administrators (org admins) are able to delete platform-level administrator accounts through both the browser-based admin interface and the REST API.

The existing authorization logic verified that an org admin could only target users within their own organization, but it did not enforce the privilege hierarchy between organization admins and platform admins. As a result, an authenticated org admin could issue a deletion request against any platform-admin account belonging to the same organization, causing the target account, its sessions, and related records to be permanently removed.

Impact:
- Loss of platform-level administrative oversight
- Potential disruption of platform-wide management functions
- Removal of higher-privilege accounts that should be protected from lower-privilege roles

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0
CAPEC-126 Privilege Escalation

solutions.value: The fix introduces an explicit privilege-hierarchy check in both the browser and API deletion routes. Before any session invalidation or account deletion is performed, the system now verifies whether the target user holds platform-admin capability. If the requester is a pure organization admin and the target is a platform admin, the request is rejected with a 403 response, preserving the intended authorization boundary while leaving legitimate deletion workflows unaffected.

cna.title: Hawtio: hawtio-systems: quadratic redos in flightrecordingdownloadfacade request-uri pattern

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in Hawtio. An authenticated remote attacker can cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by sending a specially crafted request URI to monitored endpoints. The FlightRecordingDownloadFacade servlet filter uses an inefficient regular expression pattern that causes catastrophic backtracking when processing certain long requests. This issue leads to excessive CPU utilization, causing handling threads to hang and degrading service availability.

affected.product: Red Hat build of Apache Camel - HawtIO 4

workarounds.value:
Restrict network access to the Hawtio management console to trusted administrative networks or localhost, or enforce request URI length limits at a reverse proxy fronting the application.

1. Restrict port access using firewalld:
```
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-source=<ADMIN_SUBNET>
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --remove-port=<HAWTIO_PORT>/tcp
firewall-cmd --reload
```

2. If fronted by a reverse proxy (such as Apache HTTP Server or NGINX), configure request-line limits (for example, `LimitRequestLine` in Apache HTTP Server) to truncate or reject abnormally long request URIs before they reach Hawtio endpoints.

Caveats: Limiting network access restricts remote access exclusively to specified administrative IP ranges. Configuring reverse proxy length limits may reject legitimate requests that require long query parameters.

Warning: Reloading the firewall configuration via `firewall-cmd --reload` applies changes immediately and may temporarily terminate active management connections.

cna.title: CsvEncoder Nests Rows Once per Key Separator of a Header, Letting a Small CSV Payload Crash PHP

descriptions.value:
CsvEncoder::decode() splits each header cell on the key separator, . by default, and nests the decoded rows one level per separator, with no limit. PHP frees nested arrays recursively, so freeing data that is nested deeply enough overflows the C stack and crashes the process. With a stack of 8 MB, a CSV body of 448 KB is enough.

Each row also builds all the levels of its headers again. With a deep header, a CSV body of 2 KB made of short rows allocates more than 128 MB. A body of 1 MB keeps the CPU busy for 10 seconds or more.

Any code that decodes untrusted CSV with the Serializer is affected. From Symfony 7.4.0, this included every #[MapRequestPayload] argument that doesn't restrict acceptFormat, until 7.4.23 and 8.1.11 stopped decoding CSV payloads by default.

CSV headers can now be nested up to 512 levels, the default depth of json_decode(). Decoding also stops when the rows go through more than 16 header levels, or create more than 4 arrays, per byte of data. A header row of up to 5 levels always fits, whatever the rows contain. Beyond these limits, decode() throws a NotEncodableValueException, which #[MapRequestPayload] turns into a 400 response.

Flowintel's template repository subsystem did not adequately constrain file access to the configured repository base directory. Two related weaknesses existed:

- Repository registration and editing accepted arbitrary local paths without verifying they resolved inside the configured REPOSITORY_BASE_PATH, allowing an authenticated user to point a repository at any readable directory on the host.
- Manifest and template file lookups used normalized (non-canonical) path joins and a startswith-based guard that could be bypassed by symbolic links, permitting reads of files outside the intended repository.

An authenticated user with the ability to add or edit a template repository could therefore cause the application to read and return the contents of arbitrary files readable by the service account, including configuration files, credentials, or other sensitive data.

Affected: Flowintel versions prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-126 Path Traversal

descriptions.description: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')
CWE-59 Improper Link Resolution Before File Access ('Link Following')

solutions.value: The fix introduces canonical (realpath-based) path resolution and enforces that every repository root and every child file or directory resolves within the configured REPOSITORY_BASE_PATH using os.path.commonpath. All code paths that previously performed raw os.path.join or normpath operations (registration, editing, discovery scan, entry scan, manifest read, and template file read) now go through the new validated helpers. Scans that encounter an escaping path roll back any partial database updates and return an error, preventing partial state corruption.

cna.title: Org.keycloak:keycloak-services: org.keycloak:keycloak-common: uma uri suffix matching authorization bypass

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When evaluating access permissions, Keycloak Authorization Services improperly matches resource paths containing wildcard file extensions by evaluating only the file extension suffix and ignoring configured path prefixes. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by requesting a restricted resource that shares a file extension with a more permissive resource, leading to an authorization bypass and unintended access to protected data.

workarounds.value:
Avoid using extension wildcard patterns in Keycloak Authorization Services resource definitions.

Review configured resource URIs within the Keycloak administration console under Clients > [Client] > Authorization > Resources. Replace any URI pattern relying on extension suffix wildcards (for example, `/public/*.json`) with explicit path definitions or standard directory wildcard patterns (such as `/public/*`).

Caveat: Modifying resource URI matching patterns may alter authorization policy evaluation and require aligning client requests or application routing with the revised resource definitions.

descriptions.value:
flowintel contains a vulnerability in the case and task classification usage endpoints that allows authenticated users to view classification data associated with cases they do not have permission to access.

The affected endpoints, which provide lists of used taxonomies, tags, galaxies, clusters, and custom tags, did not properly enforce object-level access controls. While the endpoints required authentication, they failed to filter the returned data based on the requesting user's visibility permissions for the underlying cases. This allowed any authenticated user to enumerate classification usage across all cases, including private or restricted cases belonging to other organizations or users.

This issue could lead to the disclosure of sensitive information, such as the existence of specific cases, the types of threats or indicators associated with them, and the relationships between different classification elements, potentially aiding an attacker in reconnaissance or targeting.

Affected versions: < 4.1.0
CAPEC-126 Accessing Functionality Not Properly Restricted by ID

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by enforcing object-level access controls on the classification usage endpoints. The fix ensures that the authenticated user's identity is passed to the data retrieval functions, which then filter the results to include only classifications associated with cases that the user is authorized to view. This prevents the disclosure of classification data from private or restricted cases to unauthorized users.

descriptions.value:
flowintel contains a log injection vulnerability in its case history (audit log) subsystem. The case history is stored as a line-delimited file where each line represents a single event attributed to a specific user. User-controlled fields, including user names, event messages, and case titles used during case merging, were written to the history file without sanitizing embedded line separator characters (such as carriage return, line feed, vertical tab, form feed, and Unicode line/paragraph separators).

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify case history entries could embed line separators in these fields. Upon writing, the injected separators would split a single intended entry into multiple lines, each of which the history format interprets as a distinct event. This allows an attacker to forge additional history entries attributed to arbitrary users, corrupting the audit trail and undermining the integrity of case records.

The vulnerability affects the case history append and merge operations. No authentication bypass or privilege escalation is required beyond normal case-management access.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-66 HTTP Request/Response Splitting

descriptions.description: CWE-117 Improper Output Neutralization for Logs

solutions.value: The fix introduces a sanitization helper that replaces all splitlines()-recognized line separator characters (CR, LF, VT, FF, file/group/record separators, NEL, Unicode line and paragraph separators) with a single space before any user-authored content is written to the case history file. The helper is applied to the author name, the event message, and the case title during merge operations, ensuring each history entry remains on exactly one line and cannot be split into forged entries.

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Revoked keys no longer sign protected events,
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix enforces key revocation in signature validation by skipping any key whose revoked flag is set before attempting PGP verification. It corrects the key-sync query to retrieve all stored keys (not just the first), ensures revocations are persisted and never lifted by a subsequent push, properly removes keys absent from the pushed list, and computes a fingerprint for entries that lack one so they match their stored counterpart. A signed protected event with no keys is now refused with a proper error response instead of an unhandled 500.
assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; all versions prior to this commit are assumed affected.
The attacker is assumed to be an authenticated sync user with permission to add or edit protected events; unauthenticated exploitation is not evidenced.
The secondary integrity impact (SI:H) assumes a multi-instance MISP sync deployment; in a single-instance deployment the secondary impact may be lower.
CAPEC-124 is selected as the closest available pattern; no CAPEC specifically covers cryptographic key revocation bypass, so the mapping is approximate.
The Co-Authored-By line for Claude Opus 5.5 is treated as a tool credit; it is unclear whether this represents AI-assisted development or a placeholder.
The 500-error issue (signed event without keys) is treated as a minor robustness defect subsumed under the primary revocation-bypass vulnerability rather than a separate issue.
CVSS AT:N is used because the only options are N or P; the attacker does perform active interaction (submitting a signed event), but no special passive observation position is required.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In CryptographicKey.php: (1) validateProtectedEvent() now checks $supplied_key['revoked'] and continues (skips) if set, before calling verifySignature(). (2) captureCryptographicKeyUpdate() changes find('first') to find('all') so all stored keys are considered. (3) A pre-loop computes a fingerprint via extractKeyData() for pushed entries that lack one. (4) The revocation branch is restructured: it now saves only the revoked flag (id + revoked=1) and the condition uses !empty() checks to ensure a revocation is never lifted. (5) The $existingKey array access is flattened (removing the nested 'CryptographicKey' key). (6) deleteAll() is guarded with an empty check on $toRemove. (7) The no-keys error message includes the event UUID and the log entry uses event ID 0. In tests/testregressions.py: a new ProtectedEventKeyRevocation test class adds nine regression tests covering revoked-key rejection, unrevoked-key acceptance, revocation persistence, non-lifting of revocations, key removal, fingerprint-less entry match
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application; the attacker interacts via the HTTP API. AC:L: exploitation requires only signing an event with a revoked key and submitting it; no race conditions or special timing. AT:N: no special targeting beyond network reachability to the MISP instance. PR:L: the attacker must be an authenticated sync user with permission to add/edit protected events. UI:N: no victim interaction is required. VC:N: no confidentiality impact is evident. VI:H: integrity is significantly impacted because revoked keys retain signing authority and revocations are not applied, undermining the trust chain for protected events. VA:N: the 500-error issue is minor and does not constitute a meaningful availability impact. SC:N: no secondary confidentiality impact. SI:H: in a multi-instance MISP sync network, events signed by revoked keys can propagate to peer instances, extending the integrity compromise. SA:N: no secondary availability impact.

capecRationale.rationale: The revoked-key state is an exceptional condition in the key lifecycle that the application failed to handle correctly during signature validation and key synchronization. The attacker exploits the system's failure to treat a revoked key as an exceptional (invalid) state. This is the closest CAPEC pattern; a more specific 'key revocation bypass' pattern does not exist in the CAPEC catalog, so CAPEC-124 is the best available match.

The key-sync path is vulnerable to manipulation of the pushed key list: by omitting keys or crafting entries without fingerprints, an attacker can prevent revocations from being applied or cause valid keys to be removed. This is a secondary attack vector enabled by the same code defects. The mapping is approximate because the primary issue is a logic flaw rather than direct parameter injection.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The signature verification routine validated the cryptographic signature but failed to verify the authenticity/validity of the signing key by checking its revocation status. A revoked key was treated as a valid signing authority, which is a failure to fully verify data authenticity.

The system accepted a revoked key as a valid credential for signing protected events, effectively failing to authenticate the signer's current authorization status. The key revocation mechanism was bypassed.

solutions.value: The fix enforces key revocation in signature validation by skipping any key whose revoked flag is set before attempting PGP verification. descriptions.value:
MISP, a threat intelligence sharing platform, contains a vulnerability in its cryptographic key management for protected (PGP-signed) events. Two related defects allow a revoked PGP key to remain effective for signing and validating protected events.

First, the validateProtectedEvent() method in the CryptographicKey model iterates over the event's stored cryptographic keys to verify a PGP signature but does not check the revoked flag on each key. A key explicitly marked as revoked is still used to validate signatures, meaning an entity whose key has been revoked can continue to sign protected events and have them accepted by the MISP instance.

Second, the captureCryptographicKeyUpdate() method, responsible for synchronizing the key list when a sync user edits a protected event, contained a query bug (find('first') instead of find('all')) that caused only the first stored key to be considered. As a result, revocations of additional keys were never persisted, keys absent from the pushed list were not removed, and entries lacking an explicit fingerprint were mismatched and incorrectly deleted. Additionally, the revocation logic did not enforce the invariant that a revocation, once stored, is never lifted by subsequent pushes.

A third minor issue: a signed protected event submitted without any cryptographic keys triggered an unhandled 500 error rather than a proper rejection response.

Preconditions: the attacker must be an authenticated sync user with permission to add or edit protected events on the MISP instance. The impact is that revoked keys retain signing authority, key revocations propagated by sync partners are silently dropped, and the integrity of the protected-event trust chain is compromised. In a multi-instance MISP deployment, events signed by revoked keys can propagate to other instances, extending the integrity impact across the sync network.

cna.title: Crun: crun: tmpcopyup follows a second path lookup and copies image files onto the host

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in crun. When copying files onto a tmpfs mounted with tmpcopyup, crun opens the destination a second time by name. A container that shares a writable volume with the container being created can change that path between the two lookups, so crun copies image files onto host files, including files under /proc/sys.

workarounds.value: Do not give an untrusted container a writable volume that is also the destination of a tmpcopyup tmpfs. That includes Podman --read-only when the image symlinks /var/tmp into the volume, and --tmpfs pointed into the shared volume.

credits.value: This issue was discovered by Giuseppe Scrivano (Red Hat).

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel, a threat intelligence case management platform, contains an information disclosure vulnerability in its case serialization logic. When a case is rendered via the REST API or browser views, all connector instances associated with that case were included in the response regardless of the requesting user's permissions.

This means that any authenticated user with read access to a case could observe connector metadata belonging to other users (personal-scope connectors) or other organizations (org-scope connectors), including connector URLs, descriptions, UUIDs, and potentially embedded API credentials.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user account with at least read access to the affected case
- The case must have connector instances attached that belong to other users or organizations

Impact:
- Disclosure of personal connector endpoints and credentials of other users
- Disclosure of organization-scoped connector metadata across organizational boundaries
- Enumeration of connector infrastructure (URLs, UUIDs, descriptions) not intended for the viewer

Affected versions: < 4.1.0
CAPEC-1 Software Feature Discovery

descriptions.description: CWE-668 Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere

solutions.value: The fix introduces viewer-scoped authorization checks during case serialization. Connector instances are now filtered based on the acting user's permissions: administrators and assigned case-administrators retain full visibility, while regular users only see connectors whose sharing scope (personal, org, or global) grants them access. When no authenticated user context is available, connector metadata is omitted entirely. Credential-use checks for module execution remain unchanged.

cna.title: @fastify/rate-limit vulnerable to failed-login limit bypass via a race condition in the documented flow

descriptions.value: @fastify/rate-limit is the rate-limiting plugin for the Fastify web framework. Starting in version 11.1.0, the plugin documented a manual flow for limiting failed login attempts that peeks at the limiter, runs the password check, and consumes a slot only on failure. Because the peek and the consume are two separate store operations with the password check in between, concurrent requests can all pass the peek before any slot is consumed, so in versions 11.1.0 through 11.2.2 a burst of requests runs far more failed attempts than the configured limit, and the sequential path also allowed one attempt more than configured. The default per-request limiter is not affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/rate-limit 11.3.0, which makes the manual flow atomic by reserving a slot in a single operation and refunding it only on success, and users should upgrade to 11.3.0 or later.

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel contained a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) vulnerability affecting fourteen web routes that performed destructive or state-changing operations. The affected routes accepted HTTP GET requests in addition to (or instead of) POST, which bypassed the Flask-WTF CSRF token validation that is only enforced on non-GET requests.

The vulnerable operations included:
- Case deletion and case merging
- Organisation removal from a case
- Task deletion (case and template)
- Case template and note template deletion
- Connector, connector instance, and icon deletion
- Custom tag deletion and status change
- Taxonomy and galaxy status changes

An attacker who could induce an authenticated user to follow a crafted link or load a page containing a cross-site navigation (e.g., an image tag or redirect) could trigger any of these destructive actions using the victim's session cookie, without the victim's explicit consent or awareness. No special privileges beyond a valid authenticated session with the appropriate role (editor or admin) were required on the victim's account.

Security impact: unauthorized deletion or modification of cases, tasks, templates, connectors, icons, custom tags, taxonomies, and galaxies belonging to the victim or the organisation, resulting in loss of data integrity.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0
CAPEC-124 Cross-Site Request Forgery

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by restricting all fourteen affected web routes to accept only POST requests, ensuring that Flask-WTF's CSRF token validation is enforced. versions.version: Synchronet BBS, versions 3.20b to 3.21e, with the SSH service enabled.

descriptions.value: Synchronet BBS, in versions 3.20b to 3.21e, contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the answer() function when processing the terminal attribute of the SSH service. The call to cryptGetAttributeString() does not limit the copy to the size of the destination buffer, of which 41 bytes are used. An unauthenticated remote client can send a TERM value of up to 64 bytes and overwrite adjacent fields of the session object. If the SSH service is enabled, this tampering can cause connection threads to be blocked for an extended period, even after the client has disconnected. By exhausting the available sockets, the attacker can prevent new connections and cause a denial of service requiring the software to be restarted.

cna.title: Quadratic time and memory multi-host URL validation

descriptions.value:
Validating an untrusted URL with a long scheme and many hosts into a multi-host URL field (e.g. PostgresDsn) takes quadratic time and memory: an input of about a hundred kilobytes takes around a gigabyte of memory to validate.

The parse_multihost_url() function (in pydantic-core/src/validators/url.rs) parses each host separately, prepending the whole URL prefix (including the scheme) to every one of them. As the scheme can be arbitrarily long, and is parsed and stored once per host, both time and memory grow quadratically with the input size. Allowed schemes (e.g. postgres for PostgresDsn) are only checked after parsing, so they don't prevent the issue.

The issue was fixed in commit b4028f9d87e34750e53be0ba011d70f3c0fcc94e.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into multi-host URL fields (PostgresDsn, MongoDsn, NatsDsn, or custom types built on MultiHostUrl).

Summary

Validating an untrusted URL with a long scheme and many hosts into a multi-host URL field (e.g. PostgresDsn) takes quadratic time and memory: an input of about a hundred kilobytes takes around a gigabyte of memory to validate.

Details

The parse_multihost_url() function (in pydantic-core/src/validators/url.rs) parses each host separately, prepending the whole URL prefix (including the scheme) to every one of them (L644-L649):

let extra_urls: Vec<Url> = hosts
    .iter()
    .map(|host| {
        let reconstructed_url = format!("{prefix}{host}");
        parse_url(&reconstructed_url, input, strict)
    })
    .collect::<ValResult<_>>()?;

As the scheme can be arbitrarily long, and is parsed and stored once per host, both time and memory grow quadratically with the input size. Allowed schemes (e.g. postgres for PostgresDsn) are only checked after parsing, so they don't prevent the issue.

The issue was fixed in commit b4028f9d87e34750e53be0ba011d70f3c0fcc94e.

Impact

Denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into multi-host URL fields (PostgresDsn, MongoDsn, NatsDsn, or custom types built on MultiHostUrl).

descriptions.value:
flowintel is a case management application that enforces an approval workflow for tasks in privileged cases. Tasks in such cases are required to start in a Requested status, meaning they must receive explicit approval before becoming active.

A logic flaw in the task-creation path allowed tasks to be initialized with a Created status (bypassing the approval step) in two scenarios:

- When a task was created from a template and no acting user was supplied, the privileged-case check was skipped entirely, leaving the task in Created status.
- When a case was created from a template, all copied tasks were unconditionally assigned the Created status regardless of the case's privileged designation.

An authenticated user with the ability to create tasks from templates or to instantiate cases from templates could therefore place tasks directly into an active state within privileged cases, circumventing the intended approval gate. This may expose restricted case content or permit actions that should require supervisory sign-off.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-108 Parameter Tampering

solutions.value: The approval-workflow enforcement for privileged cases is now applied unconditionally at task creation time. The privileged-case check no longer depends on the presence of an acting user, and template-based case creation explicitly assigns the configured Requested status to tasks when the target case is privileged. Ordinary (non-privileged) cases retain the default Created status, preserving existing behavior.

descriptions.value: In JetBrains Datalore before 2026.4.1 improper authorization allowed notebook viewers to read attached environment variable values

Flowintel contains a privilege escalation vulnerability in its Matrix relay (bot) integration. When the relay forwarded API requests on behalf of a represented user, the authorization and permission checks evaluated the relay bot's elevated role while the request handlers acted as the lower-privileged represented user. This mismatch allowed users with restricted roles (e.g., Read Only) to perform write operations, directory lookups, calendar modifications, assignment changes, template creation, and import actions they were not authorized to perform.

Additionally, relay authority was determined by matching editable user profile fields (name and email) rather than a protected, non-spoofable identifier. An ordinary user who modified their profile to match the expected bot name could be recognized as the trusted relay, enabling impersonation of the bot and potential access to its elevated privileges.

Preconditions:
- A valid Flowintel user account with a restricted role (e.g., Read Only)
- Access to the Matrix relay integration or the ability to send API requests with the relay's API key and a MATRIX-ID header
- For the impersonation vector: ability to edit one's own profile name fields

Security impact:
- Unauthorized write operations by users with read-only or otherwise restricted permissions
- Potential impersonation of the trusted relay bot by ordinary users
- Bypass of organization-level access controls and role-based restrictions
- Unauthorized modification of cases, tasks, calendar events, templates, and user directory entries

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0
CAPEC-126 Exploiting Incorrectly Adjusted Privileges

solutions.value: The fix introduces a protected, non-editable is_bot database marker to identify trusted relay accounts, replacing the previous reliance on editable name and email fields. The user resolution function now returns the same principal for both authentication/permission checks and request handlers, ensuring that a represented user's actual role governs all operations. Relay requests without a valid MATRIX-ID, bot-to-bot requests, and ordinary API keys carrying a MATRIX-ID header are all refused. New bot accounts are assigned the Read Only role instead of Admin. Only administrators can edit or delete registered bot accounts, preventing OrgAdmins from resetting bot credentials. An operator script (bin/register_matrix_bot.py) provides explicit, ID-based bot registration without relying on profile fields.

descriptions.value:
Flowintel contains multiple SSO identity and organisation trust boundary violations that collectively allow account takeover, privilege escalation, and unauthorized access to private case data.

- Keycloak SSO accepted unverified email claims, and all SSO providers (Keycloak, Entra ID, SimpleSAML) could resolve a claimed email address to an existing account that was created via a different sign-in method, enabling cross-provider account collision and unauthorized access to another user's account and data.

- Entra ID role mapping relied on group display names, which tenant members could duplicate by creating a group with the same name as a privileged group (e.g. FlowintelAdmin), resulting in unauthorized role escalation.

- SSO provisioning reused organisations whose display names matched user-controlled profile names, granting the new SSO user access to that organisation's private cases without explicit administrator assignment.

- Case sharing via the API resolved organisations by name using a first-match query, so ambiguous names could silently resolve to the wrong organisation.

Preconditions: an attacker must have a valid SSO identity (Keycloak, Entra ID, or SimpleSAML) or be a member of the relevant Entra tenant. No local administrator access is required.

Security impact: unauthorized access to private case data, privilege escalation to Editor or higher roles, and account takeover across authentication providers.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-126 Exploiting Incorrectly Handled Edge Cases

descriptions.description: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

solutions.value: The fix enforces strict identity and organisation trust boundaries across all SSO providers. Keycloak now requires a verified email claim and no longer falls back to preferred_username. A new shared identity-resolution function rejects any email that maps to an account registered under a different sign-in provider, preventing cross-provider account collision. Entra ID role mapping now requires configured group object IDs (UUIDs) instead of display names, eliminating the name-duplication escalation vector. Default organisation creation always allocates a new organisation rather than reusing one by name match. Case sharing via the API now rejects ambiguous organisation names and requires an explicit organisation ID.

cna.title: Keycloak: org.keycloak:keycloak-saml-adapter-core: org.keycloak:keycloak-saml-core: saml logoutrequest signature validation accepts a signed assertion nested in extensions in place of a signature on the request

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in Keycloak. This vulnerability allows an authenticated remote attacker to cause a denial of service by terminating active sessions of arbitrary users. When processing Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) documents that lack a root signature, Keycloak accepts the request as long as any assertion within the document is signed, without verifying its context or placement. An attacker holding a validly signed assertion can embed it into an unsigned logout request for another user, causing Keycloak to accept the forged request and terminate the victim's session.

flowintel contains multiple related flaws that allow an authenticated attacker to inject arbitrary HTML or script into pages viewed by other users.

- Timeline rendering: the timeline library's autolinking feature rewrote already-sanitised case notes and imported MISP attribute values into generated HTML link elements. Crafted text containing quote characters could break out of the generated attribute context, altering the surrounding markup and enabling script execution in the victim's browser.

- Search highlighting: the highlight injection logic used a regular expression to locate text between angle brackets and spliced <mark> elements into the resulting string. Because the pattern could match inside HTML attribute values, the rewrite could corrupt or inject content into attributes of already-sanitised markup, again leading to DOM-based cross-site scripting.

- Content-Type confusion: three analyser selection endpoints returned session-stored JSON strings with a text/html content type. A browser receiving such a response will parse and render the body as HTML, so any HTML or script embedded in the stored value is executed in the victim's context.

Preconditions: the attacker must be an authenticated user with the ability to create or import case content (notes, MISP attributes) containing specially crafted quote or angle-bracket sequences. The victim must subsequently open the affected case timeline, run a search, or request one of the selection endpoints.

Impact: successful exploitation yields DOM-based cross-site scripting in the victim's browser session, potentially allowing disclosure of case data, session manipulation, or execution of arbitrary actions under the victim's identity.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.
CAPEC-6 DOM Based XSS
CAPEC-1 XSS - Reflected

descriptions.description: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input in Web Page ('Cross-site Scripting')

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by eliminating the three injection paths: (1) autolinking is disabled on every timeline event so the library no longer rewrites sanitised HTML; (2) search and auto-highlight marks are now created by walking the DOM text nodes and setting textContent, which cannot alter existing attributes or split character entities; (3) the three selection endpoints now decode the stored JSON once, respond with application/json and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and reject malformed or excessively nested payloads with a 400 JSON error, preventing the browser from interpreting the body as HTML.

assumptions: The affected_version field in the metadata is recorded as '0', which is treated as a placeholder meaning all versions prior to 4.1.0 are affected; no earlier version boundary is specified.
The CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker needs an authenticated account to create the malicious case content; if unauthenticated import paths exist, PR could be N.

capecRationale.rationale: The primary exploitation path is client-side: attacker-controlled text (case notes, MISP values, search terms) is processed by JavaScript in the browser (TimelineJS autolinking, regex-based highlight injection) and the resulting DOM manipulation injects executable markup. The content-type confusion endpoint is a secondary vector but the dominant pattern is DOM-based script injection. CAPEC-6 is the closest standard attack pattern; the mapping is confident because the patch explicitly addresses client-side HTML rewriting of user-supplied content.

The three selection endpoints that returned session JSON as text/html could be leveraged as a reflected XSS vector if the session content is influenced by a prior request parameter. This is a secondary, less certain mapping; CAPEC-6 remains the primary pattern. Included because the content-type confusion path is a distinct mechanism from pure DOM manipulation.

x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N – the application is a web service reachable over the network. AC:L – crafting quote-bearing text in case notes or MISP attributes is straightforward; no race or special timing is needed. AT:N – no active attack or prior compromise is required beyond normal authenticated use. PR:L – the attacker needs an authenticated account to create or import the malicious content (endpoints are login_required). UI:A – the victim must actively open the case timeline, run a search, or request a selection endpoint for the injected markup to execute. VC:L – XSS can expose case data, session tokens, or other sensitive information visible in the browser. VI:L – the attacker can modify displayed content or trigger actions in the victim's session. VA:N – no evidence of denial-of-service impact beyond the nested-JSON guard. SC:N – no cross-component or cross-origin impact is demonstrated. SI:L – other authenticated users viewing the same case could be affected by the stored malicious content. SA:N – no elevation of security authority is indicated.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The vulnerability is remediated by eliminating the three injection paths: (1) autolinking is disabled on every timeline event so the library no longer rewrites sanitised HTML; (2) search and auto-highlight marks are now created by walking the DOM text nodes and setting textContent, which cannot alter existing attributes or split character entities; (3) the three selection endpoints now decode the stored JSON once, respond with application/json and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and reject malformed or excessively nested payloads with a 400 JSON error, preventing the browser from interpreting the body as HTML.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In case_history.js and timeline_view.js, an autolink: false property is added to each TimelineJS event object to suppress linkification. In smart-render.js, the previous regex-based string replacement (html.replace(/>([^<]*)</g, ...)) is replaced with a DOM TreeWalker that iterates text nodes, builds <mark> elements via document.createElement and textContent, and splices them into a DocumentFragment, preserving all existing attributes and entities. A new count_html_matches helper counts matches across text nodes. The plain-text fallback branches that performed raw regex replacement on escaped strings are removed. In misp_modules.py, a new _selected_json_response helper decodes the session value with json.loads, wraps it in jsonify, sets X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and returns a 400 JSON error on TypeError, ValueError, or RecursionError. The three get_*_selected endpoints are updated to call this helper instead of returning the raw session string.

descriptions.value: A heap-based buffer overflow was found in Corosync's Totem SRP membership commit token handling. The sanity check for memb_commit_token messages validates only minimum length and address-entry counts, not an upper bound against the fixed commit_token_storage buffer. A network-adjacent attacker who can deliver a crafted oversized commit token to a node in the GATHER membership state may overflow the heap-allocated totemsrp instance, leading to memory corruption and denial of service.

cna.title: Quadratic time timedelta validation in Pydantic V1

descriptions.value:
Validating an untrusted ISO 8601 duration string into a timedelta field with Pydantic V1 takes quadratic time: an input of a few dozen kilobytes takes seconds to validate.

The iso8601_duration_re regular expression used to parse ISO 8601 durations (in pydantic/datetime_parse.py) contains an unescaped ".", which also matches digits. On a string of digits, the repeated groups overlap and the regex engine backtracks in quadratic time.

The issue was fixed in commit 62791e66a9f8f118e465ed760c9e2ede9ae3055e. Users relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2 should upgrade to 2.14.2 or later.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into timedelta fields.

supportingMedia.value:
Summary

Validating an untrusted ISO 8601 duration string into a timedelta field with Pydantic V1 takes quadratic time: an input of a few dozen kilobytes takes seconds to validate.

Details

The iso8601_duration_re regular expression used to parse ISO 8601 durations (in pydantic/datetime_parse.py) contains an unescaped ., which also matches digits:

iso8601_duration_re = re.compile(
    r'^(?P<sign>[-+]?)'
    r'P'
    r'(?:(?P<days>\d+(.\d+)?)D)?'
    r'(?:T'
    r'(?:(?P<hours>\d+(.\d+)?)H)?'
    r'(?:(?P<minutes>\d+(.\d+)?)M)?'
    r'(?:(?P<seconds>\d+(.\d+)?)S)?'
    r')?'
    r'$'
)

On a string of digits, the repeated groups overlap and the regex engine backtracks in quadratic time.

The issue was fixed in commit 62791e66a9f8f118e465ed760c9e2ede9ae3055e.

If you are relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2, upgrade to V2.14.2 or later.

Impact

Denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into timedelta fields.

cna.title: Live Components Configured With a Custom Route Can Still Be Reached Through the Default Route

descriptions.value:
#[AsLiveComponent(route: '...')] makes a live component send its requests to another route. The documentation suggests it so that the component lives under a specific firewall, for example. The default /_components/{_live_component}/{_live_action} route still served the component, though. A request to it rendered the component and ran its actions outside the firewall and the access rules of the configured route.

The request needs props signed by the application, which a page that rendered the component provides. Controller attributes on the component, like #[IsGranted], still applied.

A live component is now only served by the route it is configured with.

descriptions.value:
flowintel contains a CSV injection vulnerability in its audit log CSV export functionality. Attacker-influenced text recorded in audit logs could be interpreted as spreadsheet formulas when an administrator opened the exported CSV file in a spreadsheet application.

The vulnerable behavior allowed an attacker who could influence audit log content (for example by generating network traffic that is captured and logged) to embed formula-like strings (such as =CMD() or =HYPERLINK()) into audit entries. When the resulting CSV export was opened in a spreadsheet application, these strings could be executed as formulas, potentially leading to data exfiltration, data manipulation, or execution of further malicious actions within the spreadsheet context.

Preconditions:
- An attacker must be able to influence content that is recorded in flowintel audit logs.
- An administrator or user must export the audit logs to CSV and open the file in a spreadsheet application that interprets formulas.

Security impact:
- Potential information disclosure from the spreadsheet or linked resources.
- Potential integrity impact on data within the spreadsheet application.
- No direct compromise of the flowintel application itself.

Affected version: <4.1.0

cna.title: Storage-location Disclosure in Elasticsearch ES|QL Query Responses

descriptions.value: Elasticsearch ES|QL query responses can disclose dataset storage locations and provider identity details to users who are allowed to query a dataset but cannot read its definition. Storage paths and storage-client error text can appear in read-failure messages or query-profile plan strings. An authenticated dataset reader can obtain this information without permission to view the dataset configuration. This issue does not disclose stored credentials or the dataset contents beyond the caller's query access.

flowintel contains an authorization bypass in the file-to-note conversion feature for case tasks. When a task is in a restricted workflow state (Requested, Rejected, or Request Review) within a privileged case, the conversion endpoint did not enforce elevated role requirements. Any authenticated user with basic case membership (e.g., editor or queuer) could invoke the conversion action, causing the system to read the attached file contents and create a note on the restricted task.

This bypasses the intended workflow restriction that only Admin, Case Admin, or Queue Admin roles may modify tasks in those states. An attacker with a low-privilege account in a privileged case could:
- Extract file contents into note format, potentially circumventing file-level access controls
- Create unauthorized notes that alter the task's note count, modification timestamp, and case history
- Disrupt the review/approval workflow on restricted tasks

The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with at least editor-level access to the affected case and a task in one of the restricted states.

Additionally, a null-check for the task object was added to prevent processing when the task target does not exist, returning a 404 response. Audit logging is recorded on denial.

cna.title: @fastify/middie vulnerable to path-scoped middleware bypass via request path matching mismatches

descriptions.value: @fastify/middie is the middleware engine for the Fastify web framework. In versions up to and including 9.3.7, middie matches path-scoped middleware against its own reading of the request path, which can differ from the path Fastify's router uses to dispatch the request. When the two disagree, the router can route a request to a handler covered by a middleware mount while middie skips that middleware, so an unauthenticated client reaches a handler that an authentication, authorization, or rate-limiting middleware was meant to protect, with no special configuration required. The mismatch is triggered by empty parameter or wildcard values, request targets that do not begin with a slash, and literal percent characters in a mount path. The issue is fixed in @fastify/middie 9.3.8, and users should upgrade to 9.3.8 or later.

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Refresh alert ownership scope on duplicate

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Refresh alert ownership scope on duplicate
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix ensures that on every duplicate alert update, the ownership and visibility scope fields are unconditionally refreshed from the current connector scope, regardless of the alert's review status. This prevents alerts from retaining a stale, potentially broader visibility scope after the connector's scope has been narrowed or reassigned.
assumptions: The affected version range is not precisely specified in the patch metadata; the affected_version field contains '0' which is treated as a placeholder. All versions prior to commit c158e1bd are assumed affected.
The CAPEC-10 mapping is the closest available match but the vulnerability is more accurately described as a stale-state authorization defect rather than an active exploitation of trust relationships.

The severity of the confidentiality impact (VC:L) assumes that the exposed alert content is sensitive but that the exposure is limited to a subset of alerts whose scope changed; if all alerts are affected or contain highly sensitive data, VC could be rated Higher.
The platform is assumed to be a multi-tenant or multi-organization security alerting system where visibility scoping is a core authorization mechanism.
No evidence of active exploitation or public PoC was found in the patch or metadata.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/alerting/alerting_core.py, within the _update_existing_alert function, two lines were added before the terminal-review-status conditional block: existing.owner_user_id and existing.owner_org_id are now assigned from the normalized incoming data on every duplicate update. Previously these fields were only set during initial alert creation and were not refreshed when a duplicate alert was ingested, leaving the stale scope in place.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N - the platform is network-accessible. AC:L - the vulnerability is inherent in the duplicate-update code path; no special race or timing is needed. AT:N - no manipulation of the attack target is required. PR:L - an authenticated user with prior access to the alert is needed. UI:N - no user interaction beyond normal platform use. VC:L - confidential alert data is exposed to users outside the intended scope, but only for alerts affected by a scope change. VI:N, VA:N - no integrity or availability impact. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N - no secondary impacts. The overall severity is moderate: limited to a subset of alerts whose scope changed, requiring prior legitimate access.

capecRationale.rationale: The closest plausible attack pattern is leveraging a trusted relationship: a user or organization that previously had legitimate access to an alert (because it was within their scope) retains that access after the scope should have been narrowed. The attacker leverages the stale trust/visibility binding. This mapping is uncertain because the vulnerability is more of a stale-state authorization bug than an active exploitation of trust, but CAPEC-10 is the best available match for unauthorized access via a previously valid relationship.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The alert resource remains exposed to a broader set of users/organizations (the wrong sphere) because the ownership/visibility fields are not updated when the connector scope changes. The resource is accessible to entities outside its intended authorization boundary.

The system fails to enforce the current authorization scope on duplicate updates, effectively missing the authorization check that would restrict visibility to the correct set of users and organizations.

solutions.value: The fix ensures that on every duplicate alert update, the ownership and visibility scope fields are unconditionally refreshed from the current connector scope, regardless of the alert's review status. This prevents alerts from retaining a stale, potentially broader visibility scope after the connector's scope has been narrowed or reassigned.

descriptions.value:
FlowIntel contains an authorization flaw in its duplicate alert ingestion logic. When a duplicate alert is received and its content is updated, the ownership and visibility scope fields (owner user and owner organization) were not refreshed to reflect the connector's current scope. As a result, an alert that was originally created under a broader visibility scope retained that broader scope even after the connector's scope was narrowed or changed.

This means that users or organizations that should no longer have visibility into a given alert could continue to access it, because the stale ownership fields were never updated during the duplicate-update path. The issue affected all duplicate updates, including those involving alerts in terminal review states and those recovered from uniqueness conflicts.

Security impact:
- Unauthorized disclosure of security alert content to users or organizations outside the intended visibility scope.
- Stale access persists indefinitely until the alert is independently re-scoped or deleted.

Affected version: <4.1.0.

descriptions.description: CWE-668 Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere

cna.title: spi: spi-fsl-lpspi: fix teardown order issue (UAF)

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

spi: spi-fsl-lpspi: fix teardown order issue (UAF)

There is a teardown order issue in the driver. The SPI controller is
registered using devm_spi_register_controller(), which delays
unregistration of the SPI controller until after the fsl_lpspi_remove()
function returns.

As the fsl_lpspi_remove() function synchronously tears down the DMA
channels, a running SPI transfer triggers the following NULL pointer
dereference due to use after free:

| fsl_lpspi 42550000.spi: I/O Error in DMA RX
| Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual address 0000000000000000
[...]
| Call trace:
|  fsl_lpspi_dma_transfer+0x260/0x340 [spi_fsl_lpspi]
|  fsl_lpspi_transfer_one+0x198/0x448 [spi_fsl_lpspi]
|  spi_transfer_one_message+0x49c/0x7c8
|  __spi_pump_transfer_message+0x120/0x420
|  __spi_sync+0x2c4/0x520
|  spi_sync+0x34/0x60
|  spidev_message+0x20c/0x378 [spidev]
|  spidev_ioctl+0x398/0x750 [spidev]
[...]

Switch from devm_spi_register_controller() to spi_register_controller() in
fsl_lpspi_probe() and add the corresponding spi_unregister_controller() in
fsl_lpspi_remove().

cna.title: nvdimm/bus: Fix potential use after free in asynchronous initialization

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvdimm/bus: Fix potential use after free in asynchronous initialization

Dingisoul with KASAN reports a use after free if device_add() fails in
nd_async_device_register().

Commit b6eae0f61db2 ("libnvdimm: Hold reference on parent while
scheduling async init") correctly added a reference on the parent device
to be held until asynchronous initialization was complete.  However, if
device_add() results in an allocation failure the ref count of the
device drops to 0 prior to the parent pointer being accessed.  Thus
resulting in use after free.

The bug bot AI correctly identified the fix.  Save a reference to the
parent pointer to be used to drop the parent reference regardless of the
outcome of device_add().

cna.title: mm/userfaultfd: fix hugetlb fault mutex hash calculation

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/userfaultfd: fix hugetlb fault mutex hash calculation

In mfill_atomic_hugetlb(), linear_page_index() is used to calculate the
page index for hugetlb_fault_mutex_hash().  However, linear_page_index()
returns the index in PAGE_SIZE units, while hugetlb_fault_mutex_hash()
expects the index in huge page units.  This mismatch means that different
addresses within the same huge page can produce different hash values,
leading to the use of different mutexes for the same huge page.  This can
cause races between faulting threads, which can corrupt the reservation
map and trigger the BUG_ON in resv_map_release().

Fix this by introducing hugetlb_linear_page_index(), which returns the
page index in huge page granularity, and using it in place of
linear_page_index().

cna.title: xfrm: clear trailing padding in build_polexpire()

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfrm: clear trailing padding in build_polexpire()

build_expire() clears the trailing padding bytes of struct
xfrm_user_expire after setting the hard field via memset_after(),
but the analogous function build_polexpire() does not do this for
struct xfrm_user_polexpire.

The padding bytes after the __u8 hard field are left
uninitialized from the heap allocation, and are then sent to
userspace via netlink multicast to XFRMNLGRP_EXPIRE listeners,
leaking kernel heap memory contents.

Add the missing memset_after() call, matching build_expire().

cna.title: usb: typec: ucsi: validate connector number in ucsi_notify_common()

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

usb: typec: ucsi: validate connector number in ucsi_notify_common()

The connector number extracted from CCI via UCSI_CCI_CONNECTOR() is a
7-bit field (0-127) that is used to index into the connector array in
ucsi_connector_change(). However, the array is only allocated for the
number of connectors reported by the device (typically 2-4 entries).

A malicious or malfunctioning device could report an out-of-range
connector number in the CCI, causing an out-of-bounds array access in
ucsi_connector_change().

Add a bounds check in ucsi_notify_common(), the central point where CCI
is parsed after arriving from hardware, so that bogus connector numbers
are rejected before they propagate further.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: fireworks: bound device-supplied status before string array lookup

cna.title: ext4: fix use-after-free in update_super_work when racing with umount

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The vulnerable ext4 paths are reached through local filesystem operations such as mounting/unmounting an ext4 image, reading ext4 procfs state, or writing ext4 sysfs controls; there is no direct network packet path.
AC:L - The race is between queued ext4 superblock error work and teardown, and a crafted/ext4-error scenario can repeatedly drive the work while unmount/cleanup proceeds; under the required rule, this attacker-influenced race is Low complexity.
PR:N - Directly initiating mount/umount or sysfs error injection requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the initial namespace, but a highest-severity reasonable scenario is an attacker-supplied crafted ext4 filesystem image mounted/unmounted by a victim or privileged automounter, requiring no attacker privilege.
UI:R - Exploitation in the no-attacker-privilege scenario requires a victim or privileged system component to mount and later unmount/process the malicious ext4 filesystem image.
S:U - The corruption occurs inside the kernel filesystem/sysfs/kernfs lifetime management for the same host kernel security authority; it is not a VM escape or cross-authority boundary break.
C:H - The bug is a use-after-free of a kernfs_node reached through sysfs_notify after kobject deletion, and kernel UAFs are treated as capable of enabling high-impact information disclosure.
I:H - The stale kernfs_node is refcounted and used after free, giving a memory-corruption primitive that is defensibly treated as potentially exploitable for kernel control-flow or data modification.
A:H - At minimum the UAF can crash or oops the kernel during ext4 unmount/error-work processing, causing high availability impact.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ext4: fix use-after-free in update_super_work when racing with umount

Commit b98535d09179 ("ext4: fix bug_on in start_this_handle during umount
filesystem") moved ext4_unregister_sysfs() before flushing s_sb_upd_work
to prevent new error work from being queued via /proc/fs/ext4/xx/mb_groups
reads during unmount. However, this introduced a use-after-free because
update_super_work calls ext4_notify_error_sysfs() -> sysfs_notify() which
accesses the kobject's kernfs_node after it has been freed by kobject_del()
in ext4_unregister_sysfs():

  update_super_work                ext4_put_super
  -----------------                --------------
                                   ext4_unregister_sysfs(sb)
                                     kobject_del(&sbi->s_kobj)
                                       __kobject_del()
                                         sysfs_remove_dir()
                                           kobj->sd = NULL
                                         sysfs_put(sd)
                                           kernfs_put()  // RCU free
  ext4_notify_error_sysfs(sbi)
    sysfs_notify(&sbi->s_kobj)
      kn = kobj->sd              // stale pointer
      kernfs_get(kn)             // UAF on freed kernfs_node
                                   ext4_journal_destroy()
                                     flush_work(&sbi->s_sb_upd_work)

Instead of reordering the teardown sequence, fix this by making
ext4_notify_error_sysfs() detect that sysfs has already been torn down
by checking s_kobj.state_in_sysfs, and skipping the sysfs_notify() call
in that case. A dedicated mutex (s_error_notify_mutex) serializes
ext4_notify_error_sysfs() against kobject_del() in ext4_unregister_sysfs()
to prevent TOCTOU races where the kobject could be deleted between the
state_in_sysfs check and the sysfs_notify() call.

cna.title: smb: client: fix off-by-8 bounds check in check_wsl_eas()

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix off-by-8 bounds check in check_wsl_eas()

The bounds check uses (u8 *)ea + nlen + 1 + vlen as the end of the EA
name and value, but ea_data sits at offset sizeof(struct
smb2_file_full_ea_info) = 8 from ea, not at offset 0.  The strncmp()
later reads ea->ea_data[0..nlen-1] and the value bytes follow at
ea_data[nlen+1..nlen+vlen], so the actual end is ea->ea_data + nlen + 1
+ vlen.  Isn't pointer math fun?

The earlier check (u8 *)ea > end - sizeof(*ea) only guarantees the
8-byte header is in bounds, but since the last EA is placed within 8
bytes of the end of the response, the name and value bytes are read past
the end of iov.

Fix this mess all up by using ea->ea_data as the base for the bounds
check.

An "untrusted" server can use this to leak up to 8 bytes of kernel heap
into the EA name comparison and influence which WSL xattr the data is
interpreted as.

cna.title: drm/i915: Unlink NV12 planes earlier

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/i915: Unlink NV12 planes earlier

unlink_nv12_plane() will clobber parts of the plane state
potentially already set up by plane_atomic_check(), so we
must make sure not to call the two in the wrong order.
The problem happens when a plane previously selected as
a Y plane is now configured as a normal plane by user space.
plane_atomic_check() will first compute the proper plane
state based on the userspace request, and unlink_nv12_plane()
later clears some of the state.

This used to work on account of unlink_nv12_plane() skipping
the state clearing based on the plane visibility. But I removed
that check, thinking it was an impossible situation. Now when
that situation happens unlink_nv12_plane() will just WARN
and proceed to clobber the state.

Rather than reverting to the old way of doing things, I think
it's more clear if we unlink the NV12 planes before we even
compute the new plane state.

(cherry picked from commit 017ecd04985573eeeb0745fa2c23896fb22ee0cc)

cna.title: futex: Clear stale exiting pointer in futex_lock_pi() retry path

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

futex: Clear stale exiting pointer in futex_lock_pi() retry path

Fuzzying/stressing futexes triggered:

    WARNING: kernel/futex/core.c:825 at wait_for_owner_exiting+0x7a/0x80, CPU#11: futex_lock_pi_s/524

When futex_lock_pi_atomic() sees the owner is exiting, it returns -EBUSY
and stores a refcounted task pointer in 'exiting'.

After wait_for_owner_exiting() consumes that reference, the local pointer
is never reset to nil. Upon a retry, if futex_lock_pi_atomic() returns a
different error, the bogus pointer is passed to wait_for_owner_exiting().

  CPU0			     CPU1		       CPU2
  futex_lock_pi(uaddr)
  // acquires the PI futex
  exit()
    futex_cleanup_begin()
      futex_state = EXITING;
			     futex_lock_pi(uaddr)
			       futex_lock_pi_atomic()
				 attach_to_pi_owner()
				   // observes EXITING
				   *exiting = owner;  // takes ref
				   return -EBUSY
			       wait_for_owner_exiting(-EBUSY, owner)
				 put_task_struct();   // drops ref
			       // exiting still points to owner
			       goto retry;
			       futex_lock_pi_atomic()
				 lock_pi_update_atomic()
				   cmpxchg(uaddr)
					*uaddr ^= WAITERS // whatever
				   // value changed
				 return -EAGAIN;
			       wait_for_owner_exiting(-EAGAIN, exiting) // stale
				 WARN_ON_ONCE(exiting)

Fix this by resetting upon retry, essentially aligning it with requeue_pi.

scenarios.value:
AV:N - RxRPC is carried over UDP and the vulnerable server-side RXGK RESPONSE processing is reached from received network packets on an AF_RXRPC service endpoint.
AC:L - There is no race or condition outside the attacker's control once an RXGK-capable service and enctype are in use; a crafted short decrypted authenticator deterministically reaches the missing length check.
PR:N - The vulnerable code runs during the RXGK authentication handshake before the service connection is accepted. No local privilege on the target is required by a remote peer sending the RESPONSE packet.
UI:N - No victim user action is required after the RxRPC service is listening; packet processing occurs in the kernel receive path.
S:U - The impact is confined to the kernel/service host processing the RxRPC connection and does not cross a VM, IOMMU, or comparable security boundary.
C:L - The bug is a bounded buffer overread of a few bytes past the decrypted authenticator buffer, potentially exposing adjacent kernel heap data through comparison/error behavior. It does not provide an arbitrary kernel memory read.
I:N - The flaw is an out-of-bounds read before nonce/appdata parsing and does not write attacker-controlled data or corrupt memory.
A:H - The out-of-bounds read can fault or trigger hardened/debug slab checks, producing a kernel oops or panic. A remote peer can repeatedly send crafted RESPONSE packets.
