cna.title: Forge: TLS client crash on a handshake record received without a session

descriptions.value: Forge (also called node-forge) is a native implementation of Transport Layer Security in JavaScript. Prior to 1.4.3, a forge.tls client can pass a handshake record to tls.handleHandshake() while the connection has no session, including after a close_notify alert, after the application calls close(), or before handshake() is called. The handler dereferences c.session.md5 before dispatching the message, causing a TypeError to propagate from connection.process(). A malicious server or on-path attacker can deliver the record, including after a reset when the connection uses no encryption, and terminate a Node.js process if the application does not catch the exception. forge.tls servers are not affected, and there is no confidentiality or integrity impact. This issue is fixed in version 1.4.3.

descriptions.value:
Description:






When BIG-IP APM is licensed and provisioned, and a virtual server with the APM access profile is configured with a per-request policy containing a form-based Logon Page, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate.









Impact:


Traffic is disrupted while the TMM process restarts. This vulnerability allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the BIG-IP system. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.









Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [sourcecache] validate URLs before archiving to block

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [sourcecache] validate URLs before archiving to block
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces a URL validation gate (is_safe_url) that is invoked before any archiving request is made. The function restricts the scheme to http or https, resolves the hostname via DNS, and verifies that every resolved IP address is globally routable (i.e., not loopback, private, link-local, or otherwise non-global). If any check fails, the module returns an error and the fetch is never performed, preventing the server from being directed to internal or non-HTTP targets.
assumptions: The MISP server is assumed to be reachable over the network and that an authenticated user with attribute-creation permissions can submit link/url attributes; no specific MISP version or authentication model is stated in the patch.
CVSS PR:L assumes a low-privilege authenticated MISP user can create attributes; if MISP requires higher-level permissions, PR could be H.
CVSS SI:N assumes the archiving function only performs read (GET) requests; if it can issue state-changing methods, SI could be elevated.
SSVC technical_impact 'partial' is the least-assumptive choice; if cloud metadata endpoint access leads to full credential theft and infrastructure takeover, impact could be 'total'.
The CAPEC-12 mapping is high-confidence based on the explicit SSRF description in the commit message and the code changes; no uncertainty is expected.
No specific affected or fixed version numbers are provided in the patch metadata; version boundaries are marked as unspecified.

The is_global check in Python's ipaddress module covers loopback, private, link-local, and other non-global ranges, but DNS rebinding between the check and the actual fetch is not addressed by this patch and could remain a residual risk.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Adds imports for ipaddress and socket. Introduces a new is_safe_url(url) function that parses the URL, rejects non-http/https schemes, resolves the hostname with socket.getaddrinfo, and rejects the URL if any resolved address fails ipaddress.ip_address().is_global(). In the handler() function, a guard clause calls is_safe_url(tocache) before invoking __archiveLink and returns an error dict if the URL is not safe. Two new unit tests verify that http://127.0.0.1:6379/ and file:///etc/passwd are blocked and that the archive function is never called.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The MISP API is network-accessible. AC:L: Crafting a URL attribute with an internal address is trivial. AT:N: No special adversary technique is required. PR:L: An authenticated MISP user with attribute-creation rights is needed. UI:N: No victim interaction beyond the attacker's own API call. VC/VI/VA:N: The MISP server's own confidentiality, integrity, and availability are not directly compromised. SC:H: The subsequent component (internal services, cloud metadata) suffers high confidentiality impact because its data is exfiltrated into the MISP event. SI:N: The module only performs GET-style fetches; no evidence of integrity impact on subsequent components. SA:N: No availability impact on subsequent components is indicated.

capecRationale.rationale: The patch explicitly describes and remediates an SSRF: an attacker-supplied URL causes the MISP server to fetch internal resources (loopback, cloud metadata) and return the data. CAPEC-12 is the direct and most specific attack pattern for this scenario. No uncertainty is noted; the commit message and code changes align precisely with this pattern.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The module accepts a user-supplied URL and issues a server-side HTTP request to it without validating the target, allowing an attacker to direct requests to internal or non-HTTP resources. This is a textbook SSRF.

The root cause is the absence of any validation on the URL attribute value before it is used as a request target. The fix adds scheme, hostname, and IP-address validation, confirming the missing input validation was the defect.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-12 Exploiting SSRF

solutions.value: The fix introduces a URL validation gate (is_safe_url) that is invoked before any archiving request is made. The function restricts the scheme to http or https, resolves the hostname via DNS, and verifies that every resolved IP address is globally routable (i.e., not loopback, private, link-local, or otherwise non-global). If any check fails, the module returns an error and the fetch is never performed, preventing the server from being directed to internal or non-HTTP targets.

descriptions.value: The sourcecache expansion module in MISP Modules (misp-modules) contains a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability. When a user with permission to create or modify attributes of type 'link' or 'url' submits an attribute value, the module passes the URL directly to its internal archiving function without any validation of the target address. An attacker can therefore craft a URL pointing to loopback addresses (e.g., 127.0.0.1), private network ranges, link-local addresses, or cloud metadata endpoints (e.g., 169.254.169.254). The MISP server will issue an HTTP request to that target and store the response body in the event, effectively exfiltrating data from internal services to the attacker through the MISP interface. Non-HTTP schemes such as file:// are also accepted, potentially allowing local file disclosure. The vulnerability requires an authenticated MISP user with the ability to create or edit attributes of the affected types. The security impact is information disclosure from internal services reachable by the MISP server, including sensitive data such as cloud credentials, internal application data, or local files.

cna.title: Private action arguments can be set by user input on the bulk destroy and bulk update paths in Ash

descriptions.value: CAPEC-77 Manipulating User-Controlled Variables

Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes vulnerability in ash-project ash allows a user to set the value of a private action argument on the bulk destroy and bulk update paths.

Action arguments declared with public?: false are meant to be set only by trusted server-side code (for example via Ash.Changeset.set_private_argument/3) and must not be settable from end-user input. CVE-2026-55736 fixed the non-bulk changeset path to strip private arguments from user-supplied parameter maps, but the bulk destroy and bulk update paths were not covered.

Ash.Actions.Destroy.Bulk.base_changeset/5 and Ash.Actions.Update.Bulk.base_changeset/5 match every key in the caller-supplied parameter map against all of the action's arguments with no public? check, then apply the matches to the base changeset. A caller who can submit parameters to a bulk destroy or bulk update action (for example through AshJsonApi, AshGraphql, or a controller that forwards request parameters to Ash.bulk_destroy/4 or Ash.bulk_update/4) can therefore set any private argument of that action, including one referenced by an arg(...) template in the action's changes or validations. Depending on how the application uses the argument (for example an acting_user_id driving authorization or record ownership, or audit metadata), this can lead to an integrity violation or privilege escalation.

The fix requires public? in the argument matching on both bulk paths; private arguments remain settable server-side via the :private_arguments option.

This issue affects ash: from 2.17.15 before 3.33.11.

descriptions.value:

descriptions.value: vm2 through 3.12.0 (fixed in 3.12.1) does not correctly handle a nullish `this` receiver in the apply trap of its bridge (lib/bridge.js): when sandboxed code calls a host-provided non-strict (sloppy-mode) function without a receiver — e.g. `fn()`, a detached method, `fn.call()`, `fn.apply(undefined)`, `Reflect.apply(fn, undefined, [])`, or `fn.bind()()` — the undefined receiver is passed straight through to the host call, and V8 substitutes the host realm's global object for `this`. vm2 then wraps and returns that object to the sandbox, giving sandboxed script a live proxy of the host global. cna.title: Bluetooth BR/EDR SDP server blocks the Bluetooth workqueue indefinitely when the SDP buffer pool is empty

descriptions.value:
The Bluetooth Classic SDP server in subsys/bluetooth/host/classic/sdp.c allocated every response PDU through bt_sdp_create_pdu(), which expands to bt_l2cap_create_pdu() and therefore uses a K_FOREVER timeout. The allocation is made from sdp_pool, a fixed pool holding only CONFIG_BT_MAX_CONN buffers (one in the default configuration) that is shared with the SDP client role. When the pool is empty the call blocks without a bound.

The allocation is reached from bt_sdp_recv() on the Bluetooth host's RX context: the bt_workq "BT RX WQ" workqueue in the default configuration since v3.1.0, and the dedicated "BT RX" thread before that. This context processes all normal-priority HCI events and all received ACL data. The SDP L2CAP server is registered on PSM 0x0001 with no security requirement (BT_SECURITY_L0), so an unpaired, unauthenticated BR/EDR peer within radio range of a connectable device can drive it. Every malformed or unrecognised SDP PDU reaches send_err_rsp(), and the sdp_svc_search_req(), sdp_svc_att_req() and sdp_svc_search_att_req() handlers allocate as well, so a short burst of pipelined requests drains the pool and parks the RX context in the blocking allocation.

A pool buffer is released only once its response has been sent, and a peer that withholds baseband acknowledgements keeps the controller's buffers for the link full, so the response is never sent. While the RX context is blocked, the entire Bluetooth host, for all connections and both LE and BR/EDR, stops processing normal-priority HCI events and received data. In most affected releases the stall is permanent. Queued PDUs are freed only by connection or channel teardown, which waits for the normal-priority Disconnection Complete handler, and that handler runs on the blocked RX context, so the host does not recover without a reset. In v3.7.0 through v4.1.x the TX processor discards the queued response once the link supervision timeout drops the connection, so each stall ends at that timeout, but the peer can reconnect and repeat it for as long as it stays in range. The impact is limited to availability; no memory corruption or information disclosure is involved.

The fix adds sdp_svc_create_pdu() using K_NO_WAIT, pre-allocates the response buffer once in bt_sdp_recv(), stashes the request in sdp->recv_pending when no buffer is available, and retries it from a work handler once a buffer is freed by the pool destroy callback.

cna.title: Backuply <= 1.5.8 - Authenticated (Subscriber+) Second-Order SQL Injection via Restore to Privilege Escalation

affected.product: Backuply – Backup, Restore, Migrate and Clone

descriptions.value: The Backuply – Backup, Restore, Migrate and Clone plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to SQL Injection via the Biographical Info field (second-order, via restore) in all versions up to, and including, 1.5.8 due to insufficient escaping on the user supplied parameter and the lack of sufficient preparation on an existing SQL query. Backuply exports the Biographical Info value verbatim inside an INSERT statement written to the backup's SQL dump (wp_usermeta). When an Administrator later restores such a backup, the crafted payload breaks out of that INSERT statement and appends attacker-controlled SQL that executes with full database privileges. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to write arbitrary data to the database — in particular to update the default_role option in wp_options to administrator (and enable open user registration) — so that a subsequently registered account is automatically granted the Administrator role, resulting in privilege escalation and full site takeover. Because the injection executes inside an INSERT during restore with no response returned to the attacker, the primitive is used to modify database records rather than to read existing data directly.

credits.value: F5 acknowledges Matt Suiche of Tolmo, Inc., Mateusz Gierblinski, LemonTea, Toan Pham of "Team Orca, Sea Security", and zenneth (randomguy6407) for bringing this issue to our attention and following the highest standards of coordinated disclosure.

workarounds.value: To mitigate this vulnerability, do not use unnamed captures. Use named captures instead and limit their usage to the block with the regex match.

supportingMedia.value: To mitigate this vulnerability, do not use unnamed captures. Use named captures instead and limit their usage to the block with the regex match.

descriptions.value:
A vulnerability exists in NGINX Plus and NGINX Open Source when a map directive uses regex matching and the root directive or access log format references the map's regex capture variables before referencing the map output variable. Alternatively, the same result could be achieved by using a non-cacheable variable in a string expression under certain conditions. An unauthenticated attacker along with conditions beyond their control can exploit this vulnerability by sending crafted HTTP requests. This may cause a heap buffer overflow in the NGINX worker process leading to a restart. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR.

Impact: 
This vulnerability may allow remote attackers to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the NGINX system or to possibly trigger a code execution. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.

Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

cna.title: Freedesktop Poppler JBIG2Stream.cc rewind null pointer dereference

references.name: VDB-406610 | Freedesktop Poppler JBIG2Stream.cc rewind null pointer dereference
Submit #942345 | freedesktop.org Poppler 26.07.0 NULL Pointer Dereference

descriptions.value: A flaw has been found in Freedesktop Poppler 26.07.0. Impacted is the function JBIG2Stream::rewind of the file poppler/JBIG2Stream.cc. This manipulation causes null pointer dereference. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been published and may be used. Upgrading to version 26.08.0 is recommended to address this issue. Patch name: 5e49250f13b0390edeb3f90eb4c02c9941f97067. Upgrading the affected component is advised.

In Znuny through 7.3.6, an attacker can bypass specific standard login procedures and gain unauthorized access to sensitive system functions by manipulating a specific HTTP request header. Because the application incorrectly trusts this header, an attacker can impersonate any user, including administrators, without requiring a password. This grants full access to confidential data and system controls. More specifically, the HTTPBasicAuth modules for the agent (Kernel::System::Auth::HTTPBasicAuth) and customer (Kernel::System::CustomerAuth::HTTPBasicAuth) interfaces read the username to log in not only from $ENV{REMOTE_USER} (set by the web server after successful authentication), but also, as a fallback, from $ENV{HTTP_REMOTE_USER}, which is populated directly from an attacker-controllable "Remote-User" request header. On systems where HTTPBasicAuth was configured as the authentication backend, this allowed an attacker to log in as any existing user by sending a request with a forged Remote-User header, without providing any credentials.

descriptions.value: ArcadeDB (Maven artifact com.arcadedb:arcadedb-engine) through 26.8.1 contains an incomplete deny-list in the polyglot script sandbox: com.arcadedb.query.polyglot.HostClassLookupFilter.DENIED lists java.util.ResourceBundle as a bare class name, which is matched by exact equality and therefore does not cover its subclasses, while ScriptTriggerExecutor.ALLOWED_PACKAGES permits java.util.*. cna.title: NULL pointer dereference in the Bluetooth host ATT request lookup (bt_att_find_req_by_user_data)

descriptions.value:
bt_att_find_req_by_user_data() in subsys/bluetooth/host/att.c walks every ATT channel attached to a connection and dereferences chan->req->user_data without checking chan->req. An ATT channel with no client request in flight holds chan->req == NULL — that is its normal idle state, set by att_handle_rsp() when a response resolves the transaction and tested by att_req_send_process() to pick a free channel — so the lookup reads through a NULL pointer as soon as it visits an idle channel. Every other chan->req user in the file already guards the pointer.

The lookup is reached from the public bt_gatt_cancel() API and, more importantly, from the host itself: bt_gatt_unsubscribe() calls bt_gatt_cancel() while a subscribe CCC write is still outstanding (BT_GATT_SUBSCRIBE_FLAG_WRITE_PENDING), and call_notify_cb_and_maybe_unsubscribe() in subsys/bluetooth/host/gatt.c invokes bt_gatt_unsubscribe() from the RX path whenever an application notify callback returns BT_GATT_ITER_STOP. A malicious or malfunctioning peer can hold the trigger window open by withholding the ATT Write Response to the CCC write and then sending a notification for the subscribed handle. With CONFIG_BT_EATT the traversal is very likely to meet an idle sibling channel, since ATT channels are prepended to the list and a channel opened after the pending request was sent is visited first.

The dereference is a read of a small constant offset from address zero, so the impact is availability only: no memory corruption, no attacker-chosen address and no information disclosure. On platforms and configurations where a near-NULL read traps — TrustZone non-secure images, MMU targets, native_sim, or builds with CONFIG_NULL_POINTER_EXCEPTION_DETECTION_MPU/_DWT — the fault occurs in the Bluetooth RX context and results in a fatal error and device reset. On a plain Cortex-M build with the vector table mapped at address 0 and null-pointer detection disabled (the default) the read succeeds and the defect is inert.

The fix adds an explicit chan->req != NULL test to the channel traversal and additionally rejects a NULL user_data argument, which would otherwise have matched, and cancelled, an unrelated request.

cna.title: Cross-tenant BundleDeployment and Secret disclosure via spoofed cluster labels during agent-initiated registration in Fleet

descriptions.value: CAPEC-122 Privilege Abuse
CAPEC-195 Principal Spoof

A cross-tenant authorization issue was discovered in SUSE Rancher Fleet. During agent-initiated cluster registration, cluster labels supplied by the registering agent, including labels in the reserved management.cattle.io/ namespace such as the cluster display name label, were applied to the resulting upstream Cluster object. Because Fleet resolves GitRepo and Bundle targets from those cluster labels, a party able to register a cluster into a Fleet workspace namespace shared with other tenants could cause its own cluster to satisfy targeting rules that administrators intended for a different cluster.
This affects SUSE Rancher Fleet 0.16 before 0.16.1, 0.15 before 0.15.6, 0.14 before 0.14.10, 0.13 before 0.13.15, 0.12 before 0.12.19 and older versions.

descriptions.value: An unauthenticated attacker reaches a SAML consume or single-logout endpoint and posts a small compressed SAMLResponse that inflates to gigabytes, exhausting memory. A few requests crash the Erlang VM and deny service to every user of the service provider.

An unauthenticated attacker reaches a SAML consume or single-logout endpoint and posts a small compressed `SAMLResponse` that inflates to gigabytes, exhausting memory. A few requests crash the Erlang VM and deny service to every user of the service provider.

descriptions.value:
Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification) in esaml_binding in dropbox esaml allows an unauthenticated attacker to exhaust server memory and crash the Erlang VM via a crafted compressed SAMLResponse.

esaml_binding:decode_response/2 base64-decodes the attacker-supplied SAMLResponse, inflates it with zlib:unzip/1 with no bound on the output, then converts the result to a charlist with binary_to_list/1 before parsing. This runs on the SAML consume (ACS) and single-logout endpoints, which accept unauthenticated requests by design, and it runs before any signature check. A small deflate stream reaches a compression ratio near 1000 to 1, so a request body of tens of kilobytes inflates to hundreds of megabytes and then to several gigabytes of list heap, so a few requests exhaust memory and take the node down.

This issue affects esaml: from 0.1.0 onward.

2. Post it to the service provider's SAML consume (ACS) endpoint as the `SAMLResponse` form field, with `SAMLEncoding` set to the DEFLATE URI, or omitted to take the default clause.
3. `esaml_binding:decode_response/2` inflates the stream and converts it to a charlist before any signature check. A single request spikes the Erlang VM by several gigabytes. Repeat to exhaust memory and crash the node.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Input. The SAML consume (ACS) and single-logout endpoints read the request body and pass the SAMLResponse form field to esaml_binding:decode_response/2. The attacker's SAMLEncoding field selects the clause. Both clauses inflate: the explicit DEFLATE clause, and the default clause, which tries zlib:unzip/1 inside a catch whenever the body is not plain XML.

2. Unbounded inflate. decode_response/2 evaluates binary_to_list(zlib:unzip(base64:decode(SAMLResponse))). zlib:unzip/1 inflates the whole stream in one call with no cap on output size, and binary_to_list/1 then expands the inflated binary to a charlist, which costs about 16 bytes of heap per byte on a 64-bit VM.

3. Exhaustion before any check. All of this happens before xmerl_scan parses the document and before esaml_sp verifies any signature. A deflate stream of a long run of identical bytes reaches a ratio near 1000 to 1, so a request body of tens of kilobytes produces hundreds of megabytes of binary and then several gigabytes of list heap. A few concurrent requests exhaust memory and crash the node.

cna.title: Zimbra Collaboration Suite Email HTML Sanitizer Bypass via Hostname Canonicalization

credits.value: Jonah Burgess (CryptoCat), Senior Security Researcher, Rapid7

scenarios.value: No individual metric - Chain only with separately reported CalDAV CSRF

descriptions.value: A hostname canonicalization vulnerability in the email HTML sanitizers of Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) allows an unauthenticated sender to bypass the restriction on forms that target the Zimbra host. DefangFilter and the OWASP ActionAttributePolicy compare the form-action hostname with the request hostname before browser URL canonicalization. A percent-encoded hostname can therefore survive sanitization while the browser submits the form to the normal Zimbra origin with the recipient's authentication cookie. This permits authenticated form requests from a crafted email after the recipient opens it in Classic and submits the form. The issue is present in ZCS 10.1.16 and 10.1.21. It does not bypass an endpoint's CSRF-token checks; a state-changing attack additionally requires an endpoint that accepts the resulting request without that protection.

descriptions.value: The Smash Balloon Social Post Feed – Simple Social Feeds for WordPress plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via Facebook Comment Message via v-html in Admin Builder Preview in all versions up to, and including, 4.13.0 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts that will execute whenever an administrator accesses the feed builder preview page. This attack requires only a Facebook account to post a comment on the connected Facebook Page, with no WordPress credentials needed; additionally, the use of v-show rather than v-if means injected HTML — including onerror handlers — is evaluated in the DOM even when the comment section is not visually displayed. When combined with the lack of URL validation in the cff_install_addon AJAX handler (admin/addon-functions.php), an injected script running in an administrator's session can trigger arbitrary plugin installation from an attacker-controlled URL, which may result in server-side code execution.

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Shubham Raj (Causal Security) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value:
The following measures reduce risk:

1. If TFTP is not required, do not enable it. Remove --enable-tftp from the dnsmasq configuration.
2. If TFTP is required, restrict it with --tftp-interface=<interface> and avoid running TFTP-only instances that serve untrusted clients on the same network.
3. Compile without TFTP support using COPTS=-DNO_TFTP if TFTP is not needed.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in dnsmasq. The TFTP server can serve the wrong file contents because a recently used transfer cache is not invalidated when a transfer finishes. references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: vm2 3.11.8 Sandbox Escape via crypto.setFips

descriptions.value: vm2 through 3.12.0 exposes Node.js's crypto.setFips() function to untrusted guest code when an embedder explicitly allowlists the crypto builtin for a NodeVM (require.builtin: ['crypto']). The builtin sanitizer (sanitizeCryptoModule in lib/builtin.js) replaces crypto.setEngine but leaves crypto.setFips callable, and the readonly wrapper used to expose the host module does not localize side effects of forwarded host functions. Guest code can therefore call crypto.setFips() to change the FIPS mode of the entire host process; the modified mode is subsequently observed by trusted host code (crypto.getFips() changed from 0 to 1 in the reported test), crossing the NodeVM isolation boundary. Fixed in vm2 3.12.1.

cna.title: ArcadeDB before 26.9.1 Authorization Bypass via Batch Edge Connect

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: ArcadeDB before 26.9.1 Authorization Bypass via Batch Edge Connect

descriptions.value: ArcadeDB before 26.9.1 (com.arcadedb:arcadedb-engine <= 26.8.1) fails to bind the authenticated principal onto the DatabaseAsyncTransaction async worker threads used by the parallel edge-connect phase of POST /api/v1/batch/{database}. Because those workers have no current user, LocalDatabase.checkPermissionsOnFile returns early and allows the write, bypassing per-type CREATE_RECORD/UPDATE_RECORD ACL enforcement. In deployments that rely on per-type or per-group ACLs, an authenticated low-privilege user holding CREATE_RECORD on an edge type E but with CREATE_RECORD/UPDATE_RECORD revoked on a vertex type V can submit a graph edge-load batch request (with parallelFlush at its default value of true) and durably append edges to protected vertices of type V by writing records into V's <V>_out_edges/<V>_in_edges buckets, resulting in unauthorized modification of graph adjacency. Setting parallelFlush=false causes the request to be correctly rejected. This is an incomplete fix of GHSA-c23x-pqcj-7hfm, which bound the principal only on the HTTP handler thread.

cna.title: Insights-operator: gather serviceaccount has cluster-wide secret read plus nodes/proxy and cluster-reader

workarounds.value: Mitigation for this issue is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria comprising ease of use and deployment, applicability to widespread installation base, or stability.

descriptions.value:
The `insights-operator-gather` ClusterRole grants the operator's service account read access to secrets in the core API group with no namespace or resourceNames restriction — therefore, access to every secret in every namespace in the cluster.

Ref: https://github.com/openshift/insights-operator/blob/8f15e3157ff09f54ab22801f5b21da35a195cc6d/manifests/03-clusterrole.yaml#L368-L373
```
- apiGroups:
  - ""
  resources:
  - secrets
  verbs:
  - get
  - list
```

By spawning a pod with the gather service account mounted, an attacker will be able to access any secret in any namespace.

```
spec:
 serviceAccountName:"gather"
```

cna.title: Barman snapshot backup deletion trusts unverified backup catalog metadata

solutions.value: Upgrade to Barman 3.20.1 or later. Before deleting a snapshot, Barman now reads the snapshot name from the cloud provider and refuses the deletion unless it matches the backup being deleted.

workarounds.value: Restrict write access to the backup catalog in object storage to the identity Barman uses. Enable object versioning or object lock on the backup bucket, and on AWS use EBS Snapshot Lock (aws_snapshot_lock_mode) to protect snapshots from deletion.

descriptions.value: Unverified ownership in Barman snapshot backup deletion allows a principal who can write the backup catalog to cause Barman to delete unrelated cloud snapshots. When a snapshot backup is deleted, either explicitly or by retention policy enforcement, Barman reads the snapshot identifiers from the backup.info file and passes them to the cloud provider's delete API using Barman's own credentials, without verifying that the snapshots belong to that backup. An attacker who can overwrite backup.info but lacks snapshot delete permissions can substitute the identifiers of other snapshots, causing Barman to delete any snapshot its cloud identity can reach on AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud. Exploitation requires a deployment where the principal that writes the backup catalog is separate from the identity Barman uses to delete snapshots. Barman versions from 3.4.0 (Google Cloud), 3.6.0 (Azure), and 3.7.0 (AWS) up to and including 3.20.0 are affected. The issue is fixed in Barman 3.20.1.

cna.title: rclone serve docker Path Traversal via Volume Name

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: rclone serve docker Path Traversal via Volume Name

descriptions.value: rclone versions 1.56.0 through 1.75.0 contain a path traversal vulnerability in the `rclone serve docker` volume plugin. newVolume() in cmd/serve/docker/volume.go computes a volume's mountpoint as filepath.Join(drv.root, name) from the attacker-supplied `name` field of a Docker VolumeDriver.Create request without verifying that the result stays within drv.root (default /var/lib/docker-volumes/rclone), and checkMountpoint() then creates that directory with file.MkdirAll before mounting. A volume name containing enough `..` components (e.g. "../../../../../../etc") therefore resolves outside the base directory, allowing anyone able to submit a VolumeDriver.Create request to the plugin socket — normally the Docker daemon, or a workload that can request named volumes in a multi-tenant orchestration setup — to make the privileged rclone plugin process create a directory and mount a remote filesystem specified in the same request at an arbitrary host path, shadowing or disrupting system directories. The advisory notes Volume.restoreState() had the same missing validation when reloading persisted volume state. Fixed in 1.75.1.

WebSocket client accepts a handshake without verifying the full Sec-WebSocket-Accept value

descriptions.value:
The Zephyr WebSocket client validates the server's handshake response in on_header_value() in subsys/net/lib/websocket/websocket.c. The comparison was performed as strncmp(at, str, length), where length is the length of the value the server sent rather than the length of the expected value, so the check only asked whether the received value was a prefix of the expected base64(SHA-1(key || GUID)). A server that returned a handful of correct characters passed, and a response carrying an empty Sec-WebSocket-Accept: header caused strncmp() to be called with a count of zero, which returns 0 and set ctx->sec_accept_ok with no comparison performed at all. The header-value callback also cleared ctx->sec_accept_present after the first chunk, so a value split across receive-buffer boundaries was only ever examined in part.

ctx->sec_accept_ok is the sole WebSocket-specific gate in websocket_connect(); the client does not check the HTTP status code or the Upgrade:/Connection: headers. Any HTTP response containing an empty or prefix-matching Sec-WebSocket-Accept header therefore completed the handshake, after which the socket is finalized as a WebSocket and all further peer bytes are parsed as frames. The affected path is driven directly by remote input through subsys/net/lib/http/http_parser.c, and is reached by every user of websocket_connect(), including MQTT over WebSocket (subsys/net/lib/mqtt/mqtt_transport_websocket.c) and subsys/net/lib/ocpp/ocpp.c.

The Sec-WebSocket-Accept exchange is not a secret-based authentication -- an endpoint or on-path attacker that sees the request can compute the expected value -- so the impact is bounded to parties that never observed the handshake request: a caching or transparent intermediary replaying a canned response, an off-path attacker injecting a spoofed response, or a non-WebSocket endpoint the client was induced to talk to. For those, the per-connection binding that RFC 6455 requires the client to enforce provided no protection at all, letting a single crafted response convince the device it holds a live WebSocket session and causing it to send application data to, and accept frames from, an unverified peer. There is no memory-safety consequence.

The fix compares each delivered chunk against the expected value at the position reached so far, refuses a chunk that would overrun it, and accepts only once every byte of the expected value -- and no more -- has been matched; on_header_field() now also clears the flag for any other header so a partial value cannot be continued across an intervening header.

cna.title: Dancer2 versions from 2.0.0 before 2.2.0 for Perl dispatch a route that a dying hook refused when the exception handler halts the response in compile_hooks

solutions.value: Upgrade to Dancer2 2.2.0 or later.

descriptions.value:
Dancer2 versions from 2.0.0 before 2.2.0 for Perl dispatch a route that a dying hook refused when the exception handler halts the response in compile_hooks.

A hook that dies fires core.app.hook_exception, then calls cleanup unless the failing hook is the exception handler. A handler that halts does not stop that cleanup, which discards the request, response and session the dispatcher has yet to read, so the refused route runs.

The handler has to halt the response object by calling its halt method or setting is_halted: the halt keyword unwinds through with_return before cleanup runs.

A check in a before hook is not enforced: the caller gets the refusal, while the route body runs and its writes land.

cna.title: Out-of-bounds write in the DesignWare I3C driver when the device address table is full

descriptions.value:
The Synopsys DesignWare I3C controller driver (drivers/i3c/i3c_dw.c) tracks free Device Address Table (DAT) slots with get_free_pos(), which signals an exhausted table by returning -1. The helper declared its return type as uint8_t, so the sentinel was truncated to 255, and both consumers (dw_i3c_attach_device() and dw_i3c_i2c_attach_device()) also stored it in a uint8_t before testing if (pos < 0) — a comparison that is never true for an unsigned value. The exhaustion guard was therefore inert in every build.

With the guard defeated, an attach attempted on a full DAT proceeds with pos == 255: it writes data->dw_i3c_i2c_priv_data[255].id, more than 200 bytes past the end of the 32-element dw_i3c_i2c_priv_data array and past the end of struct dw_i3c_data; it stores the resulting out-of-bounds address in desc->controller_priv, from which later detach, reattach and IBI operations read the slot index back; and it performs a 32-bit MMIO store 1020 bytes beyond the hardware DAT base, outside the table the controller reports. The attach still returns success, so the upper layer believes the device is bound.

The DAT is smaller than the software array (its depth is read from DEVICE_ADDR_TABLE_POINTER, commonly 8 or 16 entries), so exhaustion is reachable. In a dual-role build (CONFIG_I3C_DUAL_ROLE with CONFIG_I3C_USE_IBI) acting as a secondary controller, the attach count is supplied by the bus's active controller: i3c_sec_handoffed() attaches one device per entry of the received DEFTGTS list, so a hostile or malfunctioning controller on the local I3C bus that declares more targets than the local DAT depth triggers the condition once per surplus entry. Exhaustion can also be reached from a devicetree that declares more devices than the table holds, or by repeated i3c attach shell commands.

Impact is bounded: the out-of-bounds store is a single byte of fixed value at a fixed displacement, with no attacker-chosen data or offset, so the realistic outcomes are corruption of neighbouring static driver state, writes into reserved controller registers, and inconsistent driver bookkeeping (a crash or a wedged I3C bus) rather than a controllable memory-write primitive. The attack vector is the local chip-to-chip I3C bus; there is no network-reachable path.

cna.title: Wild Apricot Login <= 1.0.18 - Authentication Bypass via SSO Email-Collision Account Binding on Multisite

descriptions.value: The Wild Apricot Login plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass via SSO Email-Collision Account Binding in all versions up to, and including, 1.0.18. When no WildApricot contact-ID mapping is found for an incoming SSO login, the plugin falls back to a network-global `get_user_by('email', ...)` lookup in `Module.php` to resolve a WordPress user, then `UserSynchronizer::syncWaContact()` binds and `Controller::login()` issues a session cookie via `wp_set_auth_cookie()` for that resolved user — both guarded only by `is_super_admin()` — without ever requiring proof of ownership of the matched WordPress account such as a password, local account-linking confirmation, inbox verification, or administrator approval. This makes it possible for attackers with custom-level WildApricot membership access to authenticate as an existing WordPress subsite administrator on a path-based Multisite network, obtaining a valid network-global authentication cookie for the victim without their credentials. Exploitation requires that the attacker control a WildApricot contact whose email address matches the target WordPress administrator's email — achievable via a public zero-fee membership application on the connected WildApricot organization — and that they complete the SSO flow on any subsite where Wild Apricot Login is active; because WordPress user identities and authentication cookies are network-global, the cookie issued on that subsite is equally valid on any other subsite where the victim user holds an administrator role.

cna.title: Bluetooth Classic SDP client can deadlock the Bluetooth workqueue on buffer allocation

descriptions.value:
The Bluetooth Classic SDP client built its outgoing request PDUs with bt_sdp_create_pdu(), which allocates from the sdp_pool net-buf pool with a K_FOREVER timeout and no failure handling, in sdp_client_ss_search(), sdp_client_sa_search() and sdp_client_ssa_search() in subsys/bluetooth/host/classic/sdp.c. All of these run on the Bluetooth workqueue bt_workq (via sdp_client_work_handler(), the L2CAP sdp_client_connected() callback, or the continuation-state follow-up from a received response), which is the same single thread that dispatches incoming HCI ACL and event traffic, drives L2CAP, and performs connection and channel teardown. sdp_pool holds only CONFIG_BT_MAX_CONN buffers (one by default) and is shared with the SDP server role.

An unauthenticated peer within BR/EDR range can drive both halves of the trigger. The SDP L2CAP server is registered at BT_SECURITY_L0, so any inbound SDP request makes the device allocate the pool's buffer for a response, which is held until the controller has transmitted it. The same peer can then cause a client request to be issued while the pool is empty: in-tree profiles start SDP discovery from inbound connection callbacks (for example hfp_hf_accept() calls bt_sdp_discover() through hfp_hf_create(), and hfp_ag.c mirrors this), and a peer acting as an SDP server can force repeated client requests by answering with partial responses carrying continuation state.

With the pool empty, the allocation blocks uninterruptibly and freezes the entire Bluetooth host. The stall becomes permanent when the release of the outstanding buffer itself depends on the blocked workqueue: if the link carrying the queued PDU is dropped or stalls, hci_disconn_complete() and the L2CAP channel cleanup that purges the channel TX queue are themselves bt_workq work items, so the buffer is never returned. The result is an unrecoverable denial of service of all Bluetooth functionality until reboot; there is no memory-safety, confidentiality or integrity impact.

The fix allocates client PDUs with K_NO_WAIT via a new sdp_client_create_pdu(), propagates -ENOBUFS, parks the session on a new SDP_CLIENT_FLAG_WAIT_FOR_TX_BUF flag, and adds an sdp_pool destructor that re-submits the SDP client worker when a buffer becomes available. Note that the SDP server role still allocated from the same pool with K_FOREVER at this commit; that path was addressed separately.

cna.title: Apache MINA SSHD: Remote execution of JGit "archive -o=file.zip" can write file on the server

descriptions.value:
Improper input validation in sshd-git in Apache MINA SSHD, versions up to 2.19.0 and 3.0.0-M1 to 3.0.0-M5. Apache 
MINA SSHD is a Java library for client-side and server-side SSH.




Component org.apache.sshd:sshd-git provides though class GitPgmCommandFactory a way to configure an Apache MINA SSHD server such 
that authenticated SSH clients can remotely execute git commands via the JGit library 
on git repositories stored on the server. In CVE-2026-58624 this mechanism was restricted to only a few git commands, including "git archive" without "--output" or "-o" options such that the resulting archive would not be written on the server but instead sent back to the client over the SSH connection.




The fix done for CVE-2026-58624 was insufficient as it missed removing the single-argument "-o=file.zip" version of the command parameter from the "archive" command.




Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.20.0 or 3.0.0-M6, which fix this issue.

cna.title: Out-of-bounds read logging a mismatched Sec-WebSocket-Accept header in the Zephyr websocket client

descriptions.value:
The websocket client's HTTP header callback on_header_value() in subsys/net/lib/websocket/websocket.c receives the Sec-WebSocket-Accept header value as a pointer/length pair from the HTTP parser. The referenced bytes live inside the application-supplied receive buffer and are not NUL terminated. When the received value did not match the expected accept key, the pointer was passed directly to a %s conversion in a NET_DBG() call, so the logging code measured the string with strlen() and read on past the end of the header value looking for a terminator.

The value is supplied by the peer during the WebSocket handshake, before any application-level authentication, so a malicious or man-in-the-middle server reached over a ws:// (or otherwise attacker-terminated) connection can trigger the mismatch branch at will simply by answering with a wrong accept key. By sizing the response so the header value ends at the tail of the buffer passed to websocket_connect() as wreq->tmp_buf, the peer can make the scan run off the end of that buffer and into adjacent memory. The defective log statement is compiled in only when websocket debug logging is enabled (CONFIG_NET_WEBSOCKET_LOG_LEVEL_DBG=y, or CONFIG_LOG_DEFAULT_LEVEL=4); it is absent from a default build, which bounds exposure to diagnostic configurations.

The consequence is an out-of-bounds read whose contents are emitted to the log stream: memory adjacent to the receive buffer is disclosed wherever the device's logs are collected or displayed. On targets where the memory following the buffer is not mapped, the scan can instead fault and terminate the connection or thread. No out-of-bounds write occurs, so there is no integrity impact.

The fix copies at most sizeof(got) - 1 bytes of the parser-provided slice into a bounded stack buffer, NUL terminates the copy, and logs that instead, so the formatter never reads beyond the bytes the parser actually offered.

In OpenStack Blazar before 17.0.1, the V2 lease API does not enforce object-level authorization on its update and delete operations (PUT /v2/leases/{lease_id} and DELETE /v2/leases/{lease_id}). The policy authorize() wrapper attempts to load the target lease to build the authorization target from its owner, but it looks up the lease under the keyword "lease_id" whereas the controller methods name the parameter "id" (and the wsme_pecan.wsexpose wrapper delivers it positionally). The lookup returns None, and thus authorization falls back to the requesting user's own project_id/user_id instead of the target lease owner. Any authenticated user who knows a lease ID can therefore modify or delete leases belonging to other users and projects, bypassing the intended ownership check.

cna.title: Apache MINA SSHD: Memory exhaustion DoS via unbounded SCP command line read

descriptions.value:
Uncontrolled resource consumption in component ssd-scp in Apache MINA SSHD versions up to 2.19.0 or 3.0.0-M1 to 3.0.0-M5. Apache MINA SSHD is a Java library for client-side and server-side SSH.




Component sshd-scp of Apache MINA SSHD provides a Java implementation of SCP. The SCP command protocol is line-oriented with LF-terminated lines. The protocol handler in sshd-scp did not impose any limit on the length of such protocol lines. A malicious peer just sending a junk command containing a never-ending sequence of characters but never a LF would cause the receiver to allocate memory to store this whole junk command, exhausting memory and crashing the application with an OutOfMemoryError.




Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.20.0 or 3.0.0-M6, which fix this issue by enforcing an upper limit on the length of SCP protocol lines.

descriptions.value: ArcadeDB before 26.9.1 contains an access control bypass vulnerability in the query_database tool exposed through the AI chat endpoints. cna.title: (D)TLS 1.2 client accepts early ChangeCipherSpec before ClientKeyExchange

descriptions.value: A (D)TLS 1.2 client can accept a ChangeCipherSpec message before it has sent its ClientKeyExchange. No master secret has been derived at that point, so the client installs read keys derived from a known (deterministic) key and checks the server's Finished against that same key. An out-of-order ChangeCipherSpec can therefore be used by an attacker to complete the handshake in place of the server and send data the client accepts as authentic. The client's own traffic still uses correctly derived keys, so the attacker cannot read it, and the genuine server never completes the handshake. DTLS 1.2 clients are exposed because a datagram read can deliver the out-of-order records on its own. TLS 1.2 clients are exposed when the application supplies received bytes with wolfSSL_inject() or enables read ahead. For certificate suites, the attacker must be in a man-in-the-middle position. For PSK (Pre Shared Key) connections, any fake server can succeed without knowing the PSK.

cna.title: MISP Background Job Argument Injection via Console Path Switches Enables Remote Code Execution

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Refuse console path switches in background

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Refuse console path switches in background
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces a validation layer in BackgroundJobsTool::enqueue() that rejects any job argument matching a reserved CakePHP console path switch (-app, --app, -working, --working, -root, --root, -webroot, --webroot), throwing an InvalidArgumentException before the job is queued. Additionally, the EventsController::contact() method now casts the person field to a boolean, preventing it from ever forming a switch/value pair with the adjacent message field. Together, these changes ensure that user-supplied data can never be interpreted as a console path directive by the worker process.
assumptions: The affected version boundary is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.47, 43 commits after fix); the exact first fixed release is not explicitly stated in the patch and may differ.

PR:L assumes the events/contact endpoint requires at least a low-privilege authenticated session; if the endpoint is accessible without authentication in some MISP configurations, PR should be U (Unprivileged).

The CAPEC-14 mapping is the closest available pattern; the attack is more specifically an argument injection into a framework dispatcher rather than generic parameter manipulation, but no CAPEC entry precisely describes this mechanism.

The phar:// exploitation path assumes the target PHP process has the phar stream wrapper enabled and that the attacker can place or reference a crafted archive accessible via the phar:// URI; the patch does not explicitly confirm the phar wrapper is enabled by default.
The commit date (17 Sep 2026) is in the future relative to typical CVE timelines; this is taken at face value from the patch metadata.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Three files are modified. In BackgroundJobsTool.php, a new RESERVED_ARGUMENTS constant lists the eight console path switches, and a new private validateArgs() method iterates over job arguments and throws InvalidArgumentException if any string argument exactly matches a reserved switch. The enqueue() method calls validateArgs() before dispatching. In EventsController.php, the person field assignment in contact() is changed from a raw value to (bool) cast. A new test file BackgroundJobsToolArgumentsTest.php verifies that ordinary arguments pass, free text merely containing a switch substring passes, every reserved switch is refused, and non-string arguments are unaffected.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The contact endpoint is reachable over the network via HTTP. AC:L: The attack requires only crafting two form fields with a known switch string and a phar:// path; no race conditions or special timing. AT:N: No specific target configuration or state is required beyond a standard MISP installation. PR:L: The attacker needs a low-privilege authenticated MISP account with access to the event contact action. UI:N: No victim interaction is needed beyond the attacker's own form submission. VC:H, VI:H, VA:H: Successful exploitation results in arbitrary PHP code execution as the web user, giving full control over the MISP server's data, processes, and availability. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N: The impact is confined to the MISP server itself; no evidence of lateral impact on other systems.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker manipulates the person and message parameters of the events/contact form to inject CakePHP console path switches into the background job argv. The parameters are modified so that the downstream console dispatcher interprets them as directives (setting the application root) rather than as data. This is the closest CAPEC pattern; the attack does not involve classic OS command injection (CAPEC-88) but rather argument injection into a framework-level dispatcher, making CAPEC-14 the best available match.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: User-controlled form fields (person, message) are passed as arguments to a downstream component (the CakePHP console dispatcher) where special elements (path switches like -app, -root) are interpreted as directives rather than data. The lack of neutralization of these special elements in the job argument vector is the root cause.

The background job enqueue path accepted arbitrary string arguments without validating them against the set of values that the downstream console dispatcher interprets as control switches. The fix adds explicit validation to reject reserved argument values.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a vulnerability in its background job dispatch mechanism that allows remote code execution as the web user. Background job arguments are passed directly as the argv of the CakePHP console process. CakePHP's ShellDispatcher::_parsePaths() scans the entire argv for path switches (-app, --app, -working, --working, -root, --root, -webroot, --webroot) and uses the following element as the application root. The events/contact endpoint passes user-controlled fields (message and person) into job arguments without validation. An attacker who can submit the contact form can set the person field to a reserved switch and the message field to a phar:// URI pointing to a malicious archive. The CakePHP bootstrap then includes Config/core.php from within that archive, executing attacker-controlled PHP code with the privileges of the web user. 

The vulnerability requires the ability to submit the events/contact form (or any other endpoint that forwards user input into background job arguments). No special timing or race condition is required; the attack is deterministic once the crafted parameters are accepted. The impact is full remote code execution in the context of the MISP web server process, allowing data exfiltration, persistence, and lateral movement within the host.

cna.title: Imager versions before 1.036 for Perl disclose uninitialised heap memory reading a paletted image with pixel indexes past its colour map in i_gpix_p and i_glin_p

solutions.value: Upgrade to Imager 1.036 or later.

descriptions.value:
Imager versions before 1.036 for Perl disclose uninitialised heap memory reading a paletted image with pixel indexes past its colour map in i_gpix_p and i_glin_p.

The palette is allocated uninitialised, and only the entries a reader adds count as populated. The TGA reader stores pixel indexes without checking them against the colour map. i_gpix_p() rejects only an index greater than the count, so an index equal to it reads the first unpopulated entry, and getpixel() returns it.

i_glin_p() skips any index at or beyond the count without writing that pixel to the caller's buffer. The palette-to-RGB conversion reads each row through an uninitialised buffer, so those pixels of the converted image hold prior heap contents.

Reading an attacker-supplied image through Imager->read() and then fetching its pixels or converting it to RGB discloses process heap memory.

cna.title: NULL pointer dereference in the ITE IT8xxx2 SHI host-command backend when a host transaction arrives before backend initialization

descriptions.value:
The ITE IT8xxx2 SHI host-command backend in subsys/mgmt/ec_host_cmd/backends/ec_host_cmd_backend_shi_ite.c arms the SPI peripheral before its receive context exists. shi_ite_init_registers() sets the state machine to SHI_STATE_READY_TO_RECV and calls irq_enable() while the device initializes at POST_KERNEL priority CONFIG_KERNEL_INIT_PRIORITY_DEFAULT (40), but data->rx_ctx and data->tx are only assigned later by shi_ite_backend_init(), which ec_host_cmd_init() invokes at CONFIG_EC_HOST_CMD_INIT_PRIORITY (default 80).

If the attached host processor starts a SPI transaction inside that window, the Rx-valid-length interrupt fires, shi_ite_int_handler() passes its state check and calls shi_ite_parse_header(), which stores the host-derived request length through the still-NULL data->rx_ctx. On the IT8xxx2 low addresses are not backed by RAM, and with CONFIG_NULL_POINTER_EXCEPTION_DETECTION_PMP the first bytes of the address space are explicitly made inaccessible, so the store raises a fatal access fault in interrupt context. The window widens further when CONFIG_EC_HOST_CMD_INITIALIZE_AT_BOOT is disabled and the application calls ec_host_cmd_init() itself.

The result is a kernel panic on the embedded controller: with Zephyr's default fatal handler the CPU halts, so the controller stops servicing host commands until a hardware reset. Because the trigger is traffic from the attached host processor -- an untrusted peer from the controller firmware's point of view -- software on that host can provoke the fault by forcing a controller reset and issuing transactions during the reboot, turning a recoverable reset into a persistent outage. Impact is limited to availability: the faulting address is fixed and not attacker-chosen, so no memory-corruption primitive follows.

The fix leaves the interface at SHI_STATE_DISABLED with the interrupt masked during device init, moves irq_enable() into shi_ite_backend_init() after the buffers are published, and makes shi_ite_int_handler() reject a NULL data->rx_ctx while write-clearing IT83XX_SPI_ISR and IT83XX_SPI_RX_VLISR so that an unexpected early interrupt cannot storm.

affected.product: Ultimate Member – User Profile, Registration, Login, Member Directory, Content Restriction & Membership Plugin

descriptions.value: The Ultimate Member – User Profile, Registration, Login, Member Directory, Content Restriction & Membership Plugin plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to authorization bypass in all versions up to, and including, 2.13.1 This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to view privacy-restricted member profile field values — including fields explicitly configured as owner-only, members-only, or role-restricted — by querying the publicly accessible wp_ajax_nopriv_um_get_members endpoint. The nonce required by the endpoint ('um-frontend-nonce') is emitted to all unauthenticated visitors via wp_localize_script, meaning it provides no meaningful access control and any anonymous visitor can satisfy the endpoint's authentication requirements.

cna.title: MarketKing < 2.1.72 Missing Authorization via marketking_send_refund AJAX

cna.title: Dnsmasq: dnsmasq: tcp/53 child-slot exhaustion starves dnssec validation

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Shubham Raj (Causal Security) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value:
The following measures reduce risk:

1. Increase the TCP connection limit with --max-tcp-connections=<N> to raise the number of connections an attacker must hold.
2. Limit per-source TCP connections to port 53 with firewall rules, for example iptables connlimit on tcp/53.
3. Restrict which hosts can reach TCP port 53 if TCP DNS is not required from untrusted networks.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in dnsmasq. The TCP DNS service uses a small fixed pool of child processes and does not set a receive timeout on client connections. A remote attacker can open idle TCP connections to port 53 and occupy the entire pool, preventing new TCP DNS connections and DNSSEC validation that requires TCP fallback. UDP DNS resolution continues, and occupied slots are released after a fixed lifetime.

cna.title: ArcadeDB before 26.9.1 ACL Bypass via Index and TimeSeries

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: ArcadeDB before 26.9.1 ACL Bypass via Index and TimeSeries

descriptions.value: ArcadeDB (Maven artifact com.arcadedb:arcadedb-engine) through 26.8.1 enforces its per-type/per-record access-control rules only in LocalBucket, keyed on file id. Query-execution paths that reach record data through LSM index files or the TimeSeries engine never invoke that permission check, so an authenticated user who is denied readRecord/deleteRecord on a type can still, with a single ordinary SQL statement, read the type's indexed key values and record IDs (e.g. SELECT key, rid FROM INDEX:Type[field]), read MAX/MIN values via the index shortcut, read and count TimeSeries samples, learn the type's record count, and delete index entries (DELETE FROM INDEX:Type[field]), which desynchronizes the index from the data and can defeat unique constraints. Index and type names needed for exploitation are discoverable because SELECT FROM schema:indexes is unfiltered. The issue affects both embedded and server deployments and all transports (HTTP, Bolt, Postgres, Gremlin) once a principal is bound. Fixed in 26.9.1.

cna.title: Mailspring: Stored XSS in attachment quick preview (unsanitized Markdown/DOCX/XLSX conversion)

descriptions.value: Mailspring is a fast, cross-platform, open-source email client. Prior to 1.17.0, attachment quick preview converts Markdown, DOCX, and XLSX attachments with Snarkdown, Mammoth, and SheetJS and inserts the resulting HTML into the preview document through innerHTML without sanitization. A remote sender can craft a supported attachment whose converted HTML executes script when a recipient opens quick preview. The preview renderer has no direct Node or Electron access, but injected script can reach the IPC surface exposed to the quick-preview renderer. This issue alone provides script execution in the preview renderer; separate path-traversal and renderer-controlled file-write vulnerabilities are required for the documented persistent code-execution chain. This issue is fixed in version 1.17.0.

descriptions.value: Laravel-Mediable 7.0.0 before 7.0.2 contains an incomplete patch for CVE-2026-49972 in which the .pht extension is absent from the forbidden_extensions blocklist in config/mediable.php. The blocklist introduced to address CVE-2026-49972 includes phpt but omits pht, which Apache executes as PHP via the default FilesMatch directive on Debian and Ubuntu systems. An attacker can upload a .pht file that passes all validation in MediaUploader::verifyExtension() and File::sanitizeFileName() because pht is not present in the blocklist, causing the file to be written to disk and executed as PHP when requested, enabling remote code execution with the privileges of the web server process.

In version 1.2.9 and earlier, peer_find_template() in src/netflow_plugin/netflow_collector.cpp and src/netflow_plugin/netflow_v9_collector.cpp returns a pointer into global_netflow9_templates after releasing the cache mutex. On deployments with at least two entries in netflow_ports, concurrent template redefinition and data-flowset processing can let add_update_peer_template() reassign the template and free its records vector while another listener dereferences the escaped pointer. An unauthenticated sender that can reach both NetFlow/IPFIX listener ports can trigger a heap-use-after-free and reliably crash FastNetMon. No fixed release is available as of this review.

cna.title: Apache MINA SSHD: Repeated-publickey policy bypass on server

descriptions.value:
Apache MINA SSHD is a Java library for client-side and server-side SSH. SSH servers can be configured to require multi-authentication schemes, for instance two different public keys, not just one. In OpenSSH, this would be done by setting in sshd_config AuthenticationMethods "publickey,publickey". Apache MINA SSHD provides an equivalent configuration mechanism.




In Apache MINA SSHD versions up to 2.19.0 and 3.0.0-M1 to 3.0.0-M5 the server code in component sshd-core does not enforce that the two public keys presented are different. A user can thus successfully authenticate with only one of the two key pairs required by presenting this single key twice. This is a partial authentication bypass.






Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.20.0 or 3.0.0-M6, which fix this issue.

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Shubham Raj (Causal Security) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value:
The following measures reduce risk:

1. Prefer --leasequery=<addr>[/prefix] so only designated relays may query.
2. If leasequery is not needed, do not enable it. It is off by default.
3. If unrestricted leasequery is required, use firewall rules to limit which hosts can send DHCP packets to dnsmasq.

cna.title: Dpdk: dpdk: guest-triggered out-of-bounds walk via vhost indirect descriptor length toctou

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Naseeb Dangi (AOSP Lab @Nankai University) and Xiang Li (AOSP Lab @Nankai University) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: No runtime mitigation. QEMU indirect_desc=off does not help: libvhost honours VRING_DESC_F_INDIRECT anyway. Do not expose vhost-user to untrusted guests.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the DPDK vhost library. When handling a virtio indirect descriptor table, the host reads the table length more than once from guest memory and can allocate a host copy before validating that length. A guest that changes the length between those reads, or that supplies an out-of-range next index on a small host copy in the vDPA relay path, can cause the host vhost process to walk past the validated mapping or heap copy. That can crash or disrupt the vhost process. Out-of-bounds bytes are consumed as descriptor fields for GPA translation and are not returned to the guest as payload. This is a residual issue in the non-contiguous indirect descriptor copy path introduced as part of the CVE-2018-1059 fix.

cna.title: Keycloak-services: keycloak-services: token refresh continues issuing tokens for disabled audience clients

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Moritz Theile (@Moritz-cmd) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: Mitigation for this issue is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria comprising ease of use and deployment, applicability to widespread installation base, or stability.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the OIDC protocol implementation of Keycloak, an open-source identity and access management solution. The issue occurs during the token refresh process when the server restores requested audiences from stored client IDs. Keycloak fails to verify if the target audience client is still enabled before issuing a new access token. This allows an application with an existing refresh token to continue obtaining valid access tokens for a disabled client, potentially bypassing administrative access controls for resource servers that rely on offline JWT validation.

cna.title: Bludit CMS 3.22.0 Missing Authorization via content-get-list AJAX Endpoint

descriptions.value: Bludit CMS through 3.22.0 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated users holding the Author or Editor role to read the full content of private drafts and scheduled posts belonging to any other user, including administrators, by exploiting the content-get-list AJAX endpoint in bl-kernel/ajax/content-get-list.php. Attackers can send an authenticated GET request to the admin AJAX endpoint with the draft parameter set to true, triggering getList() without ownership constraints and returning serialized page objects site-wide, exposing pre-publication material and sensitive notes stored in administrator-owned drafts.

cna.title: Imager versions before 1.036 for Perl exit the process reading a TGA with a colour map length of 32768 or more in tga_palette_read

solutions.value: Upgrade to Imager 1.036 or later.

descriptions.value:
Imager versions before 1.036 for Perl exit the process reading a TGA with a colour map length of 32768 or more in tga_palette_read.

The reader unpacks the two-byte colour map length into a signed short, so a length of 32768 or more becomes negative. tga_palette_read() casts that value to size_t and asks mymalloc() for a size near SIZE_MAX. The allocation fails and Imager's allocator calls exit(3).

Reading an attacker-supplied file through Imager->read() triggers an uncatchable exit.

cna.title: Integer Underflow → Heap Out-of-Bounds Read in `bson_new_from_buffer()

descriptions.value: A missing lower-bound validation in the bson_new_from_buffer() function of libbson allows an integer underflow when processing BSON data with a zero-length prefix. The function reads a 32-bit document length from the input buffer but does not verify that the value is at least 5 (the minimum valid BSON document size) before using it in an array index calculation. When the length field is zero, the expression used to check the document's null terminator wraps to UINT32_MAX, causing a heap out-of-bounds read that crashes the process. An unauthorized party who can supply crafted BSON input to an application using this API can cause a denial of service.

cna.title: Zimbra Collaboration Suite Pre-Authentication Reflected Cross-Site Scripting via Login Page zrememberme Parameter

descriptions.value: A reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability in the login page of Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute JavaScript through the zrememberme parameter. A crafted relogin URL selects a two-factor error display that inserts the parameter into a hidden input attribute without HTML encoding. A victim who opens the URL receives attacker-controlled script and page content under the legitimate Zimbra origin, allowing credential capture through a replacement login form. This vulnerability leads to unbounded memory accumulation within the client's Java Virtual Machine (JVM) heap, causing an `OutOfMemoryError` and a denial of service (DoS) due to a process crash.

cna.title: Mesop: Unauthenticated ANSI Escape Sequence Injection in CSP Reporting Endpoint

descriptions.value: Mesop is a Python-based UI framework that allows users to build web applications. Prior to 1.3.4, the unauthenticated /__csp__ endpoint passes attacker-controlled document-uri, blocked-uri, and violated-directive values to the csp_report handler in mesop/server/static_file_serving.py, which prints them to standard output without neutralizing terminal control sequences. When an operator views the resulting logs in an ANSI-capable terminal, injected ANSI or VT100 sequences can clear or reposition the display, hide text, or present forged messages, reducing the integrity of monitoring and incident-response output. This issue is fixed in version 1.3.4.

cna.title: Cache poisoning via unvalidated image layer DiffIDs

workarounds.value:
Do not share BuildKit daemon cache between trusted and untrusted builds. Use isolated BuildKit daemons or ephemeral builders for untrusted image sources, or prune BuildKit cache after processing untrusted images.

Disabling stargz alone is not sufficient because regular snapshotters are also affected.

supportingMedia.value:
Do not share BuildKit daemon cache between trusted and untrusted builds. Use isolated BuildKit daemons or ephemeral builders for untrusted image sources, or prune BuildKit cache after processing untrusted images.

Disabling stargz alone is not sufficient because regular snapshotters are also affected.

descriptions.value:
A malicious image can advertise DiffIDs from another image while containing different layer contents. In affected versions, BuildKit could use the advertised DiffIDs to derive cache and snapshot identity without validating that they matched the actual layer contents.

If a BuildKit daemon with shared or persistent cache first processes such a malicious image, a later build using the victim image may mount the attacker-controlled layer contents as the base image. This can allow code from the malicious image to run in the victim build, for example by replacing a commonly executed path such as /bin/sh. The attacker-controlled code may read build secrets mounted into the build, access other build resources, alter output artifacts, or hang the build.

The issue affects both regular snapshotters and lazy-pulling snapshotters such as stargz.

descriptions.value: rustls-webpki (rustls/webpki) versions 0.101.0 through 0.103.11 and 0.104.0-alpha releases before 0.104.0-alpha.6 ignore X.509 name constraints that apply to URI names, causing such constraints to be accepted rather than enforced. x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Escape object names in the Overmind
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix applies HTML output encoding to the user-controlled label variable (lbl) before it is interpolated into the innerHTML string in both affected view templates. By wrapping the label with escapeHtml(), any HTML metacharacters in object names are neutralized, preventing injected markup from being interpreted as executable HTML or JavaScript in the viewer's browser.
assumptions: The exact affected version range is not explicitly stated in the patch; the tag_version_boundary indicates the fix commit is 55 commits after v2.5.47, suggesting versions up to (but not including) the release containing this commit are affected. The precise fixed version is unspecified.

PR:L assumes the attacker needs at least low-level authenticated access to create or rename a MISP object whose name appears in the Overmind legend. If unauthenticated object creation is possible in some deployment, PR could be N.
UI:P assumes the victim simply views the Overmind dashboard page (passive interaction). If the page requires a specific navigation action beyond normal browsing, UI could be A.

SC:H and SI:H assume the XSS grants full access to the victim's MISP session (cookies, API tokens, in-page data). A more conservative assessment could rate these L if the Overmind view exposes limited data.
The CAPEC-1 mapping is direct and unambiguous for this stored XSS; no uncertainty is noted beyond the standard CAPEC granularity.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Two one-line changes in the Overmind theme view templates. In app/View/Themed/Overmind/Elements/Events/View/event_general.ctp (line 607) and app/View/Themed/Overmind/Elements/Servers/View/preview_general.ctp (line 323), the raw lbl variable used in the title attribute and inner text of the legend span element is replaced with escapeHtml(lbl). No other logic, routing, or configuration changes are made.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The vulnerability is exploitable over the network via a web browser. AC:L: Exploitation requires only creating an object with a crafted name; no race or special conditions. AT:N: The attack targets the same MISP instance. PR:L: The attacker needs low-level authenticated access to create or rename an MISP object. UI:P: The victim passively interacts by viewing the Overmind dashboard page; no click or explicit action is needed beyond normal page rendering. VC/VI/VA:N: No direct impact on the MISP server's confidentiality, integrity, or availability. SC:H/SI:H: The injected script executes in the victim's browser within the MISP origin, enabling full session compromise (cookie theft, data exfiltration, arbitrary actions). SA:N: No availability impact on the victim's browser.

capecRationale.rationale: The attack pattern involves injecting client-side script into a web application via user-controllable data (object names) that is rendered without encoding in an HTML context. CAPEC-1 is the canonical XSS attack pattern and directly matches the mechanism: attacker-controlled data flows into an innerHTML sink. No uncertainty in this mapping; the patch explicitly describes the innerHTML concatenation of unescaped labels.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: User-controlled object names are concatenated directly into an innerHTML string without HTML encoding, allowing injected markup to execute in the victim's browser. This is a textbook stored XSS via missing output encoding at an HTML sink.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the Overmind theme's statistics views. The event General card and the server/feed preview card constructed donut chart legend labels by directly concatenating object name or category keys into an innerHTML string without HTML-encoding. Because MISP object names are user-controllable by any authenticated user with sufficient permissions to create or modify such objects, an attacker could craft a name containing malicious markup. When any other user viewed the affected Overmind dashboard, the injected markup would be interpreted as live HTML/JavaScript in the victim's browser, executing in the context of the MISP application origin. This could allow session hijacking, data exfiltration, or arbitrary actions performed on behalf of the victim. 

The vulnerability requires the attacker to have low-level authenticated access to create or rename an object whose name is rendered in the legend, and the victim to view the Overmind event or server preview page. No special browser conditions or race conditions are required.
