Roller treats weblog administrators as untrusted and exposes weblog and entry data to templates only through wrapper classes, but a public accessor on those wrapper classes returned the underlying persistent object directly, including the stored password hash of the weblog's creator and of any author whose entry renders on the page. cna.title: NetBird client userspace firewall allows IP-fragmented packets without evaluating ACL rules

descriptions.value: A protection mechanism failure in the userspace firewall of the NetBird client (client/firewall/uspfilter) in NetBird versions 0.55.0 through 0.74.6 allows an attacker who controls an enrolled peer to bypass the access control rules of another peer by sending IP-fragmented packets. The packet filter returned an allow verdict for any IPv4 fragment, and for any IPv6 packet carrying a Fragment extension header, before evaluating the ACL rules. This applied to the leading fragment as well as to continuation fragments, so no part of a fragmented datagram was filtered and ports denied by policy could be reached. The userspace filter is the packet filter wherever the client does not program the kernel firewall, which includes the Android and iOS apps. The issue is fixed in version 0.74.7, in the Android app from version 0.6.0 and in the iOS app from version 0.3.3, which evaluate fragments against the same ACL rules as unfragmented packets.

solutions.value: Upgrade the NetBird client to version 0.74.7 or later, the Android app to version 0.6.0 or later, and the iOS app to version 0.3.3 or later. In these versions the userspace firewall decodes the transport header of the leading fragment, evaluates it against the same connection tracking and ACL rules as an unfragmented packet, applies that verdict to the continuation fragments of the same datagram, and drops fragments whose leading fragment was denied, never seen, or overlapped (pull request #6781).

cna.title: Pingora forwards client-nominated Connection headers to HTTP/1 upstreams, allowing ACL bypass in specific chained deployments

solutions.value:
Mitigation:

  *  

Upgrade to pingora 0.9.0 or later. By default, Pingora now removes hop-by-hop and Connection-nominated headers from upstream requests, and rejects requests whose Connection header nominates Host, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Proto, or a pseudo-header. This is controlled by PeerOptions::http_upstream_request_policy (HttpUpstreamRequestPolicy). Fix commits:  https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora/commit/28c18e6b6b04dd0bd937234e5950049e6d74cded ,  https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora/commit/ca23f1668eca8e78be7ba62ef0edbd458b40eeee 


  *  

Do not use HttpUpstreamRequestPolicy::preserve() if the origin relies on headers added by Pingora; it restores the old passthrough behavior.


  *  

If you cannot upgrade: in upstream_request_filter, remove the Connection header and every header it nominates before adding trusted headers.

descriptions.value:
Summary



Before version 0.9.0, the HTTP/1 upstream path in pingora-proxy passed the downstream request through upstream_request_filter and wrote it to the upstream without removing the client's Connection header, other hop-by-hop headers, or the headers Connection nominated, although RFC 9110 Section 7.6.1 requires intermediaries to remove them. The HTTP/2 upstream path already removed Connection and related HTTP/1-specific headers. A client could therefore nominate a header that the application adds in upstream_request_filter (for example, Connection: keep-alive, X-Forwarded-For). A downstream HTTP/1 intermediary that honors Connection would then strip the Pingora-added header before it reached the origin.




Impact



Specifically affects chained deployments where an HTTP/1 intermediary between Pingora and the origin processes Connection nominations (for example, Go's net/http/httputil.ReverseProxy) and the origin trusts headers added by that intermediary (for example, X-Forwarded-For for IP-based authorization). A remote, unauthenticated attacker can have those headers removed, potentially bypassing authorization. The reporter demonstrated access to an IP-restricted endpoint using X-Forwarded-For for IP validation on the origin. This is the same class of issue as CVE-2022-31813 in Apache HTTP Server.




Note that Cloudflare CDN customers were unaffected, as no such chained deployment as described above exists with internal Pingora services, and Connection headers are sanitized before arriving at Pingora gateways.

  *

By default, Pingora now removes hop-by-hop and Connection-nominated headers from upstream requests, and rejects requests whose Connection header nominates Host, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Proto, or a pseudo-header.   *

cna.title: Pingora HTTP/2 server memory exhaustion through unbounded default header-list and concurrent-stream limits

solutions.value:
Mitigation:

  *  

Upgrade to pingora 0.8.1 or later (fix:  https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora/commit/d193c8d49b8b7c1c1ede93183759caa4f6906bbd ). When no H2Options are supplied, Pingora now advertises and enforces a 64 KiB decoded header-list limit and at most 100 concurrent streams per connection.


  *  

Applications that supply their own H2Options are not covered by these defaults and must set max_header_list_size and max_concurrent_streams explicitly (this also works on versions before 0.8.1), or, on 0.8.1 and later, start from pingora_core::protocols::http::v2::server::default_h2_options(). H2Options::default() does not include these limits.

H2Options::default() does not include these limits.

descriptions.value:
Summary



Before version 0.8.1, Pingora's HTTP/2 server used the h2 crate's default limits unless the application set its own 16 MiB decoded header-list size and no limit on concurrent streams. A remote, unauthenticated client can send 1-byte HPACK references to a near-empty header, making the server allocate hundreds of thousands of header fields per stream across an unlimited number of streams on one connection, and use HTTP/2 flow control to keep those streams open. This can exhaust memory and degrade or terminate the Pingora process.




Impact



Remote, unauthenticated denial of service against any Pingora service that terminates HTTP/2 (h2 or h2c) without explicitly setting max_header_list_size and max_concurrent_streams. The reporter showed that a single connection could get a Pingora process with a 2 GiB memory limit OOM-killed.




Note that Cloudflare CDN customers were unaffected, as internal Pingora services at Cloudflare do not have HTTP/2 clients.



Mitigation:

  *  

Upgrade to pingora 0.8.1 or later (fix:  https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora/commit/d193c8d49b8b7c1c1ede93183759caa4f6906bbd ). When no H2Options are supplied, Pingora now advertises and enforces a 64 KiB decoded header-list limit and at most 100 concurrent streams per connection.

H2Options::default() does not include these limits.

descriptions.value:
Improper Validation of Integrity Check Value vulnerability in hexpm hex allows a package mirror to substitute the tarball that mix hex.package fetch PACKAGE VERSION --output - writes to standard output.

Hex compares a fetched tarball's inner and outer checksums with the repository's signed registry before writing it to a file or unpacking it. The standard output branch of mix hex.package fetch writes the bytes returned by Hex.SCM.fetch/3 without that comparison, and Hex.SCM.fetch/3 doesn't verify freshly downloaded tarballs itself. When a mirror configured with HEX_MIRROR_URL or mirror_url serves altered bytes, the command prints them and exits successfully, while the same fetch with --output FILE fails with a checksum mismatch.

Hex also prints diagnostics to standard output while the command runs: the body of a failed HTTP response from the update check or a registry fetch, and API warnings from the x-hex-message header. A mirror that answers one of those requests with an error whose body is a tar archive gets that archive written to standard output ahead of the verified tarball, so a pipeline that unpacks standard output extracts the mirror's files. This happens even when the checksum check then fails, because the archive is already on standard output.

This issue affects hex: from 0.20.2 before 2.5.2.

* mix hex.package fetch PACKAGE VERSION --output - calls fetch_tarball!/3, which calls Hex.SCM.fetch/3.
* For a fresh download, Hex.SCM.fetch/3 writes the response body to the cache and returns it without comparing it to the registry checksum.
* The standard output branch passes those bytes to IO.binwrite/1. The file and --unpack branches call verify_inner_checksum!/4 and verify_outer_checksum!/4 first.
* While the task runs, Hex prints messages with Hex.Shell.info/1, which writes to standard output. Hex.Utils.print_error_result/1 prints the body of an error response that way; the update checker calls it when its request for installs/hex-1.x.csv fails, and Hex.Registry.Server calls it when a registry fetch fails and the cached registry is used. Hex.HTTP prints the x-hex-message warning of each response the same way. These are printed before the tarball is written, so the mirror chooses bytes that come before the tarball on standard output.

cna.title: Stored XSS via related ticket subject on RTIR Split and Create Incident forms

descriptions.value: CAPEC-592 Stored XSS

RTIR's ticket creation forms show the subject of the related
      ticket when splitting a ticket or creating an incident from a
      report, and they render that subject without HTML escaping. A
      ticket subject containing script runs it when a user opens either
      form. RTIR grants everyone the right to create Incident Reports by
      default, so an unauthenticated sender of an emailed report can set
      that subject. The script then runs in the session of the incident
      handler who creates an incident from the report or splits it, and
      can act in RT with that user's authority. 


The issue was fixed in version 6.0.4. RTIR 5.0 is not
      affected.

workarounds.value:
1. Restrict outbound network access — use Kubernetes NetworkPolicy to limit proxy pod egress to only legitimate Azure Key Vault endpoints on port 443.
2. Monitor KMS call patterns — alert on unwrap requests targeting unexpected vault hostnames.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to enforce strict allowlist regex validation on wire-deserialized vaultName in the Azure Key Vault KMS provider before constructing outbound HTTP endpoints: upgrade to kroxylicious-kms-provider-azure-key-vault-kms 0.25.1+ (or the fixed Kroxylicious Kms Provider Azure Key Vault Kms builds), which validate Key Vault name using validateKeyVaultName to reject names containing dots, URL fragments, invalid lengths, or malformed hyphens before constructing the Key Vault URL, closing all 2 injection vectors (crafted EDEK containing an arbitrary hostname in vaultName, vaultName URL fragment injection). Until patched, this is a concern on Kafka clusters using the Kroxylicious Record Encryption filter with Azure Key Vault KMS, so restrict proxy pod outbound network egress using Kubernetes NetworkPolicy strictly to legitimate Azure Key Vault endpoints on port 443 and alert on unwrap requests targeting unexpected vault hostnames. As a compensating measure, Deploy Falco or eBPF runtime security to detect anomalous outbound network connections initiated by the Kroxylicious proxy process to unexpected destinations. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying unvalidated input SSRF defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-1315 Allowlist-Preferred Input Validation (Deny-by-Default Filtering) (high)

descriptions.value: The Azure Key Vault KMS provider in Kroxylicious accepts an untrusted vaultName from wire-deserialized EDEK bytes without format validation, enabling SSRF that exfiltrates the proxy's Azure bearer token to an attacker-controlled host. descriptions.value:

Only applications that use RemoteSyslogAppender are affected.

This issue affects Apache log4net: from 1.2.12 before 3.5.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.5.0, which fixes the issue.

cna.title: Cruise-control: streams for apache kafka cruise control: authentication bypass via extra path segment allows unauthenticated access to all admin endpoints

workarounds.value:
1. Verify Strimzi NetworkPolicy exists restricting CC :9090 to operator pods
2. Do not expose CC :9090 via Ingress or Route — must not be externally accessible
3. Confirm TLS is enabled on the CC HTTP endpoint (Strimzi default)
4. For standalone CC: deploy path-normalizing reverse proxy and restrict :9090 via firewall

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to eliminate the path discrepancy between Jetty security constraints and ParameterUtils routing by canonicalizing URI paths prior to authorization evaluation: upgrade to the fixed Cruise Control/Kafka Relations Sink/Playbook Dispatcher/Cloudservices/Kafka Relations Sink/Redhat User Workloads/Playbook Dispatcher Connect builds, which canonicalizes request URI paths prior to authorization and registers wildcard security constraints or denies uncovered HTTP methods in Jetty, closing prepending an arbitrary path segment to administrative endpoint URIs. Until patched, this is a concern on Cruise Control deployments exposing HTTP port 9090 without network policy restrictions or reverse proxy path filtering, so Enforce Strimzi NetworkPolicy restricting port 9090 access strictly to operator pods, prohibit external exposure through Ingress or Routes, and deploy a path-normalizing reverse proxy or firewall rules for standalone setups. As a compensating measure, Require authenticated identity verification at the network boundary using a zero trust gateway or identity-aware proxy before traffic reaches port 9090, Restrict network access to Cruise Control port 9090 using host-based firewalls like firewalld or nftables, Bind the Cruise Control service to localhost to ensure all incoming traffic passes through a local tunnel or controlling reverse proxy, Enforce URL path authorization rules at an upstream reverse proxy to block unmapped or manipulated URI paths, and Forward Cruise Control administrative endpoint invocations to a SIEM to detect unauthorized execution of admin actions. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying path discrepancy authentication bypass defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-921 URL Request Path Canonicalization Before Authorization (high)

descriptions.value: Cruise Control's Jetty ConstraintSecurityHandler registers security constraints on exact path specs without a catch-all wildcard constraint and without calling setDenyUncoveredHttpMethods(true). The servlet routes requests using Path.of(pathInfo).getFileName(), which strips all leading segments and trailing slashes. Requests like POST /kafkacruisecontrol/x/rebalance bypass authentication entirely but still dispatch to admin endpoints. All 15 admin endpoints become reachable without authentication. In AMQ Streams, the Strimzi operator's NetworkPolicy restricts Cruise Control port 9090 to operator pods only, reducing effective severity to Important.

cna.title: Stored XSS via crafted URLs in HTML ticket content in Request Tracker

descriptions.value: CAPEC-592 Stored XSS

workarounds.value:
Set @Active_MakeClicky to an empty list in
      RT_SiteConfig.pm and restart the web server. This disables
      automatic link creation for URLs in ticket content.

supportingMedia.value:
Set @Active_MakeClicky to an empty list in
      RT_SiteConfig.pm and restart the web server. This disables
      automatic link creation for URLs in ticket content.

descriptions.value:
RT's automatic link creation for URLs in HTML ticket content does
      not HTML-escape the URL it places in the link. A URL crafted to
      break out of the link's address can add a script that runs when the
      ticket history is displayed, with no further action by the viewer.
      Anyone who can add HTML content to a ticket can plant it. That
      includes an unauthenticated sender of HTML email to any queue that

      for a queue that accepts mail from the public. The script runs in
      the session of any user who views the ticket, and can act in RT
      with that user's authority.


This issue was fixed in version 5.0.11 and 6.0.4

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Subscription authorization policies not enforced by namespace-level backlog and unsubscribe operations and by topic expire-all

descriptions.value:
Apache Pulsar namespaces can restrict which roles may use a subscription, either with the Prefix subscription authentication mode, which requires a subscription name to start with the role name, or by granting permission on a subscription to specific roles. Topic-level subscription operations, such as consuming, skipping messages, resetting a cursor or deleting a subscription, apply these subscription policies. Several admin REST API operations that act on subscriptions did not apply them:

- the namespace-level and bundle-level clear backlog operations, both for a named subscription and for all subscriptions;
- the namespace-level and bundle-level unsubscribe operations;
- the topic-level operation that expires messages for all subscriptions of a topic.

With the default authorization provider, the namespace-level operations require only consume permission granted on the namespace, and the expire-all operation requires only consume permission on the topic. As a result, when authentication and authorization are enabled and a namespace uses the Prefix subscription authentication mode or subscription permissions, an authenticated user with such consume permission can clear the backlog of, expire messages of, or delete a subscription that the policies would deny to that user. Tenant admin or superuser access is not required. The clear backlog operations can also be applied to the cursors used for geo-replication, so that messages not yet replicated to a remote cluster are skipped. Deployments that do not configure the Prefix subscription authentication mode or subscription permissions (the defaults) are not affected by this bypass, because consume permission on the namespace or topic already allows these operations there. This impact analysis assumes that Pulsar has been configured with the default authorization provider. For custom authorization providers, the impact could be different.

The impact is on the integrity of subscription state. Clearing or expiring the backlog moves the subscription's cursor forward, so unacknowledged messages are no longer delivered to the subscription's consumers. The unsubscribe operation deletes a subscription that has no connected consumers. Skipped messages can be permanently deleted once no other subscription or the namespace's retention policy keeps them. The issue does not allow reading message contents, changing permissions or policies, or accessing other namespaces, and it does not affect the availability of the broker.

In fixed versions, the namespace-level and bundle-level operations for a named subscription apply the subscription policies to that subscription, and the operations for all subscriptions, when requested by a user who is not a tenant admin or superuser, only act on the subscriptions that the user may access. Clearing the backlog of geo-replication cursors requires tenant admin or superuser access. Topic-level subscription operations apply the subscription policies for all types of authentication data, including that of the anonymous user role.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.8.0 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

All brokers in a cluster must be upgraded before relying on the namespace-level restrictions, because brokers that have not been upgraded do not apply them when they receive the internal per-bundle requests.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately can reduce exposure by restricting network access to the broker's admin REST API to trusted administrative clients.

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: OpenAM before 16.1.3 PKCE Enforcement Bypass via OAuth 2.0 Hybrid Flows

descriptions.value: OpenAM before 16.1.3 applies its OAuth2 Provider PKCE enforcement only to authorization requests whose response_type is exactly code, so codes issued through OpenID Connect hybrid flows (code token, code id_token, code token id_token) carry no bound challenge. An attacker who intercepts such a code can redeem it for a public client's tokens with any non-empty code_verifier.

cna.title: Apache log4net: NUL character truncates EventLogAppender records

descriptions.value:
Improper Neutralization of Null Byte or NUL Character vulnerability in the EventLogAppender of Apache log4net.

A NUL character in logged content ended the Windows Event Log record at that point, so everything the layout rendered after it, including exception text and trailing fields, was silently not stored. A party whose data reaches a log message could hide the rest of that record. Only applications on Windows that use EventLogAppender are affected.

This issue affects Apache log4net: from 1.2.9 before 3.5.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.5.0, which fixes the issue.

cna.title: Plane: asset download endpoints scope file lookups to the workspace (not the project / published entity) → cross-project & unauthenticated private-file disclosure

descriptions.value: Plane is an open-source project management tool. Prior to 1.4.0, WorkspaceFileAssetEndpoint.get and WorkspaceAssetDownloadEndpoint.get resolve FileAsset records within a workspace without checking membership in the asset's project, allowing a workspace member to download assets from private projects when the asset UUID is known. EntityAssetEndpoint.get is a separate public-anchor endpoint that grants AllowAny access and scopes the lookup only to the anchor's workspace rather than its published entity or project. An unauthenticated caller who knows a valid anchor and an asset UUID can therefore retrieve issue-description or comment-description assets belonging to unpublished or private projects in that workspace. This issue is fixed in 1.4.0.

cna.title: vLLM: Mirrored multimodal IPC caches desync after a rejected request — a later request reusing the same media hash trips a receiver assertion in the engine core

descriptions.value: vLLM is an inference and serving engine for large language models. Prior to 0.28.0, the default mirrored multimodal LRU cache can commit a media hash in the frontend sender cache during multimodal rendering and before engine admission, while the engine receiver cache never receives the payload if that request is rejected. A later request reusing the same media hash causes MultiModalProcessorSenderCache to send no payload and MultiModalReceiverCache to reach an assertion with the message "Expected a cached item," producing a shared-service availability failure. This issue is fixed in version 0.28.0.

cna.title: Plane: Magic-code verifier endpoint has no rate limit, enabling 6-digit OTP brute force

descriptions.value: Plane is an open-source project management tool. Prior to 1.4.0, Plane's magic-code email login uses a six-digit numeric OTP with approximately 20 bits of entropy. The verifier has no per-code failed-attempt counter, and an incorrect code does not increment a counter, invalidate the Redis entry, or lock the email address. The verifier extends django.views.View rather than DRF's APIView, so the configured AnonRateThrottle limit does not apply. The middleware stack also contains no Django-level rate limiter such as django-ratelimit, django-axes, or an IP-throttling middleware. This vulnerability is fixed in 1.4.0.

cna.title: ColdFusion | Incorrect Authorization (CWE-863)
Apache Pulsar: Function trigger publishes to the input topic without checking the caller's produce permission

descriptions.value:
The Pulsar Functions Worker provides a REST API endpoint for triggering a function, which publishes a caller-supplied value to one of the function's configured input topics. The Functions Worker performs this publish with its own broker client, which authenticates with the Worker's configured broker-client credentials rather than the credentials of the API caller.

When authorization is enabled, in Apache Pulsar 2.4.0 and later versions, the trigger endpoint checks only that the caller is authorized to perform function operations in the function's namespace. It does not check that the caller is authorized to produce to the input topic that the message is published to. Versions before 2.4.0 do not perform a caller authorization check for the trigger endpoint at all. Function input topics are not restricted to the function's own tenant or namespace, and registering a function does not require produce permission on its input topics.

As a result, an authenticated user who is authorized to manage functions in a namespace, for example a role granted the functions permission on that namespace, can cause the Functions Worker to publish messages with caller-controlled content to a topic that the user is not authorized to produce to, including topics in other tenants. These messages are published under the identity of the Functions Worker. The issue does not require any function instance to be running or any function code to be executed. It requires that the Functions Worker's broker-client identity is itself authorized to produce to the target topic and, in Apache Pulsar 2.3.0 and later versions, to list the subscriptions of the target topic, as is the case when that identity is a superuser. The impact is on the integrity of the data in the affected topics: consumers of those topics may receive messages from a user who is not permitted to publish them. This concerns the Functions Worker REST API as called by an external, authenticated client; it does not change the security model for function code, which must be fully trusted.

In fixed versions, when authorization is enabled, triggering a function additionally requires the caller to be authorized to produce to the selected input topic before any message is published.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.0.0-rc1-incubating before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users of Apache Pulsar 2.4.0 and later versions with authorization enabled who cannot upgrade immediately can limit the permission to manage functions to trusted roles. Users of versions before 2.4.0 should restrict access to the Functions Worker REST API to trusted callers, because in these versions the trigger endpoint does not check the caller's permission to manage functions.

cna.title: Console-operator: streams for apache kafka console: cross-namespace kafkauser secret exfiltration via confused deputy

workarounds.value:
1. Restrict Console CR RBAC — remove create/update verbs on consoles.console.streamshub.github.com from tenant-facing roles. Only trusted cluster administrators should manage Console CRs.
2. Audit existing Console CRs — review all Console CRs for kafkaUser.namespace fields pointing outside the CR's own namespace.
3. Network policy (defense-in-depth) — apply NetworkPolicy to restrict operator pod egress.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to enforce strict same-namespace boundary validation on KafkaUser credentials namespace references in Console Operator custom resources to prevent cross-namespace Secret reads: upgrade to the fixed Console Operator builds, which enforce an assertNamespaceAllowed() guard with a same-namespace default check when reading KafkaUser namespace configuration, closing all 2 injection vectors (Console custom resource namespace manipulation, cross-namespace Secret reference). Until patched, this is a concern on Kubernetes clusters running Console Operator where non-admin users have create or update permissions on Console custom resources, so Remove create and update permissions on Console custom resources from tenant roles and audit existing custom resources for kafkaUser.namespace values pointing outside their own namespace. As a compensating measure, Configure Kubernetes API server audit logging to record Console custom resource modifications and cross-namespace Secret read operations performed by the operator service account. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying confused deputy cross-namespace access defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-711 Admission Controller Policy Enforcement (OPA/Gatekeeper/Kyverno) (high)

descriptions.value: The StreamsHub Console operator acts as a confused deputy: a Kubernetes tenant with permission to create a Console custom resource can set spec.kafkaClusters[].credentials.kafkaUser.namespace to any namespace. The operator, running with cluster-wide Secrets RBAC, reads the victim-namespace KafkaUser Secret (SASL credentials or TLS private keys) and writes the plaintext material into a Secret in the attacker's namespace. No same-namespace check or allowlist exists anywhere in the code path.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar Manager: Missing authentication and authorization and disclosure of the Pulsar admin credential; end of life

descriptions.value:
Apache Pulsar Manager is a web console for administering Apache Pulsar clusters. It has its own user accounts and login, and it can be configured with an HTTP authentication credential, such as a token, that it uses to call the Pulsar admin API on behalf of its users. Pulsar Manager has the following security issues:

- The operation for creating the initial administrator (superuser) account is available without authentication, and it remains available after the instance has been initialized. Anyone who can reach Pulsar Manager can create an additional administrator account at any time and log in with it. This issue affects versions 0.3.0 and later.
- Requests to the Pulsar admin API that Pulsar Manager proxies to the configured Pulsar cluster are not subject to Pulsar Manager's authentication. Version 0.2.0 checks the caller's permissions for some of these requests, but not for all of them. An unauthenticated user can therefore use Pulsar Manager to send requests to the Pulsar admin API, which the cluster processes with the credential configured in Pulsar Manager.
- The destination of a proxied request can be chosen by the requester, and Pulsar Manager attaches its configured Pulsar admin credential to the request. An unauthenticated user can make Pulsar Manager send this credential to a host of the user's choosing, and the credential can then be used directly against the Pulsar cluster.
- In versions 0.3.0 and later, Pulsar Manager does not distinguish between privilege levels of its accounts. Every account, including one created through the first issue, effectively has full administrative privileges in Pulsar Manager.

The impact depends on the version and the deployment. In versions 0.3.0 and later, any user who can reach Pulsar Manager over the network can take full control of Pulsar Manager. In all versions, when Pulsar Manager is configured with an HTTP authentication credential for a Pulsar cluster, any user who can reach Pulsar Manager can perform the Pulsar admin operations that this credential permits and can obtain the credential itself. When Pulsar Manager is configured with the token signing key of a Pulsar cluster, an administrator of Pulsar Manager can create tokens for the cluster.

Apache Pulsar Manager is no longer maintained and is completely unsupported. The Apache Pulsar PMC has retired it. There are no supported versions, and no further releases, fixes or security updates will be made for any version. These issues will not be fixed.

Using Pulsar Manager is not recommended. Users should stop using Pulsar Manager, remove existing deployments, and move to one of the alternatives described in the Administration UI documentation (https://pulsar.apache.org/docs/administration-ui). Users who have exposed Pulsar Manager configured with a Pulsar credential or token signing key should also consider replacing that credential or key.

Until a deployment is removed, users should not expose Pulsar Manager to untrusted networks, and should restrict network access to it to trusted administrators.

cna.title: Stored XSS via HTML scrubber rule in RTIR

descriptions.value: CAPEC-592 Stored XSS

RTIR extends RT's HTML scrubber to allow an internal link
      placeholder, and the extension lets through any link that merely
      contains the placeholder, including links using the executable
      javascript: scheme. The change applies to the whole RT instance
      once RTIR is installed, not only to RTIR's own queues. Anyone who
      can add HTML content to a ticket on such an instance can store
      such a link. That includes an unauthenticated sender of HTML email
      to the Incident Reports queue, which RTIR opens to everyone by
      default. Script runs when a user clicks the link, in that user's
      session, and can act in RT with that user's authority.


This issue was fixed in version 5.0.11 and 6.0.4

descriptions.value: vLLM is an inference and serving engine for large language models. Prior to 0.30.0, Harmony tool continuations submitted through "POST /v1/responses" requests rebuild the next-turn engine input without preserving the cache_salt value, placing the continuation prefix in the global unsalted cache namespace even when the caller enabled salting. On deployments with prefix caching enabled, which is the default, an authenticated tenant who can reconstruct a victim's low-entropy post-tool history can submit the same continuation and use the cached_tokens_per_turn count to determine whether the prefix was previously processed, defeating the intended tenant isolation of salted prefix caching. This issue is fixed in version 0.30.0.

cna.title: Plane: Hardcoded SECRET_KEY and LIVE_SERVER_SECRET_KEY shipped in aio/cli community deployment manifests — session forgery and live-server auth bypass

descriptions.value: Plane is an open-source project management tool. Prior to 1.4.0, the deployments/aio/community/ and deployments/cli/community/ manifests provide fixed, publicly known SECRET_KEY and LIVE_SERVER_SECRET_KEY defaults that remain active when operators do not override them. cna.title: NetBird relay server decodes unauthenticated Hello handshake data with gob before verifying the HMAC signature

descriptions.value: Deserialization of untrusted data in the relay server handshake of NetBird versions 0.29.0 through 0.74.7 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to reach the Go encoding/gob decoder with attacker-supplied bytes before any credential is checked, which can lead to denial of service of the relay server. The deprecated Hello handshake message was still accepted before authentication and its token was decoded with gob.NewDecoder (shared/relay/auth/hmac) before the HMAC signature was verified. The handshake buffer limits the input to 212 bytes and the pre-authentication phase to 10 seconds, so there is no impact on confidentiality or integrity and the impact on availability depends on a separate weakness in the gob decoder of the Go toolchain used to build the relay server, such as CVE-2024-34156. The Auth handshake, used by clients since version 0.29.1, does not use gob. The issue is fixed in version 0.75.0, which removes the Hello handshake and the gob-based token decoding.

solutions.value: Upgrade the NetBird relay server to version 0.75.0 or later. In this version the relay server no longer accepts the Hello message type, and the gob-based token and message decoding behind it has been removed. Handshake authentication runs only through the Auth message, whose token is parsed by a fixed-layout reader with explicit length checks (pull request #6783).

configurations.value: Only the NetBird relay server is affected. The severity was reassessed by the vendor from the reported High to Medium because the handshake limits the attacker-controlled input to 212 bytes.

timeline.value: Reported to the vendor through a GitHub Security Advisory

cna.title: Spice-server: spice: heap oob read/write via unchecked migration data offsets

credits.value: Upstream acknowledges Tristan Madani (Talence Security) as the original reporter.

workarounds.value:
This vulnerability is only exploitable during VM live migration by an authenticated SPICE client. If live migration is not required, disabling it eliminates the attack surface. If live migration is needed, restrict SPICE client connections to trusted networks using firewall rules and enforce strong authentication (TLS with mutual certificate validation, or SASL with strong credentials) to limit who can connect as a SPICE client.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to enforce strict bounds validation on client-supplied offsets and buffer lengths across all SPICE migration data handlers prior to memory operations: upgrade to the fixed Spice/Spice Server builds, which validate migration data offsets and read bounds against declared message lengths instead of reallocating from attacker-controlled values, closing all 4 injection vectors (RedCharDevice restore via write_data_ptr offset manipulation, smartcard restore via read_data_ptr offset manipulation, reds agent state restore via msg_header_ptr offset manipulation, DisplayChannelClient migrate data handling via surfaces_at_client_ptr offset manipulation). Until patched, this is a concern on Linux hosts running Spice Server with VM live migration enabled, so disable VM live migration if not required, restrict SPICE client network access using firewall rules, and enforce strong authentication via SASL or mutual TLS. As a compensating measure, randomize heap and binary addresses using ASLR to impede reliable exploitation of out-of-bounds reads and writes, enforce full RELRO and PIE to make Global Offset Table entries read-only and prevent control flow diversion via heap corruption, validate indirect call targets using Control Flow Integrity or shadow call stacks to block redirection upon corruption of function pointers or vtables, enable FORTIFY_SOURCE to detect buffer overflows during memory copy operations such as memcpy and abort execution, and confine the SPICE server process using SELinux in enforcing mode to restrict host access if arbitrary code execution occurs. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying unchecked migration data offsets defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-301 SELinux (Enforcing Mode) (medium)

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in spice-server. Multiple migration data handlers use client-supplied offsets from SPICE_MSGC_MIGRATE_DATA messages without bounds validation, allowing a malicious authenticated SPICE client during VM live migration to read arbitrary heap memory or trigger heap corruption via out-of-bounds read and write operations on the message buffer.

cna.title: Authenticated RCE via render-components Entry Type overrides

descriptions.value:
Craft CMS 5.10.13.2 contains an authenticated remote code execution vulnerability in the Control Panel action app/render-components.



Any authenticated user with basic Control Panel access can submit request-controlled component classes and property overrides. By first overriding an EntryType object’s uiLabelFormat and then rendering an Entry that resolves the same request-cached entry type, an attacker can cause arbitrary Twig supplied in the request to be evaluated by renderObjectTemplate().



This render path is not sandboxed. A Twig string callable can therefore reach PHP functions such as system(), resulting in operating-system command execution with the privileges of the PHP/web-server process.



The issue was reproduced with an active non-admin Craft Team user with no optional permissions enabled. No access to entry-editing, Settings, utility, user-management, project-config, filesystem, Kubernetes, or environment variables was required.

cna.title: Plane: Unauthenticated Project Invitation Email Disclosure Enables Unauthorized Project Join Without Token

descriptions.value: Plane is an open-source project management tool. Prior to 1.4.0, ProjectJoinEndpoint at GET /api/workspaces/{slug}/projects/{project_id}/join/{pk}/ uses permission_classes = [AllowAny] and returns the full ProjectMemberInvite record, including its email, token, and role, to unauthenticated callers. The corresponding POST endpoint checks only whether the submitted email matches project_invite.email and does not validate the invitation token. An attacker who knows the invitation UUID can discover the invited email, register an account with that email, and accept the invitation without receiving the original invite. This issue is fixed in 1.4.0.

descriptions.value: Formbricks before 5.4.4 and 6 before 6.0.1 allows stored XSS. The survey-level Custom Head Scripts feature did not enforce the documented Manage permission boundary. A workspace member holding only readWrite permission could configure Custom Head Scripts on a survey, an operation the documentation restricts to the Manage role. Because the configured scripts execute in the authenticated browser session of any user who opens the affected survey, a lower-privileged member can run arbitrary JavaScript (stored cross-site scripting) in the session of higher-privileged users. Fixed versions require Manage access to modify survey Custom Head Scripts.

cna.title: Langflow: Authenticated Cross-Project File Disclosure via Unscoped MCP Resource Handlers

descriptions.value: Langflow is a tool for building and deploying AI-powered agents and workflows. From 1.6.8 until 1.9.1, Langflow authenticated access to the project identifier in a project-scoped MCP connection but did not authorize the resource URI supplied to resources/read. read_resource forwarded the attacker-controlled URI to handle_read_resource, which parsed a flow_id and filename and called storage_service.get_file without verifying that the flow belonged to the authenticated user or current project. A user with access to any project-scoped MCP endpoint could therefore request another user's flow-backed file, while global handle_list_resources and handle_list_tools behavior could disclose flow and file identifiers that made targeting easier. The vulnerability disclosed uploaded documents, structured data, prompts, and other private flow artifacts across tenants but did not modify victim files or stored flows. This issue is fixed in version 1.9.1.

cna.title: Plane: SSRF via HTTP redirect in webhook delivery (allow_redirects not set)

descriptions.value: Plane is an open-source project management tool. Prior to 1.4.0, the webhook delivery task in apps/api/plane/bgtasks/webhook_task.py calls requests.post() without allow_redirects=False and does not validate redirect targets. validate_url() blocks private, loopback, link-local, and reserved addresses in the original webhook URL, but the final URL reached after one or more redirects is not checked. A user who can create a workspace can register a webhook pointing to an attacker-controlled public endpoint that returns a 302 redirect to an internal address. The Plane worker then fetches internal resources, including cloud metadata, and stores the response body in webhook_logs, where the attacker can retrieve it through the workspace webhook-logs API. This issue is fixed in 1.4.0.

references.name: Secret key base exposed in stack trace arguments on wrong-typed Plug.Crypto arguments

workarounds.value:
Check argument types in the calling code before entering Plug.Crypto, so no head guard ever fails. Pass a token to Phoenix.Token.verify/4, Phoenix.Token.decrypt/4, Plug.Crypto.verify/4 or Plug.Crypto.decrypt/4 only when is_binary(token) holds, and treat anything else as an invalid token. Call Plug.Crypto.secure_compare/2 only when both operands are binaries, treating a missing header or parameter as a failed comparison rather than passing nil.

Where the leaked value matters more than the crash, configuring the error tracker to drop stack-frame arguments also keeps the secret out of the forwarded report. For Sentry this means not sending vars with the crash report. This narrows exposure but leaves the value in the local error log.

descriptions.value:
Externally-Generated Error Message Containing Sensitive Information vulnerability in plug_crypto in elixir-plug plug_crypto allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to expose the secret key base through application logs via a wrong-typed argument. Every public function in Plug.Crypto validates argument types in a function-head guard. A failed guard makes the Erlang VM raise FunctionClauseError with the actual argument values in the top stack frame, so the secret key base, a derived key, or the value an API key is compared against lands in that frame. The library's rescue blocks and Plug.Crypto.prune_args_from_stacktrace/1 only reach exceptions raised inside a function body, so they never see a guard failure. Plug.Cowboy and Bandit write the frame to the error log and attach it as crash_reason Logger metadata, which error trackers forward.

Two entry points take request data. Plug.Crypto.verify/4 exposes the secret key base when the token is neither a binary nor nil, which Phoenix.Token.verify/4 reaches because it forwards the token unguarded. Plug.Crypto.secure_compare/2 exposes the other operand when one side is not a binary, as happens when a missing request header yields nil. Reading the leaked value needs separate access to the logs or the error tracker, so the request alone does not disclose the secret to the attacker.

This issue affects plug: from 1.6.3 before 1.7.0; plug_crypto: from 1.0.0 before 2.2.1.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Type checks in function-head guards. Every public function in Plug.Crypto validates its arguments in a head guard, for example secure_compare/2 with when is_binary(left) and is_binary(right) and verify/4 with when is_binary(key_base) and is_binary(salt) and is_binary(token).

2. The VM builds the error, not the library. When no clause matches, the Erlang VM raises FunctionClauseError and the top stack frame holds the actual argument values. The library's rescue ... reraise blocks and Plug.Crypto.prune_args_from_stacktrace/1 only apply to exceptions raised inside a function body, so a guard failure never reaches them. In plug_crypto the same commit that added prune_args_from_stacktrace/1 also added these guards.

3. Which value leaks. verify/4 and sign/4 put the secret key base in the frame. decrypt/4 has no is_binary(token) guard on its main clause, so the key is derived first and the failing guard belongs to MessageEncryptor.decrypt/4, placing the derived 32-byte key in the frame. secure_compare/2 places the other operand in the frame, which is the server-side secret when a request value is nil.

4. The frame reaches logs and error trackers. Plug.Cowboy and Bandit write the formatted frame, arguments included, to the error log and attach it as crash_reason Logger metadata. Error trackers forward it; Sentry's handler sends crash reports by default and serializes frame arguments as vars.

cna.title: Apache log4net: NUL character truncates OutputDebugStringAppender records

descriptions.value:
Improper Neutralization of Null Byte or NUL Character vulnerability in the OutputDebugStringAppender of Apache log4net.

A NUL character in logged content ended the debug output record at that point, so everything the layout rendered after it, including exception text and trailing fields, was silently lost. A party whose data reaches a log message could hide the rest of that record. Only applications on Windows that use OutputDebugStringAppender are affected.

This issue affects Apache log4net: from 1.2.9 before 3.5.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.5.0, which fixes the issue.

cna.title: Broken Access Control Leading to Cross-Device Token Issuance in Tapo Cloud MQTT Proxy

descriptions.value: CAPEC-1 Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs

The Tapo
Cloud MQTT broker contains a broken access control vulnerability in a proxy
topic used by authenticated Tapo devices to request service tokens. The broker
does not verify that the device ID supplied in a proxy request belongs to the
authenticated device. An attacker who owns a Tapo device and knows another
device's ID may obtain a device token scoped to the target device and use it to
upload attacker-controlled content to the target user's Tapo Cloud storage. The
content may then be presented in the Tapo app as a legitimate event.





Successful
exploitation may allow an attacker to upload attacker-controlled content that
is presented to a target user as a legitimate Tapo event, retrieve internal
service information through crafted proxy requests, or abuse Tapo Cloud
outbound request capability in activity that could affect service
availability.

descriptions.value:
An elevation of privilege vulnerability exists in the Network Driver Interface Specification (NDIS) when ndis.sys fails to check the length of a buffer prior to copying memory to it.
To exploit the vulnerability, in a local attack scenario, an attacker could run a specially crafted application to elevate the attacker's privilege level. An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could run processes in an elevated context. However, an attacker must first gain access to the local system with the ability to execute a malicious application in order to exploit this vulnerability.
The security update addresses the vulnerability by changing how ndis.sys validates buffer length.

descriptions.value: Any client able to call the RPC endpoint can submit malformed struct arguments or field selections and read internal Elixir terms, including any state the failing pipeline step carried, from the error response.

descriptions.value:
Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information vulnerability in ash-project ash_typescript allows an unauthenticated attacker to read internal Elixir terms from an RPC error response by provoking an error the error builder has no dedicated clause for.

AshTypescript.Rpc.ErrorBuilder.build_error_response/1 in lib/ash_typescript/rpc/error_builder.ex renders a pipeline error term that matches no specific clause with inspect/1 and places the result in details.error of the client-facing error. Ash exceptions take a separate path in AshTypescript.Rpc.Errors where unhandled cases are redacted behind an errorId, but these fallbacks have no redaction, so whatever the term carries reaches the HTTP or channel response. Two request paths hand it such terms: a struct-typed action argument with an invalid nested value, where cast_map_to_struct/2 in lib/ash_typescript/rpc/input_formatter.ex throws the raw Ash.Type cast error into the builder, and field selection on a generic action that returns a primitive, where format_field_type/1 inspects the full Ash.Info.Manifest.Type struct into vars.returnType. Resource module names in vars.resource are not treated as sensitive and are out of scope.

This issue affects ash_typescript: from 0.1.0 before 0.19.1.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Error funnel. AshTypescript.Rpc.run_action/3 runs the request through Pipeline.parse_request/3, execute_ash_action/1 and process_result/2. Any {:error, reason} from these goes to error_response/1, which calls AshTypescript.Rpc.ErrorBuilder.build_error_response/1 with the raw reason term.

2. Unredacted fallbacks. build_error_response/1 has clauses for the error tuples the pipeline is expected to emit. A two-tuple whose first element is an atom but matches no clause is rendered as field_validation_error with details.error set to inspect(error), and any other term becomes unknown_error with details.error set to inspect(other). Ash exceptions never reach these clauses because AshTypescript.Rpc.Errors handles them and redacts unhandled ones behind an errorId, so only this path has no redaction.

3. Reachable triggers. AshTypescript.Rpc.InputFormatter.cast_map_to_struct/2 throws the raw Ash.Type.cast_input/3 error, a keyword list, when a struct-typed argument fails to cast, and format/6 turns the throw into {:error, term} for the funnel. Separately, requesting fields on a generic action whose return type is a primitive produces an {:invalid_field_selection, :primitive_type, return_type, ...} tuple whose return_type is formatted by format_field_type/1, which inspects the whole Ash.Info.Manifest.Type struct, constraints and decoration included, into vars.returnType.

From 2.91.0 until 2.132.0, validate_url_safety in docling/backend/utils/image_resource_loader.py validates a hostname with a single IPv4 lookup and then allows the HTTP client to resolve and parse the original URL again, permitting DNS rebinding, mixed public and internal address records, and backslash authority parser disagreement to reach internal services. HTMLBackendOptions(render_page=True) also allows HTTP and HTTPS browser requests without validating their resolved destination. Exploitation requires remote fetching to be enabled, and response content is exposed only when it is decoded as an image or passively rendered in a page screenshot. This issue is fixed in 2.132.0.

workarounds.value:
How To Apply the Fix

  *  Open the OpenShift console and navigate to Administration > CustomResourceDefinitions. 
  *  Search for coreidp.
  *  Show coreidp instances.
  *  Select the instance associated with your MAS installation;
  *  Edit Coreidp CR for your instance with the following under spec.settings field:
  *  Under the spec.settings field, add the following configuration, replacing <version> with the value specified in the table above for your MAS release:


spec:
  settings:
    imageTags:
      coreidplogin: <version>


  *  Save the change. This will trigger the Coreidp Entity Manager operator to reconcile and recreate the coreidp-login deployment automatically.
  *  Wait for the new deployment to become ready, then follow the validation steps below. 

IMPORTANT: Only remove the imageTags override from the Suite settings AFTER updating to the October 2026 monthly update or later, as earlier versions do not include the fix. Removing it before that point will revert your installation to the vulnerable version.

cna.title: Spice-server: spice: heap buffer overflow via glz dictionary max_encoders integer truncation

credits.value: Upstream acknowledges Tristan Madani (Talence Security) as the original reporter.

workarounds.value:
This vulnerability is only exploitable during VM live migration by an authenticated SPICE client. If live migration is not required, disabling it eliminates the attack surface. If live migration is needed, restrict SPICE client connections to trusted networks using firewall rules and enforce strong authentication (TLS with mutual certificate validation, or SASL with strong credentials) to limit who can connect as a SPICE client.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to prevent integer truncation of size_t allocation calculations to int when invoking the GlzEncoderUsrContext::malloc callback in the GLZ dictionary restore path: upgrade to the fixed Spice/Spice Server builds, which prevent truncation of size_t allocation sizes to int when invoking the GLZ dictionary malloc callback, closing all 2 injection vectors (crafted SPICE_MSGC_MIGRATE_DATA message, malicious max_encoders field in GlzEncDictRestoreData). Until patched, this is a concern on 64-bit Linux hosts running SPICE server, so Disable VM live migration if not required, restrict SPICE client access to trusted networks using firewall rules, and enforce strong authentication via SASL or TLS with mutual certificate validation. As a compensating measure, Run SELinux in enforcing mode to confine the SPICE server process domain and restrict unauthorized system access if the heap overflow is exploited. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying integer truncation defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-301 SELinux (Enforcing Mode) (medium)

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in spice-server. The GLZ encoder dictionary restore path truncates a size_t allocation size to int when calling the malloc callback, allowing a malicious authenticated SPICE client during VM live migration to trigger a massive heap buffer overflow by sending a crafted max_encoders value in migration data.

cna.title: Console-operator: streams for apache kafka console: tenant-controlled container image on clusterrole-bound pod enables namespace-to-cluster privilege escalation

workarounds.value:
1. Restrict Console CR RBAC — remove create/update/patch verbs on consoles.console.streamshub.github.com from tenant-level Roles. Only cluster administrators should manage Console CRs.
2. Deploy admission webhook — use OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno policy to validate spec.containers.api.spec.image against a trusted registry allowlist.
3. Apply network policies — restrict console-api pod egress to only required endpoints.
4. Single-tenant deployment — deploy the Console operator where only trusted administrators manage Console CRs.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to eliminate unvalidated container image deployment in the Console operator by enforcing image allowlists or removing tenant image override capabilities: upgrade to the fixed Console Operator builds, which requires image allowlist validation or removal of tenant image override capability to prevent deploying unvalidated images into pods bound to cluster-wide Strimzi CRD permissions, closing all 2 injection vectors (arbitrary container image injection via spec.containers.api.spec.image, ServiceAccount token exfiltration from privileged pod). Until patched, this is only a concern on Kubernetes clusters running Streams for Apache Kafka Console where tenants have RBAC permissions to create or update Console custom resources — single-tenant Kubernetes clusters where only cluster administrators manage Console custom resources are unaffected — so remove create, update, and patch permissions on Console custom resources from tenant-level RBAC roles and deploy admission webhooks to enforce container image allowlists. As a compensating measure, configure Kubernetes API server audit logging to detect Console custom resource changes and anomalous ServiceAccount operations, apply Kubernetes NetworkPolicies to block outbound pod traffic to the API server and external endpoints, restrict outbound egress to authorized endpoints to prevent ServiceAccount token exfiltration, separate tenant custom resource creation duties from privileged workload deployment, scope the console-server ServiceAccount to minimum required namespace permissions rather than cluster-wide access, and deploy Falco or eBPF runtime security to detect ServiceAccount token file access and unauthorized processes. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying unvalidated container image specification — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-206 Network Policy (Kubernetes) (medium)

descriptions.value: A Kubernetes tenant with create permission on Console custom resources can set spec.containers.api.spec.image to an arbitrary container image. The operator deploys this image into a pod whose ServiceAccount is bound via ClusterRoleBinding to a ClusterRole granting cluster-wide get/list/watch on all Strimzi CRDs (including KafkaUsers), patch on Kafkas/KafkaRebalances, and cluster-monitoring-view. The attacker's code reads the projected SA token and gains cross-tenant Strimzi control-plane read+write access.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Improper Validation of Package Name Components Allows Cross-Tenant Package Access in Filesystem Package Storage

descriptions.value:
The Pulsar Packages Management Service can be configured to store packages on the local filesystem of the broker by using the filesystem storage provider. Package names consist of a type, tenant, namespace, name and version. Authorization of package operations is based only on the tenant and namespace, while the storage location of a package is derived from all of these components. The version component of a package name was not validated, so it could contain URL-encoded path separators and parent directory references. The filesystem storage provider resolved such a version to a location belonging to a package in a different tenant or namespace. Because that location is inside the configured storage directory, the containment check that the filesystem storage provider performs in recent releases did not prevent the access.

An authenticated user who has the packages permission on any namespace could use this to download, overwrite or delete packages stored in other tenants or namespaces for which the user has no permission. Packages overwritten or deleted in this way may be used by Pulsar Functions, Sources or Sinks, so the issue can affect the integrity and availability of these components. If authentication is disabled, the operations are available to any client that can reach the broker's admin REST API.

This issue only affects deployments in which package management is enabled with the broker setting enablePackagesManagement and the filesystem storage provider (FileSystemPackagesStorageProvider) is configured with the setting packagesManagementStorageProvider. Package management is disabled by default, and the default storage provider, which stores packages in Apache BookKeeper, is not affected.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.10.0 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

descriptions.value:
Improper Validation of Syntactic Correctness of Input vulnerability in mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to set conn.host and conn.port to values outside the RFC 3986 host grammar via the authority of an HTTP/1 absolute-form or authority-form request target. Bandit validates the Host header and answers 400 when it is malformed, but when the request target carries its own authority that authority takes precedence, as RFC 9112 requires, and Bandit.Pipeline.determine_host_and_port!/4 in lib/bandit/pipeline.ex passes it to the application unchecked. A request line such as GET http://good.example@evil.example/x HTTP/1.1 with a valid Host header yields a conn.host of good.example@evil.example, and the same path admits NUL, DEL and non-ASCII bytes, invalid IP literals and ports outside 1..65535. The HTTP/1.0 clause needs no Host header at all, and CONNECT places the unparsed port string in conn.port.

Applications that build absolute URLs from conn.host, such as through Plug.Conn.request_url/1 or Phoenix URL helpers, emit links whose authority the attacker chose. Message framing is unaffected, and no CR or LF can reach conn.host.

This issue affects bandit: from 0.6.0 before 1.13.0.

* Start Bandit over plaintext HTTP with a plug that returns conn.host and conn.port.
* Open a raw TCP connection to the listener and send GET http://good.example@evil.example/x HTTP/1.1 followed by Host: good.example and an empty line. The response is 200 and conn.host is good.example@evil.example.
* Repeat with GET http://ex\x00am.com/x HTTP/1.1 (a NUL byte in the authority) or GET http://ex.com:99999/x HTTP/1.1. Both are accepted, with the NUL byte in conn.host and 99999 in conn.port.
* Send the same bytes in the Host header of an origin-form request instead. Bandit answers 400 for the NUL byte and the out-of-range port on 1.12.5, and for every payload once the Host grammar tightening on main is released.
* Send GET http://good.example@evil.example/x HTTP/1.0 with no Host header, or CONNECT good.example@evil.example:443 HTTP/1.1. Both are accepted, and the CONNECT form leaves conn.port as the binary "443".

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Request-target parsing (lib/bandit/http1/socket.ex)

:erlang.decode_packet/3 returns an absolute-form target as {:absoluteURI, scheme, host, port, path} and an authority-form (CONNECT) target as {:scheme, host, port}. resolve_request_target!/2 unwraps both into a {scheme, host, port, path} tuple and forwards host and port as received. validate_request_line!/2 only rejects bytes at or below 0x20 and 0x7F, so userinfo, delimiters, backslashes, bytes 0x80 to 0xFF, invalid IP literals and out-of-range ports pass. For CONNECT, port is the unparsed text after the first colon.

2. Host selection (lib/bandit/pipeline.ex)

determine_host_and_port!/4 has three clauses. The HTTP/1.1 clause calls required_host_header!/1, which parses the Host header with Bandit.Headers.parse_hostlike_header!/1 and raises a 400 on a malformed value, and then discards that result whenever target_host is set, returning to_string(target_host) and target_port instead. The fallback clause used for HTTP/1.0 and for CONNECT returns the target host and port directly and never consults the Host header. The precedence itself follows RFC 9112 section 3.2.2; the defect is that the value which wins is the one never validated.

3. Effect

build_conn!/6 places the pair into the URI from which Plug.Conn.Adapter.conn/5 builds conn.host and conn.port. The application therefore sees host values Bandit rejects on every other route into the same field, and for CONNECT a binary where Plug.Conn.port_number/0 promises an integer, which makes Plug.Conn.request_url/1 raise.

workarounds.value: Install roles and collections only from trusted sources. Before installing a role, review its meta/requirements.yml (including transitive dependencies) for any "name" value containing "../" or an absolute path. Avoid using "ansible-galaxy role install --force" against untrusted content.

descriptions.value: A path traversal vulnerability (CWE-22) was found in ansible-core's ansible-galaxy role installation. An explicit role "name" taken from a role's meta/requirements.yml is used to construct the on-disk installation path without validating that the resulting destination stays within the selected roles directory. A name containing "../" escapes that directory, and an absolute name replaces it entirely. Because ansible-galaxy processes transitive dependencies from an installed role's meta/requirements.yml, a malicious role publisher can cause attacker-supplied files to be written outside the operator's chosen roles directory when the operator installs the role, and, when --force is used, can cause an existing role directory outside that path to be removed and replaced. The impact is bounded by the invoking user's filesystem permissions and requires the operator to install the attacker-influenced content.

cna.title: Penpot: SSRF guard bypass via IPv6 transition addresses (NAT64/6to4/Teredo) in webhook delivery and media download

descriptions.value: Penpot is an open-source design and prototyping platform. Prior to 2.18.0, app.util.ssrf/blocked-address? relies on Java InetAddress predicates that do not classify NAT64, 6to4, or Teredo addresses and applies additional CIDR checks only to IPv4 values. Exploitation requires routing through a NAT64 gateway or an attacker-controlled DNS AAAA record; cloud environments with NAT64 gateways are directly exploitable. A user controlling a media import URL, or an administrator controlling a webhook URL, can then supply an IPv6 transition address that embeds a cloud-metadata, loopback, link-local, or private IPv4 target and bypasses the intended SSRF restrictions. Media import can disclose response bodies, while webhook delivery can expose response status as a network-probing side channel. This issue is fixed in version 2.18.0.

descriptions.value: MsQuic is a cross-platform C implementation of the IETF QUIC protocol exposed to C, C++, C#, and Rust. Prior to 2.4.20, 2.5.11, and 2.6.1, MsQuic clients using the OpenSSL or QuicTLS TLS backend do not properly verify that a server certificate matches the intended target server hostname. cna.title: Cups: cups: argument injection in mailto notifier via notify-recipient-uri

workarounds.value: Restrict network access to the CUPS service (port 631/tcp) to trusted hosts only, and avoid exposing cupsd to untrusted networks. If email notifications are not required, do not configure mailto subscriptions or remove/disable the mailto notifier. Ensure only a trusted mail transfer agent is installed and referenced from CUPS mailto configuration. Monitor for unexpected printer subscriptions and unusual sendmail activity from the lp user.

descriptions.value: An argument injection flaw was found in CUPS. When email notification is configured, the CUPS scheduler accepts printer subscription requests that supply a mailto notify-recipient-uri. The mailto notifier passes the recipient address to the configured sendmail program without ensuring it cannot be interpreted as command-line options. A remote attacker who can reach the CUPS service could supply a crafted recipient value starting with "-" to influence sendmail behavior. Successful exploitation depends on the installed mail transfer agent and CUPS network exposure, and may lead to execution of attacker-controlled commands with the privileges of the CUPS service user.

cna.title: Docling: Unbounded table rowspan/colspan in HTML, JATS, ODS and BoxNote backends causes CPU/memory exhaustion

descriptions.value: Docling simplifies document processing by parsing diverse formats and providing integrations with the generative AI ecosystem. From 2.0.0 until 2.131.0, the HTML, JATS, OpenDocument spreadsheet, and BoxNote backends, including docling/backend/html_backend.py, docling/backend/jats_backend.py, and docling/backend/boxnote_backend.py, accept the rowspan and colspan attribute values without an upper bound and execute loops or allocate a table grid proportional to the declared span. A very small document can therefore cause sustained CPU use or multi-gigabyte memory allocation, and the document_timeout setting does not interrupt the single backend conversion call. Export through the TableData.grid property can further materialize the oversized grid. This issue is fixed in 2.131.0.

cna.title: Langflow: Cross-user flow access and vertex execution via deprecated /api/v1/build/{flow_id}/vertices endpoints

descriptions.value: Langflow is a tool for building and deploying AI-powered agents and workflows. From 1.0.0 until 1.10.1, Langflow did not verify flow ownership in the deprecated POST /api/v1/build/{flow_id}/vertices and POST /api/v1/build/{flow_id}/vertices/{vertex_id} handlers. Through version 1.7.1, an unauthenticated caller who knew another user's flow UUID could reach these handlers; from version 1.7.2 through 1.10.0, callers had to authenticate but needed no elevated privileges. Such a caller could cause retrieve_vertices_order to load and cache the private graph, enumerate its vertex identifiers, and use build_vertex to execute selected vertices and receive their results. build_graph_from_db_no_cache performed a primary-key lookup without an owner filter. This could disclose private flow structure, configured values, and selected outputs and could trigger victim-configured side effects and build-history records, although it did not expose the victim's variable-store credentials or permit modification of the stored flow. This issue is fixed in Langflow 1.10.1 and langflow-base 0.10.1.

cna.title: Joplin Web Clipper pairing allows cross-origin theft of a permanent API token

descriptions.value: Joplin is an open source note-taking and to-do application that organises notes and lists into notebooks. Prior to 3.7.13, when Joplin Desktop is running with the opt-in Web Clipper server enabled, the server in packages/lib/ClipperServer.ts sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and allows an arbitrary website to call POST /auth and GET /auth/check because the pairing endpoints do not reject HTTP or HTTPS origins. The desktop confirmation dialog does not identify the requesting origin, so a victim who approves the generic prompt authorizes the attacking page, which then receives the permanent API token. The token provides ongoing read and write access to notes, folders, tags, resources, and master keys. This issue is fixed in version 3.7.13.

cna.title: Unauthenticated ZeroMQ command/telemetry bus in AIT-Core allows remote spacecraft command injection and telemetry exfiltration

descriptions.value: With the shipped default configuration, the ZeroMQ command and telemetry bus is unauthenticated and network-reachable because ait-server binds to all network interfaces. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach TCP ports 5559 or 5560 can inject arbitrary data onto the spacecraft command-uplink path, read real-time telemetry and command traffic from the ground bus, inject forged telemetry into operator displays, limit checks, and the historian, or disrupt command-bus availability. Exploitation requires no plugin, credentials, or user interaction; ait-server only needs to be running and the affected ZeroMQ ports must be reachable. Successful exploitation compromises the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the spacecraft command and telemetry path.

solutions.value: Upgrade to AIT-Core 3.1.2 or later. Version 3.1.2 changes the default ZeroMQ XSUB and XPUB bind addresses to loopback. Deployments that require the ZeroMQ message bus to operate across multiple hosts should protect the bus using authenticated and encrypted transport such as ZeroMQ CURVE or an equivalent mutually authenticated TLS-protected network layer.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade to AIT-Core 3.1.2 or later. Version 3.1.2 changes the default ZeroMQ XSUB and XPUB bind addresses to loopback. Deployments that require the ZeroMQ message bus to operate across multiple hosts should protect the bus using authenticated and encrypted transport such as ZeroMQ CURVE or an equivalent mutually authenticated TLS-protected network layer.

descriptions.value: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function in the ait.core.server telemetry and command broker (ait-server) in NASA-AMMOS AIT-Core through 3.1.1 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker with network access to the ZeroMQ message bus to inject spacecraft command data, exfiltrate command and telemetry traffic, inject forged telemetry, or disrupt the command and telemetry bus. The ait-server ZeroMQ broker binds its XSUB and XPUB sockets to all network interfaces by default without authentication or transport security. An attacker able to reach TCP port 5559 can publish messages onto internal topics, including the __commands__ command topic. With the shipped default configuration, command messages are forwarded through command_stream and emitted on the command-uplink UDP path. An attacker able to reach TCP port 5560 can subscribe to command and telemetry traffic on the ground bus. AIT-Core 3.1.2 changes the default ZeroMQ bind addresses to loopback.
