cna.title: NetBird client SSH config Match line injection via peer FQDN or hostname allows local command execution

descriptions.value: CAPEC-88 OS Command Injection

timeline.value: Reported to the vendor through a GitHub Security Advisory

solutions.value: Upgrade the NetBird client to version 0.74.7 or later. In this version, buildHostPatterns accepts a peer FQDN or hostname only if it is a plain DNS name, and rejects quotes, whitespace, newlines, commas and SSH pattern metacharacters (pull request #6805).

descriptions.value: Improper neutralization of special elements in the NetBird client SSH configuration manager (client/ssh/config/manager.go) in NetBird versions 0.60.0 through 0.74.6 allows a malicious or compromised peer to execute arbitrary commands on other NetBird client hosts. The client writes a system-wide OpenSSH drop-in file (/etc/ssh/ssh_config.d/99-netbird.conf, or the equivalent under %PROGRAMDATA%\ssh\ssh_config.d on Windows) that embeds each peer FQDN or hostname inside a double-quoted Match host directive without escaping. A peer name containing a double quote breaks out of the quoted context and injects arbitrary SSH configuration directives, including exec commands, which run locally as any user on the host the next time that user runs ssh. Desktop clients on Linux, macOS, Windows and FreeBSD are affected; the Android and iOS apps are not. The issue is fixed in version 0.74.7, which accepts a peer FQDN or hostname only if it is a valid DNS name.

cna.title: Joplin whiteboard card rendering allows CSS injection into application chrome

descriptions.value: Joplin is an open source note-taking and to-do application that organises notes and lists into notebooks. A malicious note can inject style elements and remote CSS imports that modify trusted application chrome, signal when the note is opened, and potentially disclose exposed attribute values. cna.title: Koha SQL injection in reports/cat_issues_top.pl via the Criteria, Filter and Limit request parameters

descriptions.value: Koha is vulnerable to SQL injection in the Most-circulated items report. The reports/cat_issues_top.pl script (sub calculate) concatenates the user-controlled Criteria, Filter, and Limit request parameters directly into dynamic SQL. Criteria is only prefix-normalized and never validated against an allow-list, so it is inserted verbatim into identifier positions (SELECT DISTINCTROW, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, and the main calculation query). Filter values are concatenated raw into single-quoted LIKE, BETWEEN, and comparison fragments. Limit is appended raw to a LIMIT clause. An authenticated staff user with the reports module permission (not requiring superlibrarian) can inject arbitrary SQL and read any table reachable by the Koha database user, including borrowers (userid and bcrypt password hashes, two-factor secrets, personal data), api_keys, and sessions. The issue is fixed in Koha 24.11.19, 25.05.14, 25.11.08, and 26.05.03, and in the 26.11 development branch. This is the unpatched twin of reports/bor_issues_top.pl (CVE-2026-70372).

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Missing topic policy authorization on non-persistent topic entry filter endpoints

credits.value: Mingsheng Lin of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS
Xingchen Chen of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS
Qixu Liu of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS

descriptions.value:
The Apache Pulsar broker admin REST API provides endpoints to read, set and remove the topic-level entry filter policy of a topic. For persistent topics these endpoints check that the caller is authorized for the entry filters topic policy operation. The corresponding endpoints for non-persistent topics (/admin/v2/non-persistent/{tenant}/{namespace}/{topic}/entryFilters) do not perform this authorization check. The only authorization check these endpoints perform is an indirect lookup permission check, made while the topic's partition metadata is retrieved; it is present in all affected versions.

As a result, when authentication and authorization are enabled, an authenticated user who has been granted produce or consume permission on a non-persistent topic, or on its namespace, but not permission to manage the topic's policies can read, replace or remove the topic-level entry filter policy of that topic. These operations should be restricted to users with the tenant admin role or the superuser role. This impact analysis assumes that Pulsar has been configured with the default authorization provider. For custom authorization providers, the impact could be slightly different.

The practical impact is limited by two broker configuration requirements, neither of which is met by default:

- Entry filters must have been installed by the operator. Entry filter implementations are loaded only at broker startup from the broker's entry filters directory, which is empty by default. A request can only select among entry filters the operator has already deployed; setting any other filter name is rejected. The issue does not allow a caller to install or load entry filter code or to run arbitrary code in the broker.
- Topic-level entry filter policies must be allowed to override the broker-level configuration (allowOverrideEntryFilters, which is disabled by default). When this setting is disabled, the topic-level entry filter policy has no effect on message dispatch.

In deployments where both conditions are met, an unauthorized user can remove the topic-level entry filter policy of a non-persistent topic, for example one used to restrict which messages are delivered to consumers, or apply a different installed entry filter that withholds messages from subscriptions of that topic. Removing it makes the topic fall back to the namespace-level or broker-level entry filters, which are not removed. A changed policy affects only subscription dispatchers created after the change, for example for new subscriptions or when a subscription is re-created after all of its consumers have disconnected; dispatchers that already exist keep the entry filters they were created with. Because non-persistent topics do not store messages, messages withheld by an entry filter are not delivered. Reading the policy discloses only the names of the configured entry filters. The issue does not allow reading message contents, and entry filters cannot modify message payloads. Persistent topics and namespace-level entry filter policies are not affected. Apache Pulsar versions before 3.3.0 are not affected, because in those versions the entry filters topic policy check is made in code shared by the persistent and non-persistent endpoints.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 3.3.0 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 3.3.x and 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately and have deployed entry filters should keep allowOverrideEntryFilters at its default value of false, so that topic-level entry filter policies do not affect message dispatch.

cna.title: kaniko can send the build's Azure (Entra ID) access token to lookalike ACR registry hosts

solutions.value: Upgrade to kaniko 1.25.20 or later. The repository publishes no binaries or images, so rebuild the executor, the warmer and docker-credential-acr-env from 1.25.20 or later. Go module consumers should update github.com/chainguard-dev/kaniko to 1.25.20 or later. The fixed version carries a patched copy of the helper under third_party/docker-credential-acr-env that accepts a host only if it is exactly host[:port] and the hostname is mcr.microsoft.com or a well-formed name ending in .azurecr.io, .azurecr.cn, .azurecr.de or .azurecr.us.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade to kaniko 1.25.20 or later. The repository publishes no binaries or images, so rebuild the executor, the warmer and docker-credential-acr-env from 1.25.20 or later. Go module consumers should update github.com/chainguard-dev/kaniko to 1.25.20 or later. The fixed version carries a patched copy of the helper under third_party/docker-credential-acr-env that accepts a host only if it is exactly host[:port] and the hostname is mcr.microsoft.com or a well-formed name ending in .azurecr.io, .azurecr.cn, .azurecr.de or .azurecr.us.

workarounds.value: Do not let untrusted builds reach an Azure identity: remove Azure credentials, federated tokens, MSI_ENDPOINT and MSI_SECRET from the build environment, and block access to the Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254) from build pods. If kaniko's built-in ACR authentication is not needed, set AZURE_ENVIRONMENT to a value that names no Azure cloud (for example AZURE_ENVIRONMENT=none) in the kaniko container. If config.json sets "credsStore": "acr-env", replace it with per-host credHelpers entries for your own ACR registries; on its own this closes only the standalone-binary path. If untrusted Dockerfiles were built with an Azure identity available, treat access tokens issued to that identity during those builds as compromised, review Entra ID sign-in logs and Azure activity logs, and rotate secrets the identity could read through Azure Resource Manager.

supportingMedia.value: Do not let untrusted builds reach an Azure identity: remove Azure credentials, federated tokens, MSI_ENDPOINT and MSI_SECRET from the build environment, and block access to the Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254) from build pods. If kaniko's built-in ACR authentication is not needed, set AZURE_ENVIRONMENT to a value that names no Azure cloud (for example AZURE_ENVIRONMENT=none) in the kaniko container. If config.json sets "credsStore": "acr-env", replace it with per-host credHelpers entries for your own ACR registries; on its own this closes only the standalone-binary path. If untrusted Dockerfiles were built with an Azure identity available, treat access tokens issued to that identity during those builds as compromised, review Entra ID sign-in logs and Azure activity logs, and rotate secrets the identity could read through Azure Resource Manager.

descriptions.value: kaniko before 1.25.20 can send a Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) access token for Azure Resource Manager to an attacker-controlled registry host. kaniko uses the Azure Container Registry credential helper github.com/chrismellard/docker-credential-acr-env, which decides whether a host is an ACR registry with an unanchored regular expression, so any hostname containing .azurecr.io, .azurecr.cn, .azurecr.de or .azurecr.us is accepted. kaniko consults this helper for any registry that has no credentials in the Docker config and is not a Google or Amazon ECR registry, before contacting the registry. A Dockerfile that references an image on a lookalike host, such as FROM x.azurecr.io.attacker.com/img or COPY --from=<image>, causes the helper to obtain a token from the build's Azure identity (service principal environment variables, federated workload identity token, or managed identity) and POST it to https://<host>/oauth2/exchange. The attacker can use the token against Azure Resource Manager with the identity's role assignments until it expires, and can exchange it for credentials to any ACR registry the identity can access. No RUN instruction or push is required. This issue is fixed in 1.25.20.

cna.title: Plane: Pre-auth workspace invitation hijack via email-squat and self-served invitation token leak in Plane

descriptions.value: Plane is an open-source project management tool. Prior to 1.4.0, Plane's signup flow creates a logged-in User row for any submitted email without an out-of-band ownership check, while User.email is unique=True. The authenticated user can call GET /api/users/me/workspaces/invitations/, which returns each WorkspaceMemberInvite whose email matches request.user.email. WorkSpaceMemberInviteSerializer uses fields = "all", exposing the token that protects the invitation join endpoint. An unauthenticated attacker who knows a target's email can register an account using that address, enumerate pending invitations, and accept an invitation as the target, joining a workspace at the invited role. The term pre-auth describes the attacker's initial state: the attacker has no credential before signup, while the enumeration and join requests use the session created by that signup. This issue is fixed in 1.4.0.

Reading request parameters triggers ASP.NET request validation, so a request carrying content such as markup made the layout throw and the appender discarded the whole event. A sender could suppress the log record of their own request. Only applications on ASP.NET for .NET Framework whose layout uses %aspnet-request are affected.

This issue affects Apache log4net: from 1.2.11 before 3.5.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.5.0, which fixes the issue.

cna.title: Langflow: Authenticated RCE via MCP Stdio transport allows any user to execute arbitrary OS commands on the server

descriptions.value: Langflow is a tool for building and deploying AI-powered agents and workflows. Prior to 1.9.0, any authenticated Langflow user can achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE) on the server by adding an MCP server with the "Stdio" transport. The user-supplied command field is passed directly to bash -c "exec {command}" with zero validation, no allowlisting, and no sandboxing. The command executes immediately when the server list is fetched. Additionally, the env field allows arbitrary environment variable injection (e.g., LD_PRELOAD, PATH override). This vulnerability is fixed in 1.9.0.

cna.title: hex_core decompresses registry and Erlang term API responses without size limits

descriptions.value: A mirror can make every registry fetch allocate memory far beyond the size of its response: in a test against Hex main 851b938, which vendors this code, a 65 KB registry response decompressed into a 64 MiB envelope before the signature check failed. The API server, or an attacker who can alter its responses, can do the same with API responses: 8 KB of compressed Erlang term format decoded into a list of 4.2 million elements. Large enough responses stop the Erlang VM, which fails the build tool command or the program using hex_core. No package code has to run.

descriptions.value:
Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification) vulnerability in hexpm hex_core allows an untrusted repository mirror, or a server answering hex_core's API requests, to exhaust the memory of the Erlang VM running hex_core. The same code is vendored in Hex (mix_hex_repo, mix_hex_api) and rebar3 (r3_hex_repo, r3_hex_api).

hex_repo:get_names/1, hex_repo:get_versions/1, hex_repo:get_package/2 and hex_repo:get_policy/2 decompress the registry response with zlib:gunzip/1 and decode the signed envelope before verifying its signature. A mirror doesn't have the repository's private key, but it chooses the compressed bytes, so a small response decompresses into an envelope of any size before the signature check rejects it.

hex_api decodes responses with the application/vnd.hex+erlang content type through hex_safe_binary_to_term:safe_binary_to_term/1, which calls binary_to_term(Binary, [safe]). The safe option prevents atom creation, but it accepts compressed terms and doesn't limit the size of the decoded term, and the check that rejects functions and ports runs after the term has been built. The fix for CVE-2026-21619 added the safe option and that check without bounding the decoded size.

This issue affects rebar3: from 3.9.1 before 3.27.3; hex: from 2.1.0 before 2.5.2 and from 2.6.0 onward; hex_core: from 0.1.0 before 0.20.0.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
* hex_repo:get_protobuf/3, used by get_names/1, get_versions/1, get_package/2 and get_policy/2, calls zlib:gunzip/1 on the whole response body with no output limit.
* hex_repo:decode/4 then calls hex_registry:decode_and_verify_signed/2, which decodes the protobuf envelope, copying its payload and signature, before checking the signature.
* hex_api:request/4 passes every response whose content type contains application/vnd.hex+erlang to hex_safe_binary_to_term:safe_binary_to_term/1.
* safe_binary_to_term/1 calls binary_to_term(Binary, [safe]), which decompresses compressed terms and builds the whole term, and only then walks it to reject functions and ports.

solutions.value: Fixed in commit 93dc0e50739c225f5aee2e803800a47fc0feb906, which hardcodes the https scheme in the redirect. The fix is deployed to edu.chainguard.dev; no user action is required.

descriptions.value: Use of the backend-facing $scheme variable in the trailing-slash directory redirect in nginx.conf of Chainguard Academy (edu) from commit 0b75ff98057f69b044a3e7194e428066ac5ad0d4 before commit 93dc0e50739c225f5aee2e803800a47fc0feb906 allows an on-path network attacker to read or modify documentation content served to a victim via an HTTPS request for a slashless directory path, because TLS terminates at the load balancer in front of Nginx and the resulting 301 response redirects the client to a plaintext http:// URL. Browsers that ship the HSTS preload list are not affected, because the .dev top-level domain is preloaded; clients that do not enforce HSTS, such as command-line HTTP clients and scripts that follow redirects, are affected.

cna.title: Docling: Configured HTTP headers sent to every remote image host named by a document

descriptions.value: Docling simplifies document processing by parsing diverse formats and providing integrations with the generative AI ecosystem. From 2.95.0 until 2.132.0, the HTML image resource loader in docling/backend/utils/image_resource_loader.py forwards headers configured through the HTMLBackendOptions.headers setting to every remote image URL named by an untrusted document when enable_remote_fetch=True and fetch_images=True. The loader does not restrict those credentials to the source document's origin, allowing requests that carry custom headers such as API keys and cookies to follow cross-origin redirects and expose the caller's configured credentials to a document author. The default configuration is not affected because remote fetching and configured headers are required. This issue is fixed in 2.132.0.

cna.title: Apache Qpid Proton C: The OpenSSL TLS implementation adds a locally trusted certificate authority to the existing trusted system trust anchors.

descriptions.value:
When using the OpenSSL TLS implementation, both the pn_ssl_domain_set_trusted_ca_db() & pn_tls_config_set_trusted_certs() APIs added to rather than replaced the default system trust anchors. Leading to potentially trusting unexpected peer certificates.



This can be worked around by setting the SSL_CERT_FILE environment variable for the application to /dev/null.



This issue does not affect the Win32 SChannel TLS implementation.



This issue affects Apache Qpid Proton C: through 0.40.0.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 0.41.1, which fixes the issue.

cna.title: Easy Social Icons < 4.0.3 - Author+ Stored XSS via SVG Upload

descriptions.value: The Easy Social Icons WordPress plugin before 4.0.3 does not sanitise SVG files, which it adds to the list of file types that may be uploaded site-wide, allowing users with the Author role and above to upload a malicious SVG containing XSS payloads. Where another installed Easy Social Icons WordPress plugin before 4.0.3 exposes an upload route to unauthenticated visitors, the same issue can be triggered without an account.

cna.title: TLS 1.2 session resumption in ssl crosses SNI virtual-host client-certificate trust boundaries

descriptions.value: A client holding a certificate issued by the lower-trust SNI name's CA connects to the higher-trust name as a fully authenticated mTLS peer and obtains whatever that service grants on a successful client-certificate handshake. Multi-tenant or partner-facing listeners that separate trust domains by SNI name are affected.

workarounds.value:
* Set {reuse_sessions, false} in each SNI service's option set, or in the base listener options. The reporter's proof of concept confirmed that this blocks the cross-name resumption.
* Serve distinct SNI trust domains on separate listen sockets, which gives each its own session cache.
* Restrict the listener to TLS 1.3 with {versions, ['tlsv1.3']}. TLS 1.3 does not use the session-ID cache.

descriptions.value:
Improper Certificate Validation vulnerability in the ssl application in Erlang/OTP allows a client that holds a certificate trusted by one SNI virtual host to authenticate to a second SNI virtual host on the same listener by resuming its TLS 1.2 session there.

A server that serves several SNI names from one listen socket through sni_fun or sni_hosts keeps one pre-TLS 1.3 session cache per listener and does not bind a cached session to the SNI name or client trust policy that established it. When an SNI option set switches to verify_peer without naming reuse_sessions, ssl_config:update_options/3 inherits the base listener's reuse_sessions value of true, so the default that disables reuse for client-authenticating servers does not apply. On an abbreviated handshake ssl_session:is_resumable/4 checks only that the cached session uses one of the current server certificates and carries some peer certificate, and never revalidates that certificate against the CA selected for the requested name. The names must share a server certificate, which is common with wildcard or multi-SAN certificates. TLS 1.3 does not use this cache and is not affected.

This issue affects OTP from OTP 18.0 before OTP 27.3.4.19, OTP 28.5.0.8, and OTP 29.1.2, corresponding to ssl from 7.0 before 11.2.12.14, 11.6.0.7, and 11.7.8.

configurations.value: Exploitation requires all of the following. One TLS listener serves at least two SNI names through sni_fun or sni_hosts. The names use the same server certificate but select different client CAs with verify_peer. TLS 1.2 or earlier is enabled. No SNI option set sets reuse_sessions to false while the base listener's effective value is true, which is the default when the base listener uses verify_none. The attacker holds a client certificate that the lower-trust name accepts.

x_proofOfConcept.value:
* Create one server certificate with subject alternative names low.test and high.test, two self-signed client CAs (low-ca, high-ca), and one client certificate signed by low-ca.
* Start an ssl:listen/2 server on TLS 1.2 with {verify, verify_none} and an sni_fun that returns {verify, verify_peer}, {fail_if_no_peer_cert, true} and the low-ca or high-ca cacertfile for the respective name. Do not set reuse_sessions anywhere.
* Connect with openssl s_client -servername high.test -tls1_2 -no_ticket using the low client certificate. The server rejects the handshake with unknown_ca.
* Connect with -servername low.test and the same certificate, saving the session with -sess_out. The handshake succeeds.
* Connect with -servername high.test and -sess_in pointing at the saved session. The server resumes the session, ssl:connection_information/2 reports session_resumption true for high.test, and the application behind the protected name serves the request to a client whose certificate high-ca never issued.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. One session cache per listener. tls_socket:listen/3 starts one pre-TLS 1.3 session-ID tracker per listen socket via session_id_tracker/2. Every SNI virtual host served from that socket shares it, and the cached #session{} record stores the peer and server certificates but no SNI name and no client trust policy.

2. The SNI option set inherits session reuse. When the ClientHello carries a server name, ssl_gen_statem:handle_sni_extension/2 and handle_sni_hostname/2 call update_ssl_options_from_sni/2, which passes the base listener options as fallback into ssl_config:update_options/3. The base listener's verify_none has already produced reuse_sessions = true. ssl_config:opt_reuse_sessions/3 computes a false default for verify_peer, but get_opt_bool/4 finds the inherited value and keeps it when the SNI option list does not mention reuse_sessions.

3. Resumption does not revalidate the peer certificate. On an abbreviated handshake ssl_handshake:select_session/8 calls ssl_session:server_select_session/5, which accepts the cached session when ssl_session:is_resumable/4 finds that it is marked resumable, that is_owncert/2 matches one of the current server certificates, that reusable_options/2 sees any cached peer certificate when fail_if_no_peer_cert is set, and that the reuse_session fun agrees. Nothing compares the ClientHello server name with the name that created the session, and the cached peer certificate is not validated against the CA selected for the new name.

4. Result. A client whose certificate chains to the lower-trust name's CA completes a full handshake there, then presents the same session ID with the higher-trust server name. The server resumes the session, reports session_resumption as true and the low-trust peer certificate through ssl:peercert/1, and the application behind the protected name sees an authenticated mTLS peer. is_owncert/2 is why both names must share a server certificate.

cna.title: Plane: Issue Attachment Ownership Hijacking via Missing `issue_id` Scope

descriptions.value: Plane is an open-source project management tool. Prior to 1.4.0, the V2 issue-attachment PATCH endpoint accepts issue_id in the URL but omits it from the database query. A project member can use an issue_id they control in the URL while targeting another user's attachment by its pk UUID. Because the server matches only pk, workspace, and project_id, it modifies the attachment regardless of the issue_id in the URL. When the attachment is pending and has not been confirmed as uploaded, the PATCH handler sets created_by = request.user and transfers attachment ownership to the attacker. This issue is fixed in 1.4.0.

cna.title: vLLM: Unbounded Prometheus label cardinality from attacker-controlled HTTP method tokens in the vLLM Rust frontend metrics middleware (unauthenticated denial of service)

descriptions.value: vLLM is an inference and serving engine for large language models. Prior to 0.30.0, the Rust frontend's track_http_metrics middleware records the raw HTTP method token as a Prometheus label for requests reaching registered routes. An unauthenticated attacker can send unique arbitrary method tokens to unguarded routes such as /tokenize, causing Prometheus's Family::get_or_create function to permanently create counter and histogram label sets. Those label sets increase process memory usage and enlarge the /metrics response until the service or monitoring path is exhausted. This issue is fixed in version 0.30.0.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Missing authorization on transaction admin endpoints exposes transaction coordinator and transaction statistics of other tenants

descriptions.value:
The Apache Pulsar broker exposes a transaction administration REST API under /admin/v3/transactions. When authentication and authorization are enabled, most of the read endpoints of this API verify only that the request is authenticated and that the broker serves the requested topic or transaction coordinator. They do not check whether the caller is permitted to access the tenant, namespace or topic whose data is returned. The endpoints that modify state, which abort a transaction or scale the transaction coordinators, correctly require super-user access and are not affected.

As a result, any authenticated user, including one that has been granted no permissions, can read transaction coordinator and transaction information belonging to other tenants. This includes the list of transaction coordinators with the broker service URLs that serve them, transaction coordinator statistics and internal statistics, transaction metadata including the names of the topics and subscriptions a transaction involves and the principal that opened it, the list of long-running transactions on a transaction coordinator, transaction buffer and pending acknowledgement statistics and internal statistics for any topic and subscription, and whether a given message position of a subscription is currently held in a pending transactional acknowledgement.

The disclosure of transaction metadata and statistics can only occur when transaction support is enabled in the broker (transactionCoordinatorEnabled, which is disabled by default). When transaction support is disabled, these endpoints return no transaction data; the only residual effect is that one endpoint's error response can reveal whether a named topic exists in another tenant.

The impact is limited to disclosure of transaction-related metadata and statistics across tenant boundaries. The issue does not allow reading message contents, modifying or aborting transactions, or changing any configuration.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.8.0 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately and do not use Pulsar transactions should keep transaction support disabled. Where transactions are required, restricting network access to the broker's admin HTTP endpoints to trusted administrative clients reduces the exposure.

cna.title: vLLM: Qwen2-VL / Qwen3-VL video samplers bound on request-controlled max_frames, which the num_frames ceiling does not reach

descriptions.value: vLLM is an inference and serving engine for large language models. From 0.24.0 until 0.30.0, the Qwen2VLVideoBackend and Qwen3VLVideoBackend classes accept request-level values for the media_io_kwargs.video.max_frames and media_io_kwargs.video.fps fields without enforcing server-side ceilings. An unauthenticated caller can submit these values to the /tokenize endpoint, causing the sampler to decode every frame selected from attacker-controlled video input, consume disproportionate frontend memory, and potentially terminate the API process before scheduling or admission control. cna.title: Apache Roller: Cross-site request forgery in Planet administration lets an attacker make the server fetch arbitrary URLs

descriptions.value: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) in the Planet feed aggregator administration of Apache Roller 4.0 through 6.1.6 allows an unauthenticated attacker to make the Roller server fetch a URL the attacker chooses, including internal addresses, by inducing a logged-in global administrator to open a crafted web page. The action that adds a Planet subscription can be triggered cross-site; in recent releases it accepts GET requests, which Roller's CSRF token check does not cover. The action fetches the supplied URL and saves the subscription, and any fetched content that parses as a feed is then published without authentication in the aggregated Planet feed. The Planet aggregator is enabled by default. Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.7 or later, which requires POST requests with a valid CSRF token for Planet administration changes and turns the Planet aggregator off by default.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Improper Authorization of Function, Source and Sink Package URLs Allows Cross-Tenant Package Download

descriptions.value:
When package management is enabled, Pulsar Functions, Sources and Sinks can be registered or updated from a package stored in the Pulsar Packages Management Service by supplying a package URL. The Pulsar Functions worker authorized these requests only against the namespace in which the component was being registered or updated. It did not check whether the requesting user was permitted to access packages in the namespace that the package URL refers to, and it retrieved the package from the broker using the worker's own credentials. The permission check of the Packages Management Service was therefore applied to the worker's identity instead of the requesting user's. Package URLs of transform functions supplied when registering or updating a sink were handled in the same way.

An authenticated user who is permitted to register or update functions, sources or sinks in any namespace of their own tenant could use this to obtain the contents of a package stored in a namespace of another tenant, without having the packages permission on that namespace. The impact is limited to disclosure of package contents, which may include application code, business logic or embedded credentials. The issue does not allow packages to be modified or deleted and does not affect availability.

This issue only affects deployments that have authentication and authorization enabled and in which package management has been enabled: the broker setting enablePackagesManagement and, in current releases, the functions worker setting functionsWorkerEnablePackageManagement. Both settings are disabled by default.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.8.0 before 4.0.14, from 4.1.0 through 4.1.3, and from 4.2.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider uses roles from unverified tokens for HTTP requests that fall back to the anonymous user role

descriptions.value:
Apache Pulsar's MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider authorizes a client with all roles listed in a claim of its JSON Web Token (JWT). The provider is intended for use with token authentication, which verifies the token before authorization. The provider did not verify the token itself: it parsed the token's claims with the signature removed and trusted that authentication had already checked it.

When authentication and authorization are enabled with a non-empty anonymousUserRole setting, some HTTP requests whose credentials fail authentication are not rejected, but are handled as requests of the anonymous user role. For the broker's HTTP endpoints, such as the admin REST API, this fallback applies to requests that do not name an authentication method and requires strictAuthMethod to be false (the default) where that setting is available. For the WebSocket API, failed credentials can also fall back to the anonymous user role; this path does not enforce strictAuthMethod. The authentication data kept for such a request still contained the request's Authorization header. MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider then read the bearer token from that header without verifying its signature and authorized the request with the roles in the token's role claim.

As a result, in deployments that use MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider together with a non-empty anonymousUserRole and that permit this fallback, an unauthenticated client can send an HTTP request, for example to the admin REST API or the WebSocket API, with a forged or unsigned token that lists arbitrary roles, and be authorized with those roles. The impact can include super-user access when the token lists a role configured in superUserRoles, allowing the client to read and change tenants, namespaces, topics, permissions and broker configuration. No valid credentials are required.

Deployments are not affected if they use the default authorization provider (PulsarAuthorizationProvider) or another authorization provider, or if anonymousUserRole is not set (the default). Requests that authenticate successfully with a valid token are not affected, because the token that MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider reads is the token that authentication verified. Connections that use the Pulsar binary protocol are not affected by this issue, because the broker does not keep client authentication data for connections that it assigns to the anonymous user role.

In fixed versions, MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider obtains roles only from tokens that the configured token authentication provider has verified, using its configured keys and validation settings. Broker HTTP requests that are assigned to the anonymous user role are authorized only as that role, and invalid tokens cannot supply additional roles to WebSocket requests. The broker fails to start if MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider is configured with authorization enabled but without a token authentication provider.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.8.1 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately can remove the anonymousUserRole setting from the broker and WebSocket service configurations, or restrict network access to the HTTP endpoints of these services to trusted clients.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Missing Topic Authorization on Binary Protocol GetSchema and GetOrCreateSchema Commands

descriptions.value:
The Pulsar broker serves two schema commands on its binary protocol: GetSchema, which returns the schema registered for a topic, and GetOrCreateSchema, which registers a new schema version for an existing topic. The broker handled both commands after checking only that the client connection was authenticated. Unlike the broker's other topic commands, such as those for creating producers and consumers or for looking up topics, these two commands did not check whether the authenticated client was authorized for the target topic. The Pulsar REST API endpoints for schemas were not affected.

An authenticated client without any permission on the target topic, namespace or tenant could use these commands to:

- read the schema registered for a topic in another namespace or tenant, disclosing the schema definition such as record field names and types. Message payloads are not disclosed.
- register a new schema version on an existing topic in another namespace or tenant. The topic's schema compatibility and schema auto-update policies still apply. The issue does not allow message data to be read or modified, but a registered schema version can cause legitimate producers and consumers of that topic to fail with schema incompatibility errors until the schema is corrected by an administrator.

The standard Pulsar client performs an authorized topic lookup before it sends these commands, so the missing check could not be observed when testing with the standard client. A client that implements the binary protocol directly is not required to perform that lookup first.

This issue is relevant only to deployments that have authentication and authorization enabled. The GetSchema command is affected from Apache Pulsar 2.2.0, and the GetOrCreateSchema command from Apache Pulsar 2.5.0. After the fix, the broker requires the lookup permission on the topic for GetSchema and the produce permission on the topic for GetOrCreateSchema. This impact analysis assumes that Pulsar has been configured with the default authorization provider. For custom authorization providers, the impact could be slightly different.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.2.0 before 4.0.14, from 4.1.0 through 4.1.3, and from 4.2.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

A flaw in Node.js HTTP Agent connection reuse can cause a client to accept as valid a response that was sent before the client has sent the request. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-48931.

The guard that destroys idle keep-alive sockets when unexpected data arrives only runs when the event loop polls for I/O. If an unsolicited response has already reached the socket but has not been read yet when the socket is handed to a new request, for example because the event loop was busy with synchronous work, the guard is removed without seeing it and the data is parsed as the response to the new request.

This vulnerability affects Node.js **26.x**, **24.x**, and **22.x**.

cna.title: HTTP/2 blocked-send deadlines reset on every WINDOW_UPDATE, letting a trickle pin stream processes indefinitely in Bandit

descriptions.value: A remote, unauthenticated peer requests a response larger than a send window, then drips tiny WINDOW_UPDATE frames every few seconds. Each blocked stream process, with its Plug state and any upstream connection or file handle it holds, stays alive for as long as the trickle continues. Repeated across many streams and connections this exhausts server processes and memory.

descriptions.value:
Uncontrolled Resource Consumption vulnerability in mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to pin HTTP/2 stream processes indefinitely via a trickle of small WINDOW_UPDATE frames. A stream whose response outruns the connection or stream send window blocks until the peer grants more window, and each block carries a 15 second deadline. Both deadlines restart whenever the peer makes partial progress. Bandit.HTTP2.Connection.finish_data/5 re-queues a partially advanced send in pending_sends with a fresh expires_at, so every WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 0, and every SETTINGS frame, resets the clock. Bandit.HTTP2.Stream.send_data/3 recurses on each stream WINDOW_UPDATE and re-arms a fresh after read_timeout. A peer that grants a few bytes every few seconds keeps the blocked stream process, its Plug state and any resource it holds mid-response alive for as long as it keeps dripping, and repeats this across streams and connections to exhaust server processes and memory.

The two paths are independent. The stream-level block is reached on its own by widening the connection window with a large WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 0 and shrinking the per-stream window with a small SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE, so closing only the connection-level path leaves it exploitable.

This issue affects bandit: from 1.4.0 before 1.13.0.

Connection-level path:

* Open a stream whose response exceeds the connection send window (65,535 bytes by default).
* The server sends the window's worth and queues the remainder in pending_sends.
* Send WINDOW_UPDATE for stream 0 with an increment of 1 every few seconds, or an empty SETTINGS frame. Each one re-queues the remainder with a fresh deadline, so expire_pending_sends/1 never expires it.

Stream-level path:

* Send a large WINDOW_UPDATE for stream 0 so the connection window never blocks.
* Advertise a small SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE so each stream window is tiny.
* Request a response larger than the stream window. The server sends the window's worth and blocks in the recursive receive in send_data/3.
* Send WINDOW_UPDATE for the stream with an increment of 1 at intervals shorter than 15 seconds. Each one re-arms a fresh read_timeout.
* Repeat across streams, up to max_concurrent_streams per connection, and across connections.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Connection-level block (lib/bandit/http2/connection.ex)

A send that outruns the connection send window is queued in pending_sends with an expires_at deadline computed in finish_data/5 as now plus @pending_send_timeout (15 seconds). expire_pending_sends/1 drops any queued send whose deadline has passed whenever data arrives on the connection. do_pending_sends/2 runs on every WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 0 and on every SETTINGS frame (including an empty one, through handle_frame/3). When the granted window is smaller than the queued remainder, the leftover is re-queued through finish_data/5, which recomputes expires_at from the current time instead of preserving the original deadline. Each partial advance therefore restarts the timer, and an empty SETTINGS frame restarts it without granting any window at all.

2. Stream-level block (lib/bandit/http2/stream.ex)

send_data/3 runs in the stream process. When the stream send window is exhausted it enters a receive that waits for {:bandit, {:send_window_update, delta}} with after stream.read_timeout (the struct default of 15 seconds, never overridden in init/5). On each stream WINDOW_UPDATE it applies the delta and recurses into send_data/3 with the remainder, which re-enters the same receive with a fresh after timeout. Each partial advance restarts the 15 second wait.

cna.title: OAuth callback open redirect, login-CSRF, and cross-user state leak

descriptions.description: CWE-601 URL redirection to untrusted site ('open redirect')
CWE-362 Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization
CWE-488 Exposure of data element to wrong session

descriptions.value:
In Eclipse Che versions 7.61.0 through 7.124.0 three related defects in the SCM-OAuth flow, chain into a Medium-severity finding:



1. Open redirect (CWE-601) — `EmbeddedOAuthAPI.callback()` and the OAuth1 callback issue `307 Temporary Redirect` to whatever URL was carried in the `redirect_after_login` field of the OAuth `state` parameter. The value is fully attacker-controlled and never compared against an allow-list of permitted hosts.



2. Missing CSRF nonce in OAuth `state` (CWE-352) — `OAuthAuthenticator.prepareState()` builds the `state` parameter solely by URL-encoding the original request's query string. No random nonce is bound to the user's session, so an attacker can pre-compute a callback URL carrying _their own_ SCM authorization `code` and have a logged-in victim open it. `callback()` then stores the attacker's SCM token under the victim's Che identity (`personalAccessTokenManager.store(...)`).



3. Mutable field on a `@Singleton` (CWE-362 / CWE-488) — `EmbeddedOAuthAPI` is `@Singleton` but stores the per-request `redirect_after_login` value into the instance field `private String redirectAfterLogin`. Any user's `authenticate()` call overwrites the field for all concurrent users; the `access_denied` error-path of `callback()` then redirects to the _last writer's_ URL.

descriptions.value: Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key in JWT token authentication in Apache OFBiz 24.09.06 and 24.09.07 on all platforms allows an unauthenticated, network-reachable attacker to obtain full administrative access via a forged JWT signed with the factory-default security.token.key value that CVE-2026-31986 removed from newly generated configurations, on a deployment that upgraded from a release predating that fix while retaining its existing security.properties with security.internal.sso.enabled set to true. Upgrading alone does not replace an already-configured key: deployments that carried framework/security/config/security.properties forward from a release predating the CVE-2026-31986 fix must also run './gradlew rotateSecretKeys' after upgrading, since the existing generateSecretKeys task leaves an already-set value untouched.

cna.title: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in Git

credits.value: Thanks [taise](https://hackerone.com/taise) for reporting this vulnerability through HackerOne

descriptions.value:
Affected versions of Git have a heap buffer overflow in the three-way merge
code (xdiff), which an attacker can trigger through a repository they
control.

When Git merges a file, it first adds up the size of the merged
output, allocates a buffer of that size, and then writes the output into
it. That total was kept in a 32-bit signed integer. The
conflict-marker-size attribute, which can be set from a committed
.gitattributes file, accepts any positive integer, and the markers are
written several times for every conflict. A small file with a huge marker
size and many separate conflicts can therefore push the total past 4 GiB,
so the integer wraps to a small value and Git writes attacker-controlled
merge output past the end of a buffer that is too small. At minimum this
crashes Git, and because the overflow is large and its contents are largely
attacker-controlled, worse heap corruption is possible.

Any command that does a textual three-way merge can trigger it, such
as git-merge(1), git-rebase(1), git-cherry-pick(1), and
git-merge-tree(1). The latter is most likely a target for Git forges,
which might use git-merge-tree(1) on the server-side to check
mergeability. When the server reads attributes from trees in the
repository (for example through attr.tree or --attr-source), any
user who can push branches and request that they be merged (for
example by opening a pull or merge request) can trigger the overflow
without anyone else doing anything, and the data they push is small
because the oversized output only appears during the merge.

The problem has been patched by computing the size as size_t and
checking every addition for overflow, so Git stops with an error
instead of overflowing.

Servers that cannot upgrade right away can add

* conflict-marker-size=7

to each repository's info/attributes as a workaround, which overrides
any in-tree .gitattributes, or turn off server-side mergeability checks for
untrusted repositories.

cna.title: NetBird client netstack SOCKS5 proxy binds to all interfaces and exposes an unauthenticated proxy into the overlay network

descriptions.value: Binding to an unrestricted IP address in the netstack SOCKS5 proxy of the NetBird client (client/iface/netstack) in NetBird versions before 0.74.7 allows an unauthenticated attacker on the same network as the client to relay traffic through the client into its NetBird overlay network. When the client runs in netstack mode (NB_USE_NETSTACK_MODE=true), it starts a SOCKS5 proxy, without authentication, that is meant to bridge applications on the local host into the userspace WireGuard stack. The listener was bound to 0.0.0.0 instead of the loopback address, so any host that can reach the proxy port (1080 by default) can connect and reach peers and internal resources with the network position of the affected client. Netstack mode is not enabled by default. The issue is fixed in version 0.74.7, which binds the proxy to 127.0.0.1 by default.

descriptions.description: CWE-1327 Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address

solutions.value: Upgrade the NetBird client to version 0.74.7 or later. In this version the netstack SOCKS5 proxy listens on 127.0.0.1 by default. The NB_SOCKS5_LISTENER_ADDRESS environment variable can set a different bind address when the proxy must be reachable from other hosts; doing so exposes the unauthenticated proxy on that address (pull request #6812).

workarounds.value: If an upgrade is not possible, do not run the client in netstack mode on untrusted networks, or block inbound access to the SOCKS5 proxy port with a host firewall.

configurations.value: The client is affected only when it runs in netstack mode (NB_USE_NETSTACK_MODE=true), which is not the default.

timeline.value: Reported to the vendor through a GitHub Security Advisory

affected.vendor: Guangzhou Juan IoT Technology Co., Ltd.
Guangzhou Juan IoT Technology Co., Ltd.

descriptions.value: The endpoint exposes an observable response discrepancy when processing ID values. A request submitted with a nonexistent ID returns a distinct error response code from one submitted with a valid, registered ID, allowing an attacker holding a valid access token - but without further authentication or authorization - to distinguish valid ID values from the full 10-digit numeric search space. cna.title: Langflow: OS command injection (RCE) via arbitrary command in MCP stdio server configuration

descriptions.value: Langflow is a tool for building and deploying AI-powered agents and workflows. Before Langflow 1.10.3, the MCP stdio transport launched whatever command / args a user put in an MCP server configuration, with no allowlist and (before 1.10.3) wrapped in bash -c "exec {command} ...". Any user able to reach the MCP server settings ("Settings → MCP Servers → Add MCP Server", POST/PATCH /api/v2/mcp/servers/{server_name}) or to build a flow with the MCP Tools component could add a "server" whose command is an arbitrary OS command (touch, rm -rf, a reverse shell, ...). The command runs on the Langflow host as the Langflow process user as soon as Langflow tries to connect to the server (listing servers, loading tools, running the flow) — even when the UI then reports that the stdio server failed to start. With the default LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=true, GET /api/v1/auto_login hands out a token without credentials, so on an exposed instance running the default configuration this is reachable without an account. AUTO_LOGIN is documented as a development-only setting; with it disabled, any authenticated (non-admin) user can exploit it. This issue is fixed in Langflow 1.10.3, langflow-base 0.10.3, and lfx 1.10.3.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Functions connectors list endpoint does not apply the super-user check of the worker connectors endpoint

credits.value: Mingsheng Lin of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS
Xingchen Chen of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS
Qixu Liu of Institute of Information Engineering, CAS

descriptions.value:
The Pulsar Functions worker REST API provides two endpoints that return the catalog of Pulsar IO connectors installed on the functions worker: the worker connectors endpoint (/admin/v2/worker/connectors) and the deprecated functions connectors endpoint (/admin/v2/functions/connectors and /admin/v3/functions/connectors). When authorization is enabled, the worker connectors endpoint requires super-user access. The functions connectors endpoint, served both by the functions worker and by a broker running the functions worker, returns the same catalog without this check.

As a result, when authentication and authorization are enabled, any authenticated client can read the connector catalog through the functions connectors endpoint, regardless of the permissions granted to its role and without super-user access. Unauthenticated requests are rejected unless anonymous access is configured with an anonymous user role.

The catalog contains the connector type definitions installed in the functions worker's connectors directory: the connector name, its description, and the source, sink and configuration class names. It does not contain configured source or sink instances, their configuration values or credentials, and an installed connector type does not indicate that a connector is configured or running. The impact is limited to disclosure of this metadata, which can include the names and descriptions of custom connectors installed by the operator. The issue does not allow modifying the catalog or managing connectors. Connector definitions that have a source or sink class are also returned by the built-in sources and sinks endpoints to authenticated clients.

In fixed versions, the functions connectors endpoint applies the same checks as the worker connectors endpoint, so that it requires super-user access when authorization is enabled. Clients that are not super-users can use the built-in sources and sinks endpoints to list the available connector types.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.4.1 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

cna.title: Docling: Arbitrary local file read via draw:image xlink:href in the OpenDocument backend

descriptions.value: Docling simplifies document processing by parsing diverse formats and providing integrations with the generative AI ecosystem. From 2.107.0 until 2.120.3, docling/backend/opendocument_backend.py uses the xlink:href attribute value of a draw:image element as a filesystem path when the referenced part is not found in the document archive. The _image_ref_from_odf_image function reads that attacker-controlled path without a scheme check, extraction-directory confinement, or the enable_local_fetch setting used by other backends. Readable files that Pillow can decode as images are embedded in converted output, and other existing paths can be distinguished through the attempted read. This issue is fixed in 2.120.3.

cna.title: vLLM: GLMGA video sampling permits request-driven CPU and memory exhaustion

descriptions.value: vLLM is an inference and serving engine for large language models. Prior to 0.30.0, a caller can use the request-level media_io_kwargs field to select the GLMGA video backend and supply large values for the fps and max_frames options without a strict work ceiling. GLMGA constructs and deduplicates an attacker-sized pre-decode frame-index list, allowing a compact request and tiny valid video to consume disproportionate CPU time and memory in the shared media-loading executor. This issue is fixed in version 0.30.0.

cna.title: Penpot: Anonymous share-link token disclosure & page-scope bypass via get-view-only-bundle

descriptions.value: Penpot is an open-source design and prototyping platform. Prior to 2.18.0, the unauthenticated get-view-only-bundle RPC returns every share-link row for a file even when the caller authenticated with only one scoped share link. A holder of a restrictive link can obtain other links' secret IDs, page scopes, comment permissions, and inspection permissions, then replay a more permissive token to access page data that was not included in the original share. This issue is fixed in version 2.18.0.

cna.title: Apache Pulsar: Improper authorization of WebSocket consumer dead letter topic allows writes without PRODUCE permission

descriptions.value:
The Apache Pulsar WebSocket service allows a WebSocket consumer to configure a dead letter policy through query parameters of the consumer endpoint, including the deadLetterTopic parameter that names the topic to which messages are written after the maximum number of redeliveries is exceeded. When authorization is enabled, the WebSocket service checks only that the connecting user holds the CONSUME permission on the subscribed topic. It does not check whether the user holds the PRODUCE permission on the topic named in deadLetterTopic. The dead letter messages are then written by the WebSocket service using its own broker client identity rather than the identity of the connecting user.

As a result, an authenticated user who holds the CONSUME permission on at least one topic can cause messages to be written to a topic of their choosing in any existing namespace, including namespaces belonging to other tenants, provided the role used by the WebSocket service to connect to the brokers is authorized to produce to that topic and the topic accepts a producer that registers no schema. The dead letter producer created by the WebSocket service registers no schema, so it is rejected when the target topic has a schema and schema validation is enforced for that topic or its namespace; this setting is not enabled by default. The same user is refused when attempting to produce to that topic directly. Where automatic topic creation is enabled, which is the default, the named topic is created if it does not already exist. The issue can only be triggered when the WebSocket service is enabled, either in the broker (webSocketServiceEnabled, which is disabled by default) or as a standalone WebSocket proxy.

The impact is unauthorized injection of messages into topics the user is not permitted to produce to. The user can determine the content of the injected messages when they also control the messages on the subscribed topic. The issue does not allow reading, modifying or deleting existing messages in the target topic. Injected messages carry the dead letter message properties and a dead letter producer name, so they can be distinguished from messages produced normally; however, the values of these properties are not authenticated and should not be relied upon to establish the origin of a message. Whether an injected message has further consequences depends on how the applications consuming the target topic process it. Repeated injection also consumes storage and backlog capacity in the target namespace.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.3.0 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately and do not require the WebSocket service should disable it. Where the WebSocket service is required, restricting network access to it and limiting the permissions granted to the role the WebSocket service uses to connect to the brokers to the namespaces WebSocket clients are intended to access reduces the exposure.

cna.title: Docling: Arbitrary file read/write (and command execution when shell-escape is enabled) when rendering untrusted TikZ with the opt-in Tectonic engine

descriptions.value: Docling simplifies document processing by parsing diverse formats and providing integrations with the generative AI ecosystem. From 2.94.0 until 2.132.0, callers that opt into LatexBackendOptions(tikz_engine="tectonic") invoke docling/backend/latex/engines/tectonic.py to compile an untrusted TikZ body and document preamble without restricting TeX file primitives including \openin and \openout. Crafted input can read files available to the converter and create or overwrite writable files, and enabling the tikz_engine_allow_shell_escape option additionally permits shell commands through TeX. The default configuration, which does not enable Tectonic rendering, is not affected. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.132.0.

cna.title: Twenty: Plaintext IMAP/SMTP/CalDAV password disclosure to any workspace member via /metadata GraphQL

descriptions.value: Twenty is an open-source CRM (customer relationship management) platform. From 1.20.10 until 2.7.0, the /metadata GraphQL connectedAccounts query returned connectionParameters from ConnectedAccountDTO for every connected account in a workspace, including plaintext IMAP, SMTP, and CalDAV passwords, because the field was not hidden and the lookup did not enforce the calling user's identity or account visibility. A normal workspace member could obtain other members' external-service credentials and use them to access mail or calendars and potentially reset third-party accounts. Google and Microsoft OAuth-only workspaces were not affected. This issue is fixed in version 2.7.0.

cna.title: Authorization bypass through a user-controlled key in the Amazon Q Business Lambda hook sample in QnABot on AWS

descriptions.value: CAPEC-1 Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs

Authorization bypass through a user-controlled key in the optional Amazon Q Business Lambda hook sample ( q-business-lambda-hook https://github.com/aws-solutions-library-samples/qnabot-on-aws/blob/main/source/docs/lambda_hooks/README.md ), available with QnABot on AWS versions 7.0.0 through 7.4.5, might allow an authenticated remote user to read arbitrary Amazon S3 objects in the deploying AWS account. This sample solution provides an example Lambda hook and requires separate, manual deployment and additional setup. It is not deployed automatically with QnABot. Customers who have not deployed this optional sample hook are not affected and do not need to take action. 



To remediate this issue, affected customers should update the QnABot on AWS stack to version 7.4.6 or later and then redeploy the Amazon Q Business Lambda hook sample stack. Updating the QnABot on AWS stack alone does not deliver the fix.

cna.title: Microsoft UFO: Authenticated task-result request can deadlock UFO server session manager

descriptions.value: Microsoft UFO is an open-source framework for intelligent automation across devices and platforms. Prior to 3.0.9, the /api/task_result/{task_name} endpoint calls SessionManager.get_result_by_task() in ufo/server/services/session_manager.py, which acquires a non-reentrant lock and then calls SessionManager.get_result() to acquire the same lock again when the task name maps to a session. An authenticated caller who knows or creates a mapped task name can therefore block the request indefinitely, and in the default single-process server configuration the blocked event-loop thread prevents other HTTP, WebSocket, and dependent background interactions. Unknown task names do not reach the nested call and are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 3.0.9.

cna.title: PostgreSQL Anonymizer: The secret salt and shift of anon are readable by any role in pg_roles or pg_db_role_setting

credits.value: The PostgreSQL Anonymizer project thanks user Ilya Staroverov for reporting this problem.

workarounds.value: Configure the salt in the postgresql.conf file (or one of it's includes).

descriptions.value: PostgreSQL restricts acces to the salt and shift via the `SHOW` command for users not member of `pg_read_all_settings`. But they are visible in `pg_db_role_setting` or `pg_roles` if they were set on the database, user or both. PostgreSQL Anonymizer's documentation recommends to use ALTER DATABASE / ALTER ROLE for the salt. The problem is resolved in PostgreSQL Anonymizer 3.3.0 and later versions.

cna.title: Microsoft UFO: Authenticated Galaxy device registration can bypass WebSocket SSRF IP pinning via redirects

descriptions.value: Microsoft UFO is an open-source framework for intelligent automation across devices and platforms. Prior to 3.0.9, authenticated device registration through /api/devices can supply a permitted attacker-controlled WebSocket endpoint while aip/transport/websocket.py applies pinned_addresses only to the initial destination. The pinned websockets.connect() client follows cross-origin redirects and opens a new TCP connection before Galaxy performs its post-handshake peer-IP validation, allowing WebSocket upgrade requests to internal hosts reachable from the server. The confirmed impact is the internal connection and handshake request, and does not establish arbitrary HTTP methods, response-body disclosure, a completed AIP session, or cloud metadata access. This issue is fixed in version 3.0.9.

cna.title: Microsoft UFO: Authenticated Android shell command injection in Mobile MCP type_text and launch_app

descriptions.value: Microsoft UFO is an open-source framework for intelligent automation across devices and platforms. Prior to 3.0.10, the type_text and launch_app tools in ufo/client/mcp/http_servers/mobile_mcp_server.py pass the authenticated caller-controlled text and package_name parameters into adb shell command argument positions without comprehensive validation. The adb client joins those arguments into a remote command string that the Android shell reparses, allowing shell metacharacters to execute additional commands on an authorized connected device as the Android shell user. Exploitation requires a valid Mobile MCP API key and a reachable device authorized for ADB, and it does not establish host operating-system execution, Android root execution, or access beyond the Android shell-user privileges. This issue is fixed in version 3.0.10.

cna.title: Penpot: Share-link page-scope escalation: a share-link holder reads pages outside the link's authorized scope via the get-page RPC command

descriptions.value: Penpot is an open-source design and prototyping platform. Prior to 2.18.0, the get-page RPC accepts a share-link permission object with blanket read access but does not verify that the caller-selected page-id belongs to the link's authorized pages set. An attacker with both a valid share link and the attacker's own authenticated Penpot session can retrieve the complete shape and design data of another page in the same file when its identifier is known, because get-page requires authentication. The related get-file-fragment RPC also permits share-link access without mapping fragments to authorized pages. This issue is fixed in version 2.18.0.

cna.title: Koha authenticated OS command injection in tools/scheduler.pl via the jobid parameter when deleting a scheduled task

descriptions.value: Koha is vulnerable to OS command injection in the Task Scheduler deletion path. The tools/scheduler.pl handler accepts the jobid request parameter for op=cud-delete and passes it to C4::Scheduler::remove_at_job without validating it. Schedule::At::remove substitutes the supplied job ID into an atrm command string without quoting or escaping it and executes the command through a single-argument system() call, which invokes the shell. An authenticated staff user with the tools => schedule_tasks permission can therefore execute arbitrary operating-system commands as the Koha web/application user by supplying shell metacharacters in jobid. The issue is fixed in Koha 24.11.20, 25.05.15, 25.11.09, and 26.05.04, and in the 26.11 development branch.

cna.title: apko /etc/passwd and /etc/group UID/GID truncation writes package-supplied entries as root

descriptions.value: CAPEC-128 Integer Attacks

solutions.value: Upgrade to apko 1.4.5 or later, which rejects UID and GID values outside 0 to 4294967295 instead of truncating them. Images built with earlier versions from untrusted packages should be rebuilt.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade to apko 1.4.5 or later, which rejects UID and GID values outside 0 to 4294967295 instead of truncating them. Images built with earlier versions from untrusted packages should be rebuilt.

descriptions.value: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built from apk packages. From version 0.2.0 to before version 1.4.5, UserEntry.Parse and GroupEntry.Parse in pkg/passwd read the UID and GID fields of /etc/passwd and /etc/group entries with strconv.Atoi and convert them to uint32 without a range check. On 64-bit platforms an out-of-range value such as 4294967296 (2^32) is truncated to 0, and negative values wrap. Because apko parses the passwd and group entries supplied by the packages it installs and writes them back into the image, an attacker who controls a package installed into the image can ship an entry that appears to declare an unprivileged UID or GID but is written into the built image as UID 0 or GID 0 (root). The truncated UID is also used when resolving the image's run-as user. This issue has been fixed in version 1.4.5.

The truncated UID is also used when resolving the image's run-as user. This issue has been fixed in version 1.4.5.

cna.title: LMCache Unauthenticated RCE in multiprocess mode via pickle deserialization

scenarios.value: Multiprocess mode bound to a routable address, the documented multi-node deployment

timeline.value: LMCache v0.3.9 ships the multiprocess ZMQ transport and the pickle-backed msgpack extension
PR #5644 merged: pickle removed from device IPC descriptors
LMCache v0.5.6 released, the first version that includes the fix

solutions.value: Upgrade to LMCache 0.5.6 or later. That release replaces pickle in device IPC descriptors with versioned, typed MessagePack descriptors. Descriptors are validated before use, the wrapper type is chosen from a fixed local allowlist, and there is no pickle fallback. The change covers the ZeroMQ and gRPC paths. The wire format changed, so upgrade workers and servers together. The fix is PR #5644 and it is in the v0.5.6 tag. PR #5684, which binds the example Kubernetes deployment to localhost, and PR #5685, which runs the official images as a non-root user, were merged after the v0.5.6 tag was cut and are included in v0.5.7rc2. The v0.5.6 example deployment still passes --host 0.0.0.0, and the v0.5.6 images still run as root.

references.name: msgpack extension code 1 decoded with pickle (v0.3.9)
PR #5644: replace pickle in device IPC descriptors
PR #5684: bind example Kubernetes deployment to localhost
PR #5685: run official images as a non-root user

descriptions.value: LMCache multiprocess mode, also called distributed mode, opens an unauthenticated ZeroMQ ROUTER so worker processes can register and share KV cache blocks. Messages on that socket are msgpack. Extension code 1 is passed to DeviceIPCWrapper.Deserialize, which calls pickle.loads, while the server is still decoding request arguments and before the handler runs. A single unauthenticated ZMQ DEALER message to the transport port (default 5555) therefore executes code as the user the LMCache process runs as. Official container images run that process as root. The transport binds to localhost unless the operator sets a routable address with --host, which is how multi-node deployments let peers connect. The decode path shipped in v0.3.9 and is present through v0.5.5, including the v0.5.6 release candidates. v0.5.6, published on 2026-10-14, removes pickle.loads from this path.

cna.title: Hex release-age cooldown is lifted package-wide when the locked release is retired

descriptions.value: The cooldown exists to keep a compromised release out of projects until it can be detected and retired. An attacker who controls a package owner account can defeat it by also retiring the currently locked release, so a malicious release reaches projects that rely on the local cooldown as soon as they run mix deps.update, including automated dependency update jobs. The malicious release's code then runs when the dependency is compiled.

solutions.value: Upgrade Hex to 2.5.2 or later, for example with mix local.hex. A retired locked release then no longer lifts the release-age cooldown for its package. A locked release with a security advisory still lifts it for its package and the direct dependencies of the locked release, only in the repository the package is locked from.

descriptions.value:
Protection Mechanism Failure vulnerability in hexpm hex allows the owner of a package, or an attacker who has taken over the owner's account, to get a newly published release past the release-age cooldown.

The cooldown (cooldown config, HEX_COOLDOWN) withholds versions younger than the configured age during dependency resolution. When the release of a package locked in mix.lock is retired or has a security advisory, Hex.RemoteConverger.build_cooldown_bypass/3 and Hex.RemoteConverger.unsafe_lock_bypass/1 lift the cooldown for every version of that package and of every package the locked release depends on, so that mix deps.update can move off the unsafe release. Retiring a release needs the same package owner permission as publishing one. An attacker who publishes a malicious release can retire the currently locked release, and the next mix deps.update that unlocks the package selects the new release regardless of its age. Hex.Registry.Cooldown.versions/2 checks the bypass by package name alone, so the bypass also covers packages with the same name in other repositories. Cooldown configured through an organization dependency policy is not affected.

This issue affects hex: from 2.5.0 before 2.5.2.
